title: Run templates
text:
The examples/ directory of the devstack repository exists to answer one question: what should my run file look like? A run file is the single script that builds a ProjectFlow, defines a task tree, and executes it — the file a collaborator opens first and the file you copy when you start a project.
The directory holds four kinds of material:

title: Run templates
text:
Where the files are
The templates are Python files in the devstack repository, not on this site. Browse or copy them here:

examples/run_templates/ — the copy-me set
examples/run_templates_annotated/ — the same code with the reasoning written out
examples/input_research_scripts/ — real run files and the raw scripts they replace

Clone the repo, or copy a single file straight out of GitHub.

title: Run templates
text:
Start here
The four numbered templates run with nothing downloaded — each generates its own synthetic arrays — so you can execute all of them before touching base data. (run_template_seals_example.py in the same directory is the exception: it drives a real model. See the note under the rung table.)
conda activate env1
cd earth_economy_devstack/examples/run_templates
python run_template_1_minimal.py
Then run it a second time. It finishes almost instantly: every task is behind an existence check, so ProjectFlow skips what it already computed. That skip-if- already-computed behavior, one output folder per task, and logging are the whole payoff of the ~25 lines in template 1.
Outputs do not land in the repo. Because the script lives inside a cloned repo, bare hb.ProjectFlow() places the project directory just outside it, at <repo_parent>/projects/<name derived from the filename> — the stem minus the run_ prefix, so run_template_1_minimal.py writes to Files/projects/template_1_minimal/. Look inside: input/, intermediate/, output/, and a folder per task.

title: Run templates
section: Three axes, and the one that is numbered
text:
Three axes, and the one that is numbered
A run file’s complexity is three independent questions, and a project sits somewhere on each:

Configuration — how a run varies. Levels 1–4, the four templates below.
Code layout — where the code lives: single file → split (<project>_tasks.py, _functions.py, _utils.py, _initialize_project.py) → library package.
Ownership — who owns the code you run: self-contained → devstack developer → downstream user, where the library is a read-only dependency in your own repo.

Only configuration is numbered, because only configuration is a ladder climbed in order. The axes are independent — global_invest’s service runners are configuration level 2 with a library-package layout. Every template’s docstring states its position on all three. The full model is in levels_of_complexity.qmd.

title: Run templates
text:
The four configuration levels
Templates 1–4 hold code layout and ownership fixed (single file, self-contained), so configuration is the only thing changing between them — that is what makes them readable as a diff. Read them in order. Each adds exactly one mechanism, and each docstring says when to move up — the point is to earn complexity rather than adopt it.



#
file
adds
promote when




1
run_template_1_minimal.py
one task function, p.add_task(), p.execute()
you add a second task


2
run_template_2_script_with_tree.py
build_task_tree(p); several tasks that chain by publishing paths; constants inline in __main__
you want a second variant of the run


3
run_template_3_canonical.py
run_project(p) + a scenarios CSV; variants are data, not forked code
a machine-specific value tries to enter the code


4
run_template_4_data_driven.py
a parameters CSV, nested tasks via parent=, a cross-scenario report task
you need parallel iterators or more CSV classes



Alongside the four rungs, run_templates/run_template_seals_example.py is the same anatomy applied to a real model: build_task_tree delegates unchanged to seals_initialize_project.build_standard_task_tree(p), and run_project sets the base data dir and the processing resolution and loads the scenarios CSV, which ships in seals’ tracked input_template/ and is read in place (runtime CSV generation was retired 2026-08; it returns typed as generate_scenarios_csv_from_model_spec). Copy this one to start a standalone SEALS project. It is the one template that moves along the other two axes while staying at configuration level 3: its code layout is a library package (nothing in the file defines a task) and its ownership is devstack developer (seals is imported, and you could edit it). Moving along code layout changed exactly one function — build_task_tree, which now delegates instead of containing. One practical difference from templates 3 and 4: it needs seals installed and will download base data on its first run, so it is not a five-second toy like the others. For ownership one step further — seals as a read-only dependency in your own repo — copy run_template_downstream_user.py instead.

title: Run templates
text:
The other two axes
Two further templates in run_templates/ hold configuration fixed at level 4 and move along one of the other axes each. Both compute exactly the same numbers as run_template_4_data_driven.py, which is the point — diff them against it and the only difference is the axis named.



file
axis it moves
what changes




run_template_split_layout.py
Code layout → split
tasks leave the run file for four siblings: caloric_yield_tasks.py, _functions.py, _utils.py, _initialize_project.py. Exactly one function in the run file changes — build_task_tree now delegates instead of containing.


run_template_downstream_user.py
Ownership → downstream user
imports caloric_yield_initialize_project as a read-only dependency, then adds its own task after the library builder returns. Note it is back to a single-file layout while being further along ownership — the axes really are independent.



The _utils / _functions split is the rule worth internalising: <project>_utils.py is science-unaware and therefore a promotion queue — when a second project needs one of those helpers, it belongs in hazelbean. <project>_functions.py encodes the model’s domain knowledge and is terminal. If nothing ever leaves your _utils, you are not applying the rule.
run_template_downstream_user.py also states the one thing the ownership axis has not solved: attaching a task to a specific library task (parent=p.yield_analysis_task) works only because builders assign p.<name>_task as a side effect, and no contract says which of those names are public API. Until one exists, attach at the top level and depend on published paths rather than on task objects.
Rung 3 is the canonical anatomy, and all four of its parts are required at that level:

build_task_tree(p) — what the pipeline is. Nothing but add_task calls.
run_project(p) — how it is executed. Returns p.
the __main__ guard — importing a run file must never start a run. It is also where this project’s own configuration lives.
a scenarios CSV — the rows of work.


The rule that runs through rungs 3 and 4

run_project(p) sets what no variant ever changes. The caller sets what a variant might.

The caller builds the ProjectFlow and hangs configuration on it; run_project only runs it. When a constant starts varying, it moves one line up — out of run_project, into the caller. There is no signature to edit, no keyword to add, and no default that can drift out of sync. One deliberate exception (2026-08 amendment): the full definitions-filename block (parameters, scenarios, outputs, figures, sections, descriptions) is set by the caller even though most members never vary — it is the project’s interface manifest, and variants copy the block and override only the member that differs. Template 4 shows it working: the block sits in __main__, and run_project only loads it via hb.initialize_parameters / hb.initialize_scenarios. The split, downstream and seals templates additionally end their init with the model’s initialize_project(p) — the model-initializer anatomy.
The cost, stated honestly: bare run_project() no longer works — the caller must hand it a ProjectFlow, and a variant wrapper is four lines instead of three. In exchange every knob a run uses is visible at the call site, and forgetting one raises a named AttributeError instead of silently using somebody else’s default.


A variant run is its own file, never a fork
This is the habit the ladder exists to build. run_templates_annotated/run_template_3_canonical_test.py is the whole answer to the “copy the run file and change one line” instinct:
import hazelbean as hb
from run_template_3_canonical import run_project

if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = hb.ProjectFlow(project_name='..._test', run_mode='check')
    p.scenario_definitions_filename = 'template_3_scenarios_test.csv'
    # p.tasks_to_skip = ['yield_summations']
    run_project(p)
It imports the pipeline unchanged. What differs is data (a one-row CSV) and placement (its own project dir) — never code. Both sets carry this file, because a wrapper is something you copy: run_templates/run_template_3_canonical_test.py is the one to start from.


run_mode
Templates 3 and 4 pass run_mode to the constructor:

'check' — reuse the stable project dir; recompute only what is missing. The default working mode.
'fresh_intermediate' — redo all computation but keep input/. Test projects only.
'full' — a fresh, timestamped project dir; everything re-runs.



input_template/ and the machine-specific values
Both template sets keep their CSVs in a tracked input_template/ directory next to the run file. get_path reads them in place, after checking the project’s untracked input/, and nothing is copied into input/ automatically. That is why template_4_parameters.csv ships with data_credentials_path blank: to fill it, copy that one CSV into your machine’s input/ and edit the copy, which shadows the template and never reaches the code or git. If a template later changes underneath your copy, the run warns and names both files.







CSV
what it is




template_3_scenarios.csv
four scenario rows (scenario_label, yield_offset, year)


template_3_scenarios_test.csv
the same schema, one row — the variant run


template_4_scenarios.csv
scenarios for template 4


template_4_parameters.csv
key,value constants: ndv, n_rows, n_cols, and blank data_credentials_path



The three-column scenarios CSV in these templates is illustrative only. The real schema is specified in proposed_changes.qmd; worked instances of it are in scenario_definitions_examples/.

title: Run templates
text:
The two template sets
run_templates/ and run_templates_annotated/ are the same four rungs computing the same toy project (sum caloric yield across scenarios). They differ only in how much they say:

run_templates/ — concise. Comments only where a line is non-obvious. This is the set to copy into a new project.
run_templates_annotated/ — the same code with long docstrings covering what each level is for, what it deliberately does not have, why the conventions are what they are, and when to move along an axis. Read these once; copy from the other directory.

run_templates/ additionally holds run_template_split_layout.py and run_template_downstream_user.py (the other two axes) with their caloric_yield_* modules; the annotated set covers the configuration axis only. The input_template/ CSVs are otherwise identical between the sets.
Templates 1 and 2 use bare hb.ProjectFlow() in both sets, so they share a project directory across the sets — harmless, since they compute the same thing. Templates 3 and 4 carry distinct project names and get their own directories.

title: Run templates
text:
input_research_scripts/
Real scripts collected as source material: the input to conversion work, and the reference implementations that conversion produces. Read these; copy from run_templates/. Three groups:
Reference implementations — the conventions at full scale:

run_invest_carbon_in_projectflow.py — the run_project(p) convention on the global_invest InVEST carbon task tree. The variant knob is p.aoi (an ISO3 code or 'global'); paths resolve through p.get_path(), which searches the project input dir, then base data, then the cloud.
ngfs_pnas.py — the largest reference implementation of the canonical anatomy: a two-pass GTAP+SEALS pipeline whose build_task_tree is driven by a shock_config column in the scenarios CSV. It shows the anatomy holding at a scale where the task tree runs to hundreds of lines: run_project(p) is still nothing but constants, and every knob a run varies is still visible in the __main__ guard.
ngfs_pnas_test.py — its pared test run: same task tree, a minimal scenarios CSV, one policy scenario, one year, one region. The variant-is-a-file habit at full scale.
seals_standard.py — a standard SEALS run, identical to run_templates/run_template_seals_example.py.

Converted, but not exemplary — useful for what they get wrong:

yanxu_carbon.py, cc_carbon.py — GEP carbon runs on ProjectFlow, with hardcoded absolute base_data_dir paths pointing at somebody else’s machine. cc_carbon.py also has no __main__ guard, so importing it starts a run.

Not on ProjectFlow at all — the before-pictures:

research_script.py — a working pollination analysis with hardcoded D:\Shared drives\... paths throughout. The canonical example of a script that cannot run on any other machine.
research_script_relative_paths.py — the same script after one improvement: paths built from a single base_data_dir. Still not a ProjectFlow run file; a useful intermediate step.
invest_carbon_script.py — an InVEST-generated standalone script, the form the InVEST UI exports. Compare with run_invest_carbon_in_projectflow.py to see what wrapping it in a task tree buys.

title: Run templates
text:
Data examples
scenario_definitions_examples/ holds instances of the v2 scenario definitions schema specified in proposed_changes.qmd:

single_stage_seals.csv — a SEALS-only project, including a hindcast year.
multi_stage_ngfs.csv — GTAP + SEALS: a 2020-anchored canonical clock with a gtap stage clock.
hindcast_example.csv — a minimal demonstration of backward years.

title: Run templates
text:
Where to go next

title: GTAPPy release notes
text:
NoteHistorical record, not a guide



These are dated notes from the 2022–2023 build-out of GTAPPy, kept because they record why several conventions are the way they are and what was still open at the time. The code shown has since moved to the run_project(p) run-file convention described in Conventions, so do not copy from it. For current usage start at GTAPPy.




The open question this entry records: how to get from an Erwin-style mapping workbook to the EE spec correspondence format.
This is what a region correspondence looks like as it arrives:



GTAP-ctry2reg as downloaded, before conversion


Two problems with it as a machine-readable input. First, the file has to be renamed to say what it actually maps — gtapv7_r251_r160_correspondence.xlsx (and it has to stay .xlsx rather than CSV, because the mapping spans multiple worksheets). Second, No. is used twice in the same sheet, once numbering the r160 regions and once the r251 ones. Any parser reading it positionally gets this wrong, so the input format needs to disambiguate the two.
Legend information is also carried inside the region correspondence sheet, which is the wrong home for it — it needs a deliberate place of its own rather than being attached to whichever correspondence happened to need it.
The same pattern applies to sectors, which is the converted, EE-spec shape:



The converted correspondence: regions, sectors, activities and commodities as parallel blocks


A terminology note worth preserving: “sector” is used here specifically for the case where you are not distinguishing COMM (commodities) from ACTS (activities) — at the time these notes were written the distinction had not been pinned down.



Proposals raised against the model release layout, and how they resolved.
Naming.

In the release’s Data folder, the aggregation label gtapaez11-50 should be v11-s26-r50 — database version, sector count, region count.
The most recent release carries no timestamp; dated versions of a same-named model or aggregation take the timestamp of when they were first released.
CMF files renamed from cwon_bau.cmf to gtapv7-aez-rd_bau.cmf, and cwon_bau-es.cmf to gtapv7-aez-rd_bau-es.cmf — hyphens join parts of one variable, underscores split the name into its list of fields.
SIMRUN becomes just the experiment name (bau) rather than project name plus experiment.

Project structure.

Drop set PROJ=cwon from the CMF — the project is defined by the ProjectFlow object, not the command file.
Separate data and output from the code release:
set MODd=..\mod      set CMFd=.\cmf
set SOLd=..\out      set DATd=..\data%AGG%
SOLd and DATd deliberately live outside the release.
The goal is that a release can be run either by calling the batch file or by calling the Python run script, so the two are kept as close as possible. The asymmetry is intentional and one-directional: the batch file can only reproduce a resource-depletion run without ecosystem services, so the Python script can wrap the batch file but not the reverse.
CMF command-line options renamed to match what they are: gtap_base_data_dir, starting_data_file_path, output_dir, starting_year, ending_year (previously positional p1–p5). experiment_label may not be renameable, as it appears to be fixed by the CMF filename.

Answers from Erwin.

Can the raw GEMPACK output be read to estimate progress, for a progress bar? Yes, when running with automatic accuracy — GEMPACK reports its position:
+++> Beginning subinterval number 4.
---> Beginning pass number 1 of 2-pass calculation, subinterval 4.
Beginning pass number 6 of 6-pass calculation, subinterval 6
Could years drop the Y prefix (Y2018), which breaks string→int conversion? No — keep the Y. GEMPACK variable names cannot begin with a non-numeric… that is, cannot begin with a numeral.
There is no bau-SUM_Y2050, though there is for VOL and WEL — is that intentional? No: SUM describes the starting database, so a terminal-year SUM is meaningless. Relatedly, welfare cannot be produced in a resource-depletion run because there is no discount rate.
Is everything stored in the .sl4, making the other files redundant? No. Conversions such as results in volume terms are not in the .sl4 and have to come from sltoht or ViewSOL.




Shocks implemented at this point: population file replacement, GDP change, and (tentatively) yield changes.
The run file of the era created the ProjectFlow object at the top and added tasks to it — the ancestor of today’s task tree:



The 2022-era run file: ProjectFlow object, aggregation and experiment labels, tasks added explicitly


Note the shape already visible here: a list of aggregation labels ('10x10', '65x141') and a list of experiment labels ('agpr20b', 'beef50', 'rtms5'), iterated over as a cross product. That is the multi-aggregation philosophy described on the GTAPPy home page, present from the start.
And the task that generated a CMF and called the executable:



run_gtap_v7_executable: per-aggregation, per-experiment CMF generation and invocation


The interesting part is the if not hb.path_exists(expected_sl4_path) guard — skip-if-already-computed, done by hand before it was pushed down into ProjectFlow — and the per-aggregation override of xSets, xSubsets and Shock, since the 10×10 aggregation needs different set members than the 141×65 default.
What was hard. The open problem at this date was making shocks work generally: producing xSets, xSubsets and Shock statements per scenario, with READFROMFILE in the TABLO CMF as the mechanism for file-driven values. The taxonomy that came out of it is on Running GTAP by hand.
A distinction from this entry worth restating, because it caused confusion: there are shocks and there are data updates, and replacing an elasticity file is the latter. If you swap in basedata2 with a matching default2.prm and apply no shock, the model reproduces that database — the elasticities are, in that sense, calibrated to it. A supply-response elasticity behaves differently and will move the results.
Population shocks needed one more preprocessing step: the value has to be a percentage change over the default POP in the base data, so an external population file is read in and processed against the base rather than used directly.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text: Local climate regulation is urban cooling. Vegetation lowers city temperatures, buildings spend less electricity on air conditioning, and the account values that saved electricity. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is avoided energy cost.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Quantity
InVEST urban cooling gives each city-month a vegetation cooling effect, which the calculation converts into an electricity difference in kilowatt-hours, the kwh_diff column of the committed city-month files.
The cooling-degree measure behind that conversion is temp_degc_to_cdd_smooth, v04’s smoothed exceedance. Below the base minus the window it returns zero, above the base plus the window it is linear in temperature, and across the window it follows smoothstep01, the cubic \(t^2(3-2t)\) on [0, 1].

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Price
The national electricity price in USD per kilowatt-hour, the price_usd_per_kwh column.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Valuation
\[
\text{total\_savings\_usd} = \text{kwh\_diff} \times \text{price\_usd\_per\_kwh}
\]
city_savings_identity recomputes that product at rtol 1e-6 and raises if it breaks. Summing cities to countries gives the December 2025 version of the accounting table.
The current final applies v04’s correction, written explicitly in that version’s code and ported verbatim in apply_country_marginal_consumption. It divides out the old global marginal-consumption slope embedded in the v02 values and multiplies by each country’s own consumption per cooling-degree-day, which is cooling energy per capita over the IEA-CMCC 2019 humid-CDD total.
\[
\text{corrected} = \frac{\text{value}}{\text{URBAN\_COOLING\_OLD\_GLOBAL\_MC}} \times \text{consumption per CDD}
\]

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
What the library reports
gep_calculation reads the committed final table, parses its dollar-formatted string column through parse_dollar_column, and joins it onto the r250 country list by label.
Three things verify against staged data. The kilowatt-hour times price identity is exact. The merged-sum identity against the December 2025 version is exact on every country tested. The current final’s parse and totals check out.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the local_climate_regulation service:

local_climate_regulation_final_path, the committed final accounting table.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, and local_climate_regulation_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Method constants

URBAN_COOLING_OLD_GLOBAL_MC = 1.71737465916468, the old global marginal-consumption slope that v04 divides out.
URBAN_COOLING_CDD_BASE_C = 18.0, the humid cooling-degree-day base the calculation uses (CDDhum18).
URBAN_COOLING_SMOOTH_WINDOW_C = 1.0, the width of the smoothing window either side of the base.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
Taken as given
The InVEST urban cooling run itself and the national electricity prices.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Local Climate Regulation
text:
What is open
The v04 correction’s own inputs are not reproducible here. The IEA-CMCC cooling-degree-day file and the v2_nkd energy workbook live only on the author’s machine, and the staged VERSION4 energy CSV is a different vintage that does not validate the inversion. Those two files are the named asks.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text: Value the carbon held in the world’s three mapped coastal blue-carbon habitats (mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass) as part of Gross Ecosystem Product. The quantity is mapped habitat area multiplied by a per-habitat carbon density; the price is the same annual rental social cost of carbon that terrestrial carbon storage is valued at (Parisa et al. 2022). The service values storage only. The figure it reports is the carbon standing in the base year, not a flow between years.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text: Value the carbon held in the world’s three mapped coastal blue-carbon habitats (mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass) as part of Gross Ecosystem Product. The quantity is mapped habitat area multiplied by a per-habitat carbon density; the price is the same annual rental social cost of carbon that terrestrial carbon storage is valued at (Parisa et al. 2022). The service values storage only. The figure it reports is the carbon standing in the base year, not a flow between years.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text:
Method

Extent
Each habitat comes from its own published extent map, read as polygons:







Habitat
Extent




Mangrove
Global Mangrove Watch v3, 2019 (Bunting et al. 2018, 2022)


Salt marsh
GLC_FCS30D 2019, a 30 m land-cover product; the marsh class extracted to global_salt_marsh2019.gpkg (Zhang et al. 2024)


Seagrass
UNEP-WCMC013-014 SeagrassPtPy v7.1 (UNEP-WCMC and Short 2021)



Seagrass is optional at the tree level (include_seagrass). A tree built with seagrass but no extent file raises rather than running, so a data gap cannot quietly understate the coastal total; a tree built without seagrass writes every seagrass column at zero, so the combined table has the same shape either way.


Aggregation surface
Coastal habitat is aggregated on the marine surface, eemarine_r566 (one row per exclusive economic zone and coastal region) rather than on the land country surface the other services use. Each habitat layer is clipped to every marine region in turn, and the clipped pieces are measured in the equal-area projection EPSG:6933 (NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 Global), which is what turns polygon geometry into hectares.
Salt marsh additionally runs a zonal pass over the hectares-per-cell pyramid, written out as salt_marsh_with_area.gpkg for inspection. The area that reaches the country table is the equal-area geometric area, the same measure the other two habitats use.


Carbon density
Density is resolved per pixel for mangrove and salt marsh, and per polygon for seagrass. Every pool is reported in Mg C per hectare, and soil carbon throughout is the stock in the top 20 cm. The external soil products report the top 1 m, and are taken as a linear share of that profile.
Mangrove. Above-ground biomass follows the Hamilton & Friess latitude regression (Hamilton and Friess 2018), AGB (t/ha) = −6.4305 × |lat| + 271.747, floored at zero (the line crosses zero at roughly 42°, and the floor is what stops it going negative beyond that). Below-ground biomass is AGB times the IPCC zone-specific root-to-shoot ratio (IPCC 2014): 0.49 in the wet tropics, 0.29 in the dry tropics, 0.96 subtropical, with the tropical boundary at |lat| = 23.5° and the wet/dry split at 2000 mm mean annual precipitation. Biomass converts to carbon at 0.48 for AGB (Hamilton and Friess 2018) and 0.39 for BGB (Howard et al. 2014). Soil carbon is read from the Sanderman 30 m mangrove soil map (Sanderman et al. 2018). Where no precipitation raster is supplied the whole tropics take the wet ratio; where no soil raster is supplied, soil falls back to a latitude step function running from 80 Mg C/ha at the equator down to 50 Mg C/ha poleward of 25°.
Salt marsh. Above-ground biomass is the Chmura median of 5 t/ha (Chmura et al. 2003), raised by a factor of 1.2 below |lat| = 25° for tropical productivity. Below-ground biomass is 2.5 times AGB, for the extensive root systems of tidal marsh. Carbon fractions are 0.45 for AGB and 0.41 for BGB. Soil carbon is read from the Maxwell MarSOC map of tidal marsh soils (Maxwell et al. 2024); the fallback step function runs the other way from mangrove, 36 Mg C/ha in the tropics up to 70 Mg C/ha poleward of 45°.
Seagrass. Biomass carbon is genus-specific, from the Gomis global synthesis (Gomis et al. 2025), and is the one density that is an attribute of the polygon rather than of the pixel, the extent map carries a GENUS field. Genera group by life-history strategy: persistent (Posidonia at 9.78 Mg C/ha, the other persistent genera at 3.70), opportunistic (Zostera, Syringodium, Halodule at 0.94) and colonising (Ruppia 0.33, Halophila 0.19). A polygon whose genus is unknown, unreported or absent from the table takes the global mean, 1.55 Mg C/ha. Biomass splits 30% above ground and 70% below. Soil carbon is a constant 22 Mg C/ha, the Fourqurean global mean for the top 20 cm (Fourqurean et al. 2012). Freshwater genera present in the extent map (Trapa, Myriophyllum, Valisneria, Najas and the rest) are zeroed across every pool, soil included, so they contribute nothing to a country’s stock.


Stock
For mangrove and salt marsh, stock is accumulated pixel by pixel on the 10 arc-second grid. Each pixel’s density is evaluated at its latitude, multiplied by the hectares in that cell, and added to the marine region it falls in. A pixel counts only where the habitat mask is set, a region id is present and the cell has area. A no-data pixel inside a soil raster contributes zero soil rather than a missing value, and its biomass still counts. The pass runs in row blocks and skips any block the habitat does not reach.
For seagrass, stock is each clipped polygon’s genus density multiplied by its hectares, summed to the region.
Every habitat therefore reports four columns per region: above-ground, below-ground and soil carbon, and their sum. The total is always the three pools added, never a separately computed figure, so it cannot drift away from the parts it is printed beside.


Price and valuation
The price is the annual rental social cost of carbon for the base year, read from the carbon price series (carbon_prices.xlsx) under the run’s price convention, the same series and convention terrestrial carbon uses, so the two carbon services are priced identically. GEP is then
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{coastal carbon}} = \text{carbon stock (Mg C)} \times \text{rental SCC (\$ per Mg C)}
\]
applied pool by pool, so the written table carries a value for above-ground, below-ground and soil carbon as well as the habitat total. The year and the price used travel in the table beside the values.


Collapse to one row per country
The service produces two tables. The first, gep_by_country_base_year_r566, is the full marine surface: per-habitat area, stock pools and storage values for each of the r566 marine regions, with a matching GeoPackage for mapping. Regions with no coastal habitat at all are dropped from it, they are ocean rows, not zero-value countries.
The second, gep_by_country_base_year, is the country table. Building it takes two steps that each guard against counting the same coast twice:

Keep the _EEZ rows. The marine surface carries a country’s coast more than once, as an EEZ row plus land and territorial rows over the same habitat. Only the _EEZ rows are valued.
Collapse through the canonical r264 row. The r264 correspondence splits large countries into sub-regions (China ×6, India ×6, and four two-way splits), so it is filtered to ee_r264_label == iso3_r250_label before the join. Without that filter the join repeats a split country once per sub-region and the sum multiplies its value. Countries with no coastal habitat report zero rather than dropping out.

title: Coastal blue carbon
section: Open question: EEZ-only versus all rows
text:
Open question: EEZ-only versus all rows
Step 1 above is a choice, not a cleanup. Valuing every r566 row instead of the _EEZ rows returns a strictly larger total, and the gap is exactly the non-EEZ rows, the same coastal habitat counted again under a land or territorial label. The two totals answer different questions. What the module writes is the EEZ-only figure; the all-rows figure is what summing the r566 table gives, and the module does not compute it. The arithmetic of the distinction is pinned in test_eez_only_is_a_strict_subset_of_all_rows.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text:
Sensitivity worth naming
The latitude fallbacks, mangrove soil without the Sanderman raster, salt marsh soil without MarSOC, and the mangrove root ratio without a precipitation raster, change the number a run produces. Which source each run used is written to the log at the point the raster is aligned.

title: Coastal blue carbon
text:
Outputs
Per habitat, in the habitat’s own task directory:

<habitat>_area_by_countries2019.{gpkg,csv} (hectares per marine region.
<habitat>_carbon_stock_by_countries2019.csv) the four stock pools per marine region (Mg C).
<habitat>_storage_value_by_countries2019.csv, the stock pools priced (USD), with the year and the rental SCC used.

Then, across habitats:

combined_ecosystem_areas.csv, every habitat’s area and stock on one row per marine region, plus total coastal area and total carbon stock.
gep_by_country_base_year_r566.{csv,gpkg} (the marine-surface GEP detail.
gep_by_country_base_year.csv) one row per country, the service’s GEP result.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text: This section outlines how we value carbon sequestration as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. The analysis focuses specifically on carbon sequestration provided by terrestrial ecosystems, which is appraised in terms of its contribution to climate change mitigation. By quantifying the carbon sequestration capacity of these ecosystems, we aim to capture their role in reducing atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, thereby contributing to global climate regulation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text:
Estimating Quantity
We followed the methodology outlined in Johnson et al. (2023) to quantify global carbon sequestration. To estimate the quantity of carbon sequestered, we implemented a two-stage modeling framework, as illustrated in panels (a) and (b) of Figure 1.
First, we utilized an advanced global carbon density map developed by Spawn et al. (2020) to update the carbon pool. This dataset consists of harmonized vegetation-specific maps that integrate both aboveground and belowground biomass into a single, comprehensive spatial representation for the year 2010, thereby enabling more accurate assessments of carbon stocks across diverse ecosystems. To construct the carbon pool table or carbon density lookup table, we combined the 300 m land use and land cover (LULC) data from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative Land Cover (ESA CCI LC) with the carbon zone map employed by Ruesch and Gibbs (2008). This integrated methodology enhances both the spatial resolution and contextual relevance of carbon stock estimations.
Second, we applied the updated carbon density lookup table and the carbon zone map to a time series of LULC data, also derived from ESA CCI LC, to enable dynamic assessments of carbon storage over time.






Figure 1: Workflow for quantifying and valuing global carbon storage. (a) The Data Preparation phase integrates the carbon zone map employed by Ruesch and Gibbs (2008), base-year ESA LULC data, and carbon density data from Spawn et al. (2020) to generate a carbon density lookup table. (b) The Application phase applies the lookup table to the base-year LULC and carbon zone maps to obtain per-cell carbon density, then multiplies by cell area to obtain per-cell carbon stocks. The same calculation applies to any LULC time series for dynamic assessment. (c) The Valuation phase sums carbon stocks per country and multiplies by the annual rental social cost of carbon to yield GEP by country.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text:
Estimating Price
To estimate the value of carbon sequestration, we employed the rental social cost of carbon (SCC) (Parisa et al. 2022) as the pricing metric. Parisa et al. (2022) provides the theoretical rationale for quantifying the value of short-term carbon storage, which corresponds to carbon sequestration. Following this approach, and within the framework of Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP), we estimate the annual value of carbon sequestration as follows:
\[
\text{Carbon Rental Rate} = P_C(t) - P_C(t+1)e^{-r} = P_C(t)\left(1 - e^{-r} \right)
\]
where \(P_C(t)\) denotes the social cost of carbon in year \(t\), and \(r\) represents the net discount rate equal to the difference between the discount rate and the rate of growth of carbon prices. This formulation reflects the rental valuation approach, capturing the annualized benefit of temporarily storing one metric ton of CO2 for one year. This measure represents the annualized marginal damage cost of emitting an additional metric ton of CO2, thereby aligning our valuation approach with established climate policy frameworks and principles of intertemporal cost-benefit analysis. We adopt a carbon price of $678.33 per metric ton of carbon (C), corresponding to the mean social cost of CO2 of roughly $185 per metric ton of CO2 estimated by Rennert et al. (2022) (converted to a per-carbon basis by the 44/12 mass ratio). This value is employed for \(P_C(t)\), the carbon price at time \(t\), and a discount rate of 2% is applied, following the same source. The rental rate the model applies is read year by year from the carbon-price series (rental scc r2% in carbon_prices.xlsx); for the base year 2019 it is approximately $13.19 per ton of C. A flat 2% rate applied directly to $678.33 would give $13.43; the difference reflects the net discount rate \(r\) defined above, which nets out the growth in carbon prices.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Terrestrial Carbon Storage
text:
Valuation
After estimating both the quantity and price of carbon sequestration, the economic value of carbon sequestration, is calculated as:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{carbon storage and sequestration}} = Q \cdot P \cdot \lambda = \text{Carbon Storage} \times \text{Rental SCC} \times 1
\]
where \(Q\) represents the quantity of carbon storage (in metric tons), and \(P\) denotes the annual rental SCC per ton. This formulation aligns with the GEP framework, translating biophysical carbon sequestration into monetary value.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text: Extractive energy provision covers natural gas, coal and petroleum. The account values it as the resource rent each country earns from extraction, read from the World Bank’s Changing Wealth of Nations 2024 package at the GEP base year of 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Quantity and price
There is no separate quantity step and no separate price step. CWoN reports the rent itself, in current USD per country per year, so the module reads that number and carries it through. The price convention recorded for this service in es_config.csv is resource rent.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Valuation
fuel_rent_by_country_from_cwon takes one CWoN table and returns one row per country holding the YR<year> column at the requested year. The CWoN tables are wide, keyed on countrycode with World Bank codes that match iso3_r250_label directly, Kosovo included as XKX.
extractive_energy_gep_from_cwon runs that read once per fuel and sums the three components with min_count=1. A country absent from one fuel’s table stays NaN in that component and still receives a service total from the components that do exist, so a country with only coal is a coal country rather than a missing one. Components sum by the same commodity convention that extractive materials provision uses.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, all scoped to the extractive_energy service:

extractive_energy_cwon_gas_path, extractive_energy_cwon_coal_path and extractive_energy_cwon_oil_path, the Stata rent tables the valuation computes from. Each carries a _source_url row pointing at the World Bank reproducibility archive and a _source_archive_member row naming the file inside it, under Reproducibility package/Output/Latest/.
extractive_energy_gas_path, extractive_energy_coal_path and extractive_energy_oil_path, the three committed per-country CSVs from the consortium drive, kept as the replication anchor.

The shared country references come from initialize_country_paths, which publishes the r264 correspondence and loads p.df_countries.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory. The columns are the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, the three per-fuel columns extractive_energy_gas_gep, extractive_energy_coal_gep and extractive_energy_oil_gep, and their sum extractive_energy_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Method constants
EXTRACTIVE_ENERGY_FUELS = ('gas', 'coal', 'oil') names the three components and fixes the order the summation reads them in.
COMMITTED_DUPLICATE_VALUE_ROWS records eight rows of the committed drive CSVs that carry another country’s full rent value. Bouvet Island and Svalbard take Norway’s, Christmas Island and the Cocos Islands take Australia’s, Tokelau takes New Zealand’s, Western Sahara takes Morocco’s, Palestine takes Israel’s, and Kosovo takes Serbia’s. In the Kosovo row the committed name column itself reads “Serbia”. The values were verified equal in every fuel where the row is non-empty.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
Taken as given
The CWoN rent estimation is upstream science and is used as published.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Energy Provision
text:
What is open
The eight duplicate rows are a name-join artefact that counts the source countries twice, and for Kosovo it overrides the CWoN table’s own coal value. CWoN carries no rows at all for the first six. The module therefore computes from the CWoN tables, one country one row, rather than adopting the committed CSVs. gep_calculation logs the computed total beside the committed total so the gap stays visible on every run.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Groundwater Recharge
text:
Groundwater recharge is valued as the pumping energy it saves. Recharge keeps the water table higher, so every cubic metre withdrawn is lifted a shorter distance; the service value is that avoided lift, priced at the country’s electricity tariff. The base year is 2019.
⚠ The construction values ONE year’s recharge as a one-year head increment on that year’s withdrawals, which is why the totals are millions where neighbouring services are billions: the marginal metre of lift costs a fraction of a cent per cubic metre. The magnitude is the method’s own, not an error.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Groundwater Recharge
text:
Quantity
Two quantities. The country’s mean local recharge depth (l_mean_mm), the seasonal water yield model’s output read from the staged country table – the model itself runs elsewhere, per watershed, and is taken as given. And the country’s fresh groundwater withdrawal, FAO AQUASTAT, in billions of cubic metres at the year set by groundwater_recharge_withdrawal_year.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Groundwater Recharge
text:
Price
The country’s average electricity price per kilowatt hour, from the staged 2021 global pricing table, deflated from 2021 to the 2019 base year by the shared US CPI factor (the tariffs are USD, so one scalar carries every country). Lifting one cubic metre by one metre takes gamma / (eta x 3.6e6) kilowatt hours, with gamma the specific weight of water (9810 newtons per cubic metre) and eta the pump efficiency (groundwater_recharge_pump_efficiency, 0.5).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Groundwater Recharge
text:
Valuation
groundwater_gep is the whole product:
\[
\text{GEP}_i = \frac{\gamma \, e_i}{\eta \times 3.6 \times 10^6} \; \bar{L}_i \; Q_i
\]
where \(e_i\) is the electricity tariff, \(\bar{L}_i\) the mean recharge depth in metres and \(Q_i\) the withdrawal volume in cubic metres. A country missing any input carries NA with the absence named in a note column, never a silent zero. The committed ground_water_gep.csv is carried beside the result as the replication anchor, and the run log reports the per-country agreement.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Groundwater Recharge
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the groundwater_recharge service key: the recharge table, the AQUASTAT withdrawal extract, the electricity price table, the pump efficiency and the committed reference, each with a source row beside it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text: Water supply is built one component at a time. Hydropower direct use is complete and is what water_supply_gep currently carries. A water-use calculation covering agriculture, industry and municipal withdrawals is ported and reported beside it as separate columns. The price convention recorded in es_config.csv is resource rent (CWoN 2024), and the base year is 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Hydropower

Quantity and price
The hydropower valuation has no separate quantity and price step. CWoN 2024 publishes a capitalised hydropower wealth per country, and the annual rent that wealth implies is what the account wants.


Valuation
annuity_factor is the present value of one dollar a year over the CWoN horizon,
\[
A = \sum_{t=1}^{100} \frac{1}{(1+r)^t}, \qquad r = 0.04
\]
and hydropower_rent_from_wealth divides each country’s YR2019 wealth by it. Countries without wealth stay NaN, because no data is not zero rent.
The method was identified by reverse-engineering against the drive’s committed 2019 output, whose script is not on the drive. It is exact across all 94 valued countries, with the ratio constant to 1e-10. The test suite asserts the annuity identity and the exact replication. An earlier direct-use script on the drive, price times quantity from EIA and World Bank series dated November 2024, is superseded by this method and is not ported.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Water use

Quantity and price
Withdrawal volumes in cubic metres per sector come from the withdrawal table. The price is the AQUASTAT SDG 6.4.1 water-use efficiency series in US dollars per cubic metre, one series per sector.


Valuation
clean_aquastat_water_efficiency is script 01 of the drive’s R calculation. It keeps the US$/m3 rows of the four SDG 6.4.1 series and pivots them wide by country and year.
water_use_gep_by_country_year is script 02. It applies three country renames onto the withdrawal table’s spellings, fills iso codes for the names its country map does not carry, drops the regional aggregate rows, merges the two tables, restricts to the survey years, and multiplies efficiency by withdrawal per sector to give gep_water_agricultural, gep_water_industrial and gep_water_municipal.
water_use_components_from_chain takes the latest survey year per country and keys it to r250 by exact country-name match, first on iso3_r250_name and then on name_long. A calculation country with no match keeps an empty iso3, so a name drift is visible instead of dropped.
Both of the R calculation’s own outputs replicate. The cleaned efficiency table matches bit-exactly. The country-year GEP table matches to the anchor CSV’s own 15-significant-digit rounding, maximum relative difference 3e-15.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the water_supply service:

water_supply_cwon_hydro_wealth_path, the CWoN hydro_wealth_cd table, with a _source_url row for the World Bank reproducibility archive and a _source_archive_member row naming the file inside it.
water_use_efficiency_input_path, the raw AQUASTAT export, with a _source_url row for the AQUASTAT data API.
water_use_withdrawal_path, the withdrawal table.
water_use_agriculture_path and water_use_all_sector_path, the drive’s committed per-country tables, held as comparison anchors.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Outputs

hydropower_rent.csv from the hydropower_rent task.
aquastat_water_efficiency_cleaned.csv, water_use_gep_by_country_year.csv and water_use_components.csv from the water_use_components task.
gep_by_country_base_year.csv from gep_calculation, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, hydropower_gep, water_use_agriculture_gep, water_use_all_sector_gep and water_supply_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Method constants

water_supply_hydropower_capitalization_rate = 0.04 in es_parameters, the rate CWoN capitalized their wealth figure with.
⚠ This is not the account’s discount rate and must not be harmonized onto it. The account discounts future benefits at 2 percent, with sensitivity at 1 and 3. This rate is doing the opposite job: CWoN published a capitalized wealth figure, and hydropower GEP is the annual rent inside it, so the module runs their capitalization backwards. Inverting with any rate but the one they capitalized with returns a rent CWoN never capitalized — the number would become wrong in the act of making it look consistent. The two quantities share a word and nothing else. The consistency gate knows the difference and reports both.
HYDROPOWER_HORIZON_YEARS = 100, the CWoN capitalisation horizon.
HYDROPOWER_GEP_YEAR = 2019, the wealth column the rent is read from. Current USD equals real 2019 USD in the 2019 base year, and this is the only variant that covers Venezuela.
HYDROPOWER_REFERENCE_EXCLUDED, seventeen iso3 codes set to NaN to reproduce the reference: AZE, BGR, DOM, GRC, GTM, HTI, KAZ, LBR, MAR, MKD, NIC, POL, PRT, SLV, TJK, UKR and ZAF.
WATER_USE_YEARS = (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015), the AQUASTAT survey years the calculation keeps.
WATER_USE_EFFICIENCY_SERIES, WATER_USE_COUNTRY_RENAMES, WATER_USE_ISO_LOOKUP and WATER_USE_REGIONS_DROPPED, which reproduce script 02’s name surgery verbatim.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
Taken as given
CWoN’s own hydropower wealth estimate, and the AQUASTAT efficiency and withdrawal series.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply
text:
What is open
The seventeen excluded countries are the largest open item. The reference output leaves them empty although the CWoN wealth table values them, and no available material explains the drop, because the 2026 script is not on the drive and the package lacks its raw workbook. The exclusion is encoded to reproduce the reference, the reason is an ask on the deck, and changing the list is a reviewed-commit decision.
The drive’s per-country water-use tables are not this calculation’s outputs and are held as anchors rather than adopted. The agriculture table equals 1000 times GEP_total from a separate crop-water valuation whose scripts are not on the drive. The all-sector table was computed on a newer AQUASTAT vintage with the appendix’s deflate-to-2015 step, and only 3 of 183 countries reproduce from the staged inputs, with a median committed to computed-at-2019 ratio of 0.36 over a range of 0 to 1.25.
Script 02’s lookup countries keep their AQUASTAT names, so their efficiency and withdrawal rows share an iso code but never a country name. The merge leaves them as half-rows with no products, including USA, RUS and TUR. The anchor commits that behaviour and the port reproduces it.
water_supply_gep stays the hydropower component alone. How, and whether, the water-use components combine with it is the account’s subgroup question, flagged on the deck. The agriculture and household components named on the group’s sheet are not yet built anywhere we have seen, and the module is laid out to receive them beside hydropower.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text: Stormwater retention values the runoff that land cover holds back instead of sending into drainage systems. The account prices that volume at what it would cost to replace the same capacity. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is replacement cost.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Quantity
Annual retained volume in cubic metres per country, from an InVEST Urban Stormwater Retention run over the inputs the consortium drive staged, the biophysical coefficient table, ESA 2020 land cover, WorldClim precipitation and SLGWRB soils. That run is made outside the task tree, on the drive’s own configuration, which base_data/global_invest/stormwater/run_recipe.md records. The retention_by_country task then sums the run’s retention raster inside each r250 country and writes the per-country table. The library reads that table; it does not run the retention model.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Price
USD per cubic metre retained. The committed InVEST configuration prices retention at 1, which is a placeholder rather than a valuation. The intended price is the open ask, and it is held in one named constant until the author answers.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Valuation
stormwater_gep_by_country is the whole valuation:
\[
\text{stormwater GEP} = \text{retention (m}^3) \times \text{price (USD/m}^3)
\]
The function is in place and unit-tested.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the stormwater service:

stormwater_retention_by_country_path, the per-country retention volumes the valuation prices.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding iso3_r250_label, retention_m3, year and stormwater_gep. The log line reports the total retention in cubic metres a year, the number of countries with positive retention, the resulting GEP, and the placeholder price it was computed at.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
Method constants
STORMWATER_PRICE_PER_M3_PLACEHOLDER = 1.0, the committed configuration’s price per cubic metre.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Stormwater Retention
text:
What is open
The price. Every output built on the placeholder is provisional by construction, which is why the constant is named for what it is and logged on every run. Whether the retained volumes should be masked to urban areas is the other open question. The run was made wall to wall over the global land cover, because the committed configuration carries no urban boundaries.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Value the deaths that forest root cohesion averts by holding hillslopes together. The service is computed as a difference between two runs of the same model on the same grid: one in which forest roots reinforce the soil as the land-cover map says they do, and one in which root cohesion is removed entirely. Everything else – terrain, soil, rainfall, population, roads, and the fitted statistical models – is identical between the two, so the difference in predicted deaths is attributable to root reinforcement alone.
This note describes what the code in global_invest/landslide_mitigation/ does. The science is a fold of m-braaksma/landslide_mitigation v0.2.0 (folded 2026-08-16); the arithmetic lives in landslide_mitigation_chain.py as pure functions, the raster drivers in landslide_mitigation_functions.py, and the pipeline in landslide_mitigation_tasks.py.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Value the deaths that forest root cohesion averts by holding hillslopes together. The service is computed as a difference between two runs of the same model on the same grid: one in which forest roots reinforce the soil as the land-cover map says they do, and one in which root cohesion is removed entirely. Everything else – terrain, soil, rainfall, population, roads, and the fitted statistical models – is identical between the two, so the difference in predicted deaths is attributable to root reinforcement alone.
This note describes what the code in global_invest/landslide_mitigation/ does. The science is a fold of m-braaksma/landslide_mitigation v0.2.0 (folded 2026-08-16); the arithmetic lives in landslide_mitigation_chain.py as pure functions, the raster drivers in landslide_mitigation_functions.py, and the pipeline in landslide_mitigation_tasks.py.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Grid and inputs
Everything is computed on the NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 global 1km grid (EPSG:6933), built from the authoritative EASE2_M01km.gpd grid definition rather than assumed. EASE-Grid is equal-area, so a pixel count converts to real area by one constant multiply and no latitude weighting is needed anywhere in the calculation. Every input is warped onto that exact grid and then checked against it for matching size, pixel resolution and projection before the model runs.








Input
Source
Resampling onto the 1km grid




Elevation
SEALS alt_m.tif (shared base data)
average


Agro-ecological zones

mode (categorical)


Forest cover

class weights, then average


Landslide events

coordinate transform, not a warp


Population
LandScan, per year

Soil texture, organic carbon, bulk density

Saturated conductivity
HiHydroSoil 0-5, 5-15, 15-30cm
thickness-weighted mean, then average


Soil and sediment thickness

average


Mean annual precipitation
WorldClim BIO12 (1970-2000 normal)

Annual maximum daily rainfall
ERA5-Land, per year
