Road density
GRIP4 total density, m/km²
bilinear (upsampling)



The three soil-depth intervals are combined by their own thickness (5, 10 and 15cm), and only where each interval has data, so a pixel missing the deepest layer is the mean of the two shallower ones rather than a hole.
Forest cover enters as a root-reinforcement weight, not as a binary forest mask. Closed-canopy and flooded tree-cover classes take weight 1; the two mosaic tree/shrub-herbaceous classes are 50/50 land cover and take 0.5; sparse tree cover below 15% takes 0, as being below meaningful root reinforcement. Every other class is 0. Averaging that 0-1 weight field onto the 1km grid gives each pixel a fractional forest share.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Slope
Slope is computed with gdal.DEMProcessing (Horn 1981) from the raw elevation at four times the target resolution (~250m) and then averaged down to 1km. Computing slope at 1km directly would flatten exactly the terrain the model is about. Because the grid is already in metres, no degree-to-metre scale factor enters.
The elevation used for the hydrology is separately pit-filled at 1km: the trusted 300m DEM is already pit-filled, but averaging it down to 1km can create new local minima. D8 flow direction and flow accumulation run on the pit-filled version, and the accumulated pixel count is scaled to an upslope contributing area in m².

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
section: Slope stability with and without forest roots
text:
Slope stability with and without forest roots
The stability model is the infinite-slope form used across the SHALSTAB / SINMAP / TRIGRS family. For every pixel,
\[
SI \;=\; \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\beta}
\;+\; \frac{c_{\text{soil}} + c_{\text{root}}}{\gamma\,h\,\sin\beta\,\cos\beta}
\;-\; \min\!\left(\frac{q}{T\,\sin\beta},\,1\right)
\]
where \(\phi\) is the internal friction angle, \(\beta\) the slope, \(c_{\text{soil}}\) the soil’s own cohesion, \(c_{\text{root}}\) the root reinforcement, \(\gamma\) the soil unit weight, \(h\) the soil depth, \(q\) the specific discharge and \(T\) the transmissivity. The first term is friction against geometry, the second is cohesion holding the slope together, and the third is the destabilising effect of water. Higher \(SI\) is more stable.
The four soil terms are derived from the mapped soil properties:

Friction angle \(\phi = 25 + (\text{sand}\% - \text{clay}\%)/20\), clipped to 15-40 degrees: sandier soils resist shear at a steeper angle than clay-rich ones.
Soil cohesion \(c_{\text{soil}} = 2 + 0.03\,\text{clay}\% + 0.1\,\text{organic carbon}\%\) kPa, clipped to 0-50 kPa.
Unit weight \(\gamma = \rho\,g\), converting SoilGrids bulk density in Mg/m³ to kN/m³.
Transmissivity \(T = K_{\text{sat}} \times h\), with HiHydroSoil’s integer conductivity unscaled and converted to m/day first.

The specific discharge is static rather than event-based: the WorldClim annual rainfall total is spread evenly over the year, applied to the pixel’s upslope contributing area, and divided by the cell width it enters through. The hydrological term is physically a saturation ratio, so it is capped at 1; uncapped, the heavily right-skewed upslope area drives most pixels onto the stability floor.
Root cohesion is the only thing that differs between the two runs. It is \(c_{\text{root}} = \text{forest share} \times c_{\text{root,max}}\) with \(c_{\text{root,max}} = 5\) kPa in the observed run and \(0\) in the full_impacts counterfactual.
Three exclusions and clips are part of the method rather than defensive coding, and each changes results:

Pixels flatter than 2 degrees are excluded entirely. Infinite-slope theory does not apply there, and without the exclusion both the friction and hydrological terms blow up near \(\beta = 0\) and swamp the forest-cover signal – the median observed-versus-counterfactual difference was exactly zero before it was added.
Slope is clipped to 0.5-89.5 degrees and the friction angle to 15-40 degrees before the trigonometry, since \(\tan\beta\) goes to zero at flat and diverges near vertical.
\(SI\) itself is clipped to \([-10, 10]\).

The observed index is computed for every modelling year and the prediction year; the counterfactual only for the prediction year, since a counterfactual has no meaning during calibration.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Calibrating stability to landslide probability
Recorded landslides are rare relative to land pixels, so the hazard model is fitted on a stratified case-control sample rather than on the whole grid.
Cases are UGLC events. The events are filtered to those with a usable location accuracy – the recorded accuracy must be present, positive, not one of the fill codes UGLC uses, and no coarser than 1000m – and then reprojected to EASE-Grid metres. Several events can fall in one 1km pixel, so within a year they are collapsed to one row per pixel carrying the highest fatality count of the group: the model is fitted on pixel-years.
Controls are pixel-years drawn uniformly at random over the grid and kept only where the GAEZ raster says there is land, at 25 controls per case, with a fixed seed so the draw is reproducible. Each row, case or control, is then sampled for its stability index, annual maximum daily rainfall, population, slope, road density and GAEZ zone. Rows missing stability, rainfall or zone are dropped – most of them are the near-flat pixels the stability model excluded.
An ordinary logit of case status on stability index and extreme rainfall is fitted on the modelling years. Its slope coefficients are consistent estimates of the population slopes, but its intercept carries the oversampling of cases, so it is corrected (Prentice and Pyke 1979):
\[
\alpha_{\text{corrected}} \;=\; \alpha_{\text{raw}} \;-\; \log\!\frac{\tau/(1-\tau)}{\pi/(1-\pi)}
\]
\(\tau\) is the case fraction in the sample. \(\pi\) is the prevalence in the population, and it is not assumed: it is counted from the UGLC annual panels themselves, as event pixel-years over SI-eligible land pixel-years across the same years used for training. Restricting the denominator to the pixels the stability model actually scores keeps the prevalence on the same population the model predicts over. The per-year counts behind it are exported as an audit table.
To build those panels, each UGLC event is stamped onto the grid as a disc of its own location accuracy rather than as a single pixel: the binary panel marks every pixel the disc covers, and the mortality panel spreads the event’s fatalities over the disc with a linear distance decay \(1 - d/r\), summed across events.
The fit is scored by AUC on the training years and on the held-out prediction year.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Fatalities given a landslide
Severity is a two-part hurdle model, fitted only on realized landslides (the cases) in the modelling years, on the same four covariates in both parts: log(1+population), extreme rainfall, slope and road density.

Part A, a logit, gives \(\Pr(\text{fatalities} > 0 \mid \text{landslide})\). If the maximum likelihood fit fails on separation, it falls back to an L2-regularized fit; the coefficients are then shrunk toward zero and the standard errors are not comparable to an unpenalized fit, so that fallback is a point estimate rather than inference.
Part B, an OLS on the fatal subsample, gives \(E[\log(\text{fatalities}) \mid \text{fatal}]\).

Back-transforming part B needs care: \(\exp\) of a predicted log understates the expectation by Jensen’s inequality. The correction is Duan’s (1983) smearing factor, the mean of \(\exp\) of the part-B residuals, which estimates the bias from the residuals themselves rather than assuming log-normal errors. Expected fatalities given a landslide are therefore
\[
E[\text{deaths} \mid \text{landslide}] \;=\;
\Pr(\text{fatal}) \times \exp\!\big(X\beta_B\big) \times \text{smearing}.
\]
A separate diagnostic refits both parts with the stability index in place of slope, to check whether stability subsumes slope’s information in severity. It is written to its own output and never overwrites the production coefficients.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Prediction and avoided mortality
Prediction runs tile by tile over the land-containing tiles of the grid (2000 pixels per side by default), so the global rasters are assembled from independent pieces.
For each scenario, expected deaths per pixel-year are
\[
\text{deaths} \;=\; \Pr(\text{landslide} \mid SI, \text{rain}) \times E[\text{deaths} \mid \text{landslide}].
\]
Rainfall is the prediction year’s, and the severity covariates do not vary by scenario, so the severity expectation is computed once per tile and reused. The scenarios differ only through the stability index that enters the hazard probability – which is to say, only through root cohesion.
Avoided mortality is then the counterfactual minus the observed:
\[
\text{avoided deaths} \;=\; \text{deaths}_{\text{full\_impacts}} \;-\; \text{deaths}_{\text{observed}}.
\]
Physically this cannot be negative – removing root cohesion cannot make a slope safer – so pixels where it comes out negative are counted and warned about rather than silently floored.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
Valuation
Avoided deaths are priced at the value of a statistical life, per country, in 2019 constant USD to match the rest of GEP.
The default schedule is the staged EPA life-years-lost panel (landslide_mitigation_vsl_panel_path): EPA’s adopted $7.9M (2008 USD) carried to $9,876,237 at 2019 by CPI and real-income growth at elasticity 0.4, transferred to each country by the ratio of GDP per capita (PPP) times life years lost, with World Bank region-median and global-median fallbacks. All 250 account countries are covered (199 direct, 49 region, 2 global) and each row records its tier in a vsl_source column.
Blanking that parameter row recovers the OECD schedule. There, countries with a published OECD country estimate take it directly; the published figures are 2022 USD with a power-of-ten multiplier, scaled up and deflated to 2019 by the PMPRB CPI-based cumulative price-adjustment factor of 1.050. Countries without a direct estimate take their income group’s figure from Table 6.1 of OECD (2025), Mortality Risk Valuation in Policy Assessment: 7.1 USD million for high-income OECD, 7.9 for high-income non-OECD, and 1.1 for the upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups; a row whose income group is unclassified takes the global figure of 2.7 USD million, deflated the same way. The run logs the OECD-priced total beside the panel-priced one, so the two schedules stay comparable.
The per-country values are joined onto the EE r264 correspondence and rasterized onto the 1km grid, so every pixel carries its country’s VSL. The service’s value raster is the avoided-death raster times the VSL raster, and country totals are the zonal sums of both rasters over the correspondence polygons.
Note that the r264 correspondence splits large countries into sub-regions. Each sub-region carries its country’s ISO3 and therefore its national VSL, which is what the rasterization needs; a one-row-per-country table has to sum the sub-regions back together, which is what the results report does.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
section: What the module does not do
text:
What the module does not do

The stability model is static: one specific discharge from a climatological rainfall normal, not an event-based or seasonal hydrology.
Rainfall enters the hazard model as the annual maximum daily total, so hazard is a per-pixel-year probability, not a per-storm one.
Transmissivity units are flagged as unverified in the code and have not been checked against the HiHydroSoil documentation here.
The module has been run end to end once on the cluster, but its numbers have not been replicated against a machine-readable v0.2.0 output from the author, so they remain provisional.

title: Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value
text:
References
The citations below are the ones the code itself names. They are the model family and the specific corrections applied, not a general literature review.

Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method.
Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. (The slope algorithm gdal.DEMProcessing uses.)
OECD (2025). Mortality Risk Valuation in Policy Assessment, Table 6.1.
Prentice, R. L., and Pyke, R. (1979). Logistic disease incidence models and case-control studies.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Pest Control
text:
Biological pest control is valued as the extra yield natural enemies provide on organically managed cropland, at the organic producer price. The base year is 2019.
⚠ The scope is organic agriculture only, by design: the underlying evidence measures the yield effect of predators where synthetic pesticides are absent, and no comparable estimate exists for conventional systems. The full value is attributed to nature – no human-input adjustment (lambda) is applied, unlike the neighbouring crop rows.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Pest Control
text:
Quantity
Organic production per crop and country: FiBL’s organic area extract, times the country’s conventional FAOSTAT yield, times an organic-to-conventional yield ratio per FAO crop group (pest_control_yield_ratio_*). FiBL aggregate rows with no FAOSTAT production analogue are excluded and their share logged, never guessed.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Pest Control
text:
Price
The organic producer price: the country’s FAOSTAT 2019 producer price for the crop (the item’s global median where the country reports none), times the organic-to-conventional price premium (pest_control_price_premium).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Pest Control
text:
Valuation
Per crop \(i\), country \(j\):
\[
\text{Value}_{ij} = \left(e^{\text{lnRR}_{g(i)}} - 1\right) \; A_{ij} \; y_{ij} \, r_{g(i)} \; p_{ij} \, \pi
\]
where \(\text{lnRR}_{g(i)}\) is the crop group’s meta-analytic log response ratio (pest_control_effect_lnrr_*: the cereal effect for cereals, the vegetable effect for vegetables, oilseeds and pulses, the other-crops effect for fruit, nuts and stimulants, zero for every other group), \(A\) the organic area, \(y\) the conventional yield, \(r\) the yield ratio, \(p\) the producer price and \(\pi\) the price premium. Countries sum over crops; the published table carries all 250 account countries with NA where nothing is valued.
The committed pest_control_gep.csv is carried beside the result as the comparison anchor. It is a Monte Carlo mean from a pipeline that is not on the drive, so the run log reports coverage and log-rank agreement rather than a to-the-cent match, and the total scales linearly in \(\pi\) (the committed level corresponds closely to \(\pi = 1\)).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Pest Control
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the pest_control service key: the FiBL area extract, the FAOSTAT 2019 yield and price slices, the FAO/CPC crop classification, the three effect sizes, the six yield ratios, the price premium and the committed reference, each with a source row beside it.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Vegetated landscapes intercept rainfall, slow its passage into rivers and store part of it in the soil. Where they do so upstream of towns and farmland, floods downstream are shallower than they would otherwise be, and the damage those floods cause is smaller. That reduction in damage is what this account values.
The scope is river flooding only. Coastal flooding, storm surge and pluvial flooding lie outside it, following the hazard product the account uses. Coverage is 250 countries at 537 m, reported in USD 2019.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Vegetated landscapes intercept rainfall, slow its passage into rivers and store part of it in the soil. Where they do so upstream of towns and farmland, floods downstream are shallower than they would otherwise be, and the damage those floods cause is smaller. That reduction in damage is what this account values.
The scope is river flooding only. Coastal flooding, storm surge and pluvial flooding lie outside it, following the hazard product the account uses. Coverage is 250 countries at 537 m, reported in USD 2019.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Method
Valuing this service requires answering a question that cannot be observed: how much flood damage would occur if landscapes stopped absorbing rain. The account simulates a counterfactual world in which ecosystems no longer retain water, routes the same storms through it, and takes the difference.
Everything turns on one number per location, the depth amplification: the ratio of flood depth in the degraded world to flood depth in the current one. Hydrology has no standard name for it, because it has not previously been needed – it exists here only because there is a paired counterfactual world to run.

Step 1, how absorbent each piece of land is
A curve number between 30 and 100 is assigned to every cell by crossing land cover with soil hydrologic group, from USDA field measurements:
\[S = 25400 / \text{CN} - 254\]
\(S\) is the potential maximum retention in millimetres. Forest on loam holds 208 mm; the same soil stripped bare holds 41 mm. This is the only point in the account where vegetation enters the physics.


Step 2, how much extra water runs off
\[I_a = 0.2S, \qquad Q = (P - I_a)^2 / (P - I_a + S) \text{ for } P > I_a\]
The relation saturates. As \(P\) grows large relative to \(S\), runoff approaches total rainfall regardless of land cover, so the service is concentrated in frequent events and the largest proportional effects appear where storms are small relative to what the soil can hold.


Step 3, following the water downhill
\[\text{ratio}(i) = \text{accum}(Q_\text{degraded})(i) / \text{accum}(Q_\text{current})(i)\]
Routing uses MERIT Hydro. On the Upper Mississippi, seven per cent more runoff at the point of rainfall becomes twenty-two per cent more discharge in the river: routing roughly triples the local effect, and that is what makes flood regulation a landscape service rather than a local one.


Step 4, turning more water into deeper water
\[A(i) = [\text{ratio}(i)]^{f}, \qquad f \approx 0.4\]
At-a-station hydraulic geometry gives the split between width, depth and velocity. So 21.5% more discharge produces 8% more depth. The exponent is the least constrained element of the chain and is swept over 0.3 to 0.5.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Two counterfactuals
Bare soil removes land cover entirely, setting curve numbers to the fallow values of the reference tables. This is the world a gross product asks about, and it is the reference the erosion account uses, so the two services are measured against one hypothetical landscape and can be summed.
In-situ degradation raises curve numbers less: soils compacted and canopy thinned, the land still present. Closer to what realistic degradation would produce, and reported alongside rather than as a sensitivity.
Bare soil exceeds in-situ by about 2.5, and that ratio is stable to within four per cent across both hazard products and both treatments of permanent water.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Lambda
Lambda is 1 for this service. The counterfactual already isolates the ecosystem contribution: it is a difference between two worlds identical in every respect except the ecosystem, so whatever remains in the difference is the ecosystem’s doing by construction.
The prevention share reported throughout is a different quantity and not an attribution coefficient:
\[\text{prevention share} = (\text{EAD}_\text{degraded} - \text{EAD}_\text{current}) / \text{EAD}_\text{degraded}\]
An attribution share near 1 and a prevention share near 0.01 are not two estimates of one thing.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Sign conventions
GEP is positive: it is damage that does not occur. Degradation raises expected annual damage, so the difference is non-negative by construction and a negative value indicates a routing or alignment fault rather than a result.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
text:
Compute
The amplification field is built from rainfall and flow direction rather than from the hazard maps, so it survives a change of hazard product. Building it is two weeks of single-threaded flow accumulation over 75 billion cells; everything downstream of it is hours. RUN.md documents both paths.

title: Riverine flood-control ecosystem service
section: Before trusting any rerun of the pipeline
text:
Before trusting any rerun of the pipeline
The account as it stands does not rerun the pipeline: gep_calculation reads the author’s own per-country export, so the number here is his verified one. This section matters only if that changes.

The failure that made this account wrong twice
The author’s RUN.md is explicit, and it is the most important thing in it:

Check flow-direction coverage. This is not optional, and it is the reason this account was wrong twice.

Seven MERIT flow-direction packages were missing at various points, and every absence was silent. Accumulation over a missing network writes nodata, the amplification clips to a minimum of 1.0, and the valuation reads 1.0 as no change here rather than no data here. Japan, Korea, Portugal and Kazakhstan returned zero service against 49 bn USD of exposure; Nigeria, Chad, Cameroon, Niger and the Central African Republic another 4 bn. Nothing in any log recorded a problem. Both were found because a country looked implausible. Recovering them raised GEP by 18.5 per cent and then a further 16.
python prep_merit_dir.py --check-tiles
⚠ The check has a limit the author states plainly. Its reference list was generated from a tile set believed complete, so it detects regressions — a lost file, a partial copy, an interrupted extraction — but not a package that was never downloaded, which was the original failure.
A missing amplification raster behaves the same way: the pipeline warns, falls back to current depths and returns a GEP of zero, so the job completes and the number is wrong. RUN.md carries a three-line check that the mosaic resolves, and msi/final_run.sbatch verifies the totals itself and prints ALL MATCH or the quantity that differs.


The account should compute this itself
The account computes this figure rather than reading it. That was not true until 2026-09-01 and this page said so; it is true now.
Four of the six tasks run here: task_compute_service_flow, task_compute_flood_damages, task_compute_flood_gep and task_generate_maps_and_figures. The GEP chain with the counterfactuals gives $11,403,596,548 across 250 rows, positive in 163, against the author’s published $11.40bn – his rounding to one decimal, and his committed table agrees with ours to the cent, 250 of 250 countries, largest per-country difference $0.000000. gep = ead_bare - ead_current holds to 1.2e-07 on every row, and the damage side reproduces at $887,827,659,820 / $194,256,309,530 / $551,051,565,602.
The two tasks that do not run here are task_prepare_flood_inputs and task_build_sda, which are Sections A and B. That is deliberate on the author’s part rather than a gap: his RUN.md tells a reader to copy the staged Sections B and C across because rebuilding them turns a three-hour run into an eleven-hour one. A cold start of those two began on 2026-09-01, once the inputs they need were staged into base_data – the aligned JRC depths at 1.3 GB and the service-providing-area raster at 144 MB.
⚠ What reproducing him does and does not establish. The module is his pipeline with our path handling and ProjectFlow wiring, so agreement was close to guaranteed. It is a build test: it catches our refactor breaking his arithmetic, and says nothing about whether the arithmetic is right.
⚠ The water variant moves this figure more than anything else in it. The run writes four, and gep_flood_bare is $6.29bn on 4rp, $7.34bn on v1_2016, $11.40bn on v2_2024_waterremoved – the delivered one – and $24.54bn on v2_2024_waterkept. Keeping permanent water more than doubles the headline. The author has reported about $11.4bn consistently, in correspondence and in his committed table, so waterremoved is the account’s variant; the gap is pinned by a test so it cannot drift unnoticed.


What running the remaining two needs
The inputs live on MSI at /projects/standard/jajohns/shared/flood_gep, read-only. What Sections A and B actually need from it is small – flood_depth_aligned_path and flood_spa_path, 1.5 GB with the optional population grid – and both are staged in base_data now with the template carrying the references. The 129 GB of counterfactual amplification rasters in that tree feed task_compute_flood_gep, which already runs, so they are not part of this.

title: Crop Provision
text:
Main contributors: Marta Sylla, Lijing Wang, Ryan McWay
This section outlines how we assess and value food provision as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. The analysis focuses specifically on food provision provided by terrestrial ecosystems. This analysis does not include any aquatic ecosystem; aquaculture/fisheries is covered in a different section of the GEP manuscript. By estimating and valuing crop provision, we aim to capture the ecosystem contribution to commercial crop agricultural practices.
Crop production is defined as a contribution of the ecosystem to agricultural production of crops (United Nations et al., 2021). The contribution of the ecosystem has effective biophysical impact and consecutive economic influence. Researchers often applied these two perspectives: biophysical and economic. Biophysical perspective starts at looking at the biophysical processes or biological production functions and tries to disentangle ecosystem and human contributions. Very often the common units of energy or biomass, water inputs are used. In the economic perspective, the common monetary units are used. Crop production belongs to the provisioning group of ecosystem services (CICES Version 5.1), as well as is characterized as material contribution by the classification suggested to the concept of nature contributions to people (Brauman et al 2020).
This is a final product that enters the economy via the agricultural sector. Further modifications or processing of the initial/raw products are included in the GDP of the economic sector of Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting, but also other sectors down the value chain. It should be noted, however, that according to the global study farmers receive, on average, 27% of the money consumers spend on food eaten at home, while they receive a significantly smaller share of the expenditure on food consumed outside home (Yi et al., 2021). This percentage varies across countries and regions, as well as changes with the quality of the raw product.

title: Crop Provision
text:
Data and Methods
We estimate gross ecosystem product (GEP) for crop provision for the year 2019 as:
\[
\mathrm{GEP crop}_{\text{c,k,t}} = \sum_{c,k,t} \left( \mathrm{GPV}_{c,k,t} \cdot \lambda_{c,t10} \right)
\] , where
GEP crop c,k,t is the agricultural ecosystem contribution for country c, crop item k and given year t,
GPVk,t is the FAO’s gross production value for country c, crop item k and given year ,
λc,t10 is the CWON land rent representing ecosystem contribution for country c, decade t10,
This value is aggregated at the national level for a given year (in this case, 2019). The summation can represent global GEP for food provision when aggregated across all countries, crop items and year.
FAOSTAT’s gross production value in current US dollars stops wherever its own US-dollar producer-price series stops, so a country-crop pair can carry production and no value (India’s rice in 2019 is one). At the base year those pairs take GPV from the values table the pollination module stages (fao_values_1993_2024.csv): production tonnes times that year’s US-dollar producer price, the price falling back from the country’s own to the FAO subregion, region and world medians. No price arithmetic happens in this module. The same lambda then applies to filled and read pairs alike, and each filled row records which level priced it.
This formula and method follows the Changing Wealth of Nations method presented in the 2024 report (World Bank, 2024). Lambda (λ) is “proxied by land cost shares provided by the International Agricultural Productivity database for each country and each decade. For countries where rental rates vary across decades, annual values are assumed to be constant within each decade” (World Bank, 2024). Agricultural land is further subdivided into pasture or cropland, therefore land rates are disaggregated into livestock or crop production. We do not distinguish between organic and non-organic farming, as well as intensive/extensive types of farming. In the CWON report of 2021 (Source: CWON 2021: Methods and Data, p. 48) the pastures were divided into intensive and extensive pastureland and the rental rates for extensive pasture were twice as high as for intensive. The rental rates for intensive pasture and cropland were the same. However, the data was provided by regions of several countries clustered together. Therefore, the CWON 2024 methodology constitutes a major improvement in terms of accuracy and timeframe, losing the artificially doubling the rent for extensive pastureland.

title: Crop Provision
text:
Validation
The applied method follows the CWON methodology for estimating the value of natural capital rents. For agriculture, the natural resource is land and the crop rents represent ecosystem contribution. We compared our results with the CWON 2024 for global results for the year 2019. CWON’s results are about 5% lower than ours, even though we use the same input data and values for lambda.

title: Crop Provision
text:
References

K.A. Brauman, L.A. Garibaldi, S. Polasky, Y. Aumeeruddy-Thomas, P.H.S. Brancalion, F. DeClerck, U. Jacob, M.E. Mastrangelo, N.V. Nkongolo, H. Palang, N. Pérez-Méndez, L.J. Shannon, U.B. Shrestha, E. Strombom, & M. Verma,Global trends in nature’s contributions to people, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 117 (51) 32799-32805, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2010473117 (2020).

Yi, J., Meemken, EM., Mazariegos-Anastassiou, V. et al. Post-farmgate food value chains make up most of consumer food expenditures globally. Nat Food 2, 417–425 (2021). https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-021-00279-9

World Bank (2024). The Changing Wealth of Nations: Revisiting the Measurement of Comprehensive Wealth. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099100824155021548/pdf/P178446-7dfe6e92-9cf0-4d24-ad25-20b1320904c2.pdf

United Nations et al. (2021). System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA). White cover publication, pre-edited text subject to official editing. Available at: https://seea.un.org/ecosystem-accounting.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text: Timber provision values managed forestry. The valuation runs on a 10 arcsecond grid and is reported as one row per country for the GEP base year of 2019. The price convention recorded in es_config.csv is stumpage value.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Quantity
Annual harvestable biomass yield in cubic metres per hectare, built from MC2 forest types crossed with Tian et al. timber regions and adjusted for net primary productivity. This layer is produced by the consortium drive’s Forestry calculation and is staged for the library rather than rebuilt in it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Price
The national log price in USD per cubic metre, from Siikamaki and Santiago-Avila 2014 as the Forestry calculation’s method appendix cites it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Valuation
Gross return is converted to net return with the GTAP land factor share (Damania et al. 2023) and then reduced by a per-pixel transport cost built from Weiss et al. travel time and a trucking cost. net_forest_return is that decomposition:
\[
\text{net return} = \text{land factor share} \times \text{biomass} \times \text{price} - \text{transport cost}
\]
forest_value_from_net_return keeps a pixel only where the Lesiv et al. (2022) forest management map marks current timber activity, categories 2 to 5 on forested ESA classes. Negative net returns and nodata floor to zero, which is the value raster’s own nodata convention.
gep_by_zone then sums the value raster per country. It runs blockwise with np.bincount over the 10 arcsecond r250 country-id raster, 2048 rows at a time, accumulating into an array indexed by iso3_r250_id. timber_gep_from_zone_sums keys those sums onto the country list.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
What the library reports
The reported number is the library’s own run of the zonal sum over the staged value raster. The committed Forestry CSV is the comparison anchor, logged next to the computed total and pinned in the test suite, and is never written out as the result.
Three checks are recorded against the staged rasters:

current_forest_value.tif equals forestry_land_share_return_tcost_before_2022_07_23.tif bit-exactly on every one of its 265,210,379 positive pixels, with zero mismatches globally. The remaining 802,119,863 positive net-return pixels are dropped by the management mask, which is external to the staged layers and cannot be derived from them.
The net-return decomposition reproduces the net-return raster with a per-region fitted land factor share, R2 between 0.78 and 0.9999 over twelve continental windows and median relative error between 0.5 and 4 percent. The share applies at GTAP region by AEZ level with separate plantation and natural estimates, so it enters as an input rather than as a constant.
The committed per-country table, $88.74bn over 166 countries, is the plain pixel sum of current_forest_value.tif inside each r250 country polygon, ratio 1.0000 on all countries tested. The raster is per-pixel USD.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the timber_provision service:

timber_provision_value_raster_path, the staged current-forest-value raster.
timber_provision_zone_raster_path, cartographic/ee/ee_r250_id_10sec.tif, the country-id raster the zonal sum keys on.
timber_provision_gep_path, the committed Forestry table used as the anchor.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, and timber_provision_gep.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Method constants
NET_RETURN_NDV = -99999.0 is the net-return raster’s nodata value, which forest_value_from_net_return excludes alongside negative returns.
The zonal sum is sized by n_zones = 1000 and reads rows_per_block = 2048 at a time.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
Taken as given
The upstream raster valuation, meaning the biomass yield, the aligned log prices and the transport cost surface, is taken as produced by the Forestry calculation. The management mask is not derivable from the staged layers and is likewise adopted.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Timber Provision
text:
What is open
The status sheet lists timber’s draft as In Progress. The committed output and the verified replication above correct that status.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Nature View Amenity
text:
Urban and coastal nature is valued as the room-price premium hotel guests pay for a natural view. Within one hotel on one date, a sea-, mountain-, lake- or garden-view room prices above a comparable room without the view; that difference is a market price for the view itself, because brand, location, star rating and service difference out inside the hotel. The base year is 2019.
⚠ Two of the owner’s conventions are kept and named rather than changed: the room prices are scraped at the submission’s own booking dates and applied to 2019 room-nights, and one uniform mean occupancy (from the 106 reporting countries in the UN Tourism table) applies to every country. Because the scrape is 2026 money, the published figure deflates it to 2019 by the shared US CPI factor; the owner-vintage reading is kept beside it and is what the replication anchor holds at.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Nature View Amenity
text:
Quantity
The country’s hotel room-nights carrying a natural view: UN Tourism hotel rooms 2019, times the uniform mean occupancy, times 365, times the scenic-room share – the natural-view share of displayed room availability in the sample, over records with a positive price and availability.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Nature View Amenity
text:
Price
The unit price difference per room-night: within each of the 7,270 comparable groups (same hotel, date and room configuration), the mean natural-view price minus the mean comparable non-view price. Groups outside three Excel-inclusive interquartile ranges of the log price ratio, or with a negative premium, are dropped (5,213 kept); the country figure weights each group’s difference by its scenic-room availability.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Nature View Amenity
text:
Valuation
\[
\text{GEP}_i = R_i \; \bar{o} \; 365 \; s_i \; d_i
\]
with \(R_i\) the hotel rooms, \(\bar{o}\) the uniform mean occupancy, \(s_i\) the scenic-room share and \(d_i\) the unit price difference. A country missing any input carries NA with the absence named in a note column, never a silent zero. The owner’s results workbook is carried beside the result as the replication anchor, and the run log reports the per-country agreement.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Nature View Amenity
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the nature_view_amenity service key: the raw room-price sample (read only for the coordinate-to-country mapping), the analysis-ready comparable-group workbook, the country mapping, the UN Tourism room inventory and the owner’s reference, each with a source row beside it.

title: GEP service library: status
text:
This drives the service status. Change the prose here, then run python3 docs/publish_service_status.py to refresh the group’s shared sheet from it.
Refactoring onto the library template means every service is built the same way, in two files.
One file holds the maths and never opens or saves anything. The second file does the opening and saving. It reads the input data, calls the maths, and writes the results.
Every service joins its results to the same country list and builds its results page the same way.
The fields mean: category is what the code does to produce the number, on a scale from reading a published value to running a model here. method is how the number is computed. ours is whether we can compute the number ourselves, or only read someone else’s. code is the engineering work we did. number is what the figure is and what it was checked against. need is what we are waiting on from someone else. signed off is whether the service meets the fourteen conditions below.
What signed off means.
The standard the account is built to: somebody who wants to reproduce a GEP number should be able to read this repository and follow every step, without opening anyone else’s. They will need the data — base_data holds inputs from many authors and always will — but not another codebase, and not a person to explain the missing part.
That is what signed off: green asserts. Fourteen conditions, each of which has already failed somewhere and been caught:
Stating a departure is not meeting the condition. A service that departs deliberately says so and stays amber until the account agrees the departure, because the point of the convention is that figures can be added together.
And the second half: where our code departs from theirs it departs because ours is better, and the entry says why. Reproducing somebody is the evidence that we understood their pipeline; it is not the goal. Crop subsistence reproduces theirs exactly and then publishes a different number, because their units disagree with their own sources and their extrapolation fits the own-consumption level on the largest term in the formula that produced it. Publishing their arithmetic once we knew that would have been repeating a mistake with our name on it.
⚠ The check must count qualified references. A first version excluded any name preceded by a dot, which made every crop_provision_functions.foo(...) invisible and reported 218 dead names across 21 services, nearly all of them alive. A gate that cries wolf gets switched off.
And deleting is not the only answer. Flood publishes a family of composable tree builders and two of them were called by nothing; they are deliberate API, so the fix was a test that builds every tree, which also proves each one assembles – something nothing had checked.
⚠ The reference anchors are the exception and stay FLAT at the top of the service directory. That is service_data_dir’s contract rather than an oversight: it seeds top-level files only, so an anchor moved into a subfolder stops being found on a machine that has not staged it by hand.
⚠ Measured 2026-09-02: what is missing is almost never the grid. Across every raster the runs had written, they sit on the right geotransform and fail on overviews and statistics – which hb.make_path_pog adds in a fraction of a second on a small raster. base_data/pyramids/ha_per_cell_10sec.tif failed the same way, so this was a library-wide gap rather than any one service’s, and it is why the condition is about publishing rather than about reprojecting.
⚠ It applies to the RESULTS a service distributes, not to its intermediates – 480 rasters over a megabyte sit under intermediate/, and converting those would cost a great deal to make files nobody opens readable. utilities.distribute_results does the conversion once, for every service, as results reach the output directory.
⚠⚠ gdalinfo must be on PATH or the conversion fails with 'int' object has no attribute    'info', which says nothing about the cause: hazelbean’s fallback then builds <env>/bin/bin/    gdalinfo, a doubled path. Activating the environment is enough; invoking its python by absolute path is not.
⚠⚠ A raster only reaches the output directory if a result registers it, and six services do not register theirs: coastal carbon, landslide mitigation, NTFP, recreation, stormwater and terrestrial carbon each write a GeoTIFF that stops at intermediate/. Checking the output directory alone therefore reported the library clean on the day the condition was written – silence that read as compliance and was absence. The gate now reports both halves, so a service whose map never leaves is named rather than passed over, and registering that map is part of closing the condition for it.
Green means all sixteen. amber means the number is usable and at least one condition is open, with the entry saying which. red means the number should not be quoted yet.
⚠⚠ A fidelity-only check no longer passes. This used to read that a service could be green while its only check was that it reproduced the author’s output, provided condition 5 said so. That exemption let green mean “our engineering is complete and legible” while the number rested entirely on somebody else’s data and somebody else’s method, which is not what a reader takes green to mean. Nine services reproduce their source because they share its lineage – terrestrial carbon, both fisheries rows, crop, water quality, air filtration, storm mitigation, hydropower and water use – and that agreement cannot see an error the original also makes. Pollination is the sharpest case: the dependence table, the FAOSTAT bulks, the CropGrids and Monfreda grids are all the author’s, so reproducing his pair to the cent tests our port and nothing else.
Condition 5 therefore now requires more than saying so. Either the check is independent of the source’s lineage, or the entry names what an independent check would have to be and green waits for it. Green is a claim that the number is ours and that somebody could find it wrong; a port nobody can contradict is amber however clean the code.
The five categories, in ascending order of what the code does.
1. Reads a published value — 1 account. The per-country figure already exists in a file. We open it and reshape it to the house table, and no valuation happens. Urban cooling is the one: the city-month valuations are ours, but the reported figure is parsed from a dollar column in a committed file.
2. Rescales a published rate — 2 accounts. Someone published a rate rather than a value, and one or two operations turn it into dollars. Mining production is a rent share times GDP times 0.49; extractive energy is the sum of three published per-fuel rent columns. Real arithmetic, but the economics is entirely theirs.
3. Table arithmetic — 12 accounts. A quantity, a price and an attribution multiplied over tables, with no grids involved. This is the bulk of the library: crop production, livestock, both fisheries rows, energy production, hydropower, water use, air filtration, sandstorm prevention, wildfires, water quality and coastal protection.
4. Raster arithmetic — 7 accounts. The value cannot be reached without processing grids, cell by cell, multiplied and summed into countries. Pollination multiplies 158 production grids by price and by each crop’s pollinator dependence per cell; terrestrial carbon builds density rasters. Also coastal carbon, ntfp, timber, floods and stormwater.
5. Process model run here — 3 accounts. A model with dynamics of its own runs inside the pipeline. Erosion runs InVEST SDR with sediment routing, landslides computes slope stability twice for every pixel, and recreation runs a gravity model allocating visits into scored sites.
category and ours answer different questions. A service can run a model here and still not be ours, because the coefficients or the physical quantity come from elsewhere. Wildfires is the clearest case: the valuation runs here, and the regression coefficients underneath it do not.
The ladder measures work, not confidence. Read as a quality ranking it gets things backwards. The account without a usable number sits at the top of it: stormwater reports retained volume and no dollar total because its price is a placeholder of 1. Crop production, down at table arithmetic, reproduces its reference table exactly.
One label per service hides a split. Several services compute part of the value and read the rest, and the category can only name the heaviest thing the code does. Water quality computes its dollar figure and reads the international-dollar one it reports; coastal protection computes the mangrove half and reads the coral half; ntfp computes the accessible area and reads the value per hectare. ours is where that lives.

title: GEP service library: status
text:
Terrestrial Carbon

subgroup: terrestrial
module: terrestrial_carbon
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes
method: Carbon density by climate zone and land-cover class, times hectares per cell, summed to countries, times the rental social cost of carbon. Rental is not the full social cost: the full cost is what a tonne is worth as an asset, and the rental is one year’s service from holding it. The account is an annual flow, so it takes the yearly service. The rental is P(1 - e^-r), which at 2 percent turns an asset worth $665.87 a tonne of carbon into $13.19 a year. The quantity is a carbon density raster built here from a zone-by-class density table and the land-cover map.
total: $5.365T
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Corrected division by the wrong baseline for the shock, and corrected a double-count that had entered split countries once per sub-region.
grid: WGS84 geographic on the shared 10 arc-second pyramid. Cell area is the per-latitude ha_per_cell raster, multiplied into the density in terrestrial_carbon_tasks.py:146. Correct: a geographic grid needs a per-cell area and this carries one.
reference: The manuscript total. NOT independent of us in the part that matters, since we reproduce a figure computed from the same density table and land-cover map. The double-count we fixed was ours to find, which is what an agreement of this kind cannot surface. ⚠⚠ The reference MOVED (Yanxu, email 2026-09-04), and the per-country table is now compared (his gep_by_country_base_year sheet, modified 2026-09-01): his terrestrial total is $5,330,140,459,760 at 2 percent (announced $5.33T; the sheet verifies it, along with $8.12T at 1 percent and $3.43T at 3, plus new 1.5 and 2.5 percent columns). The 1 percent SCC is replicated following Rennert et al., which answers where that column comes from. ⚠⚠ The $34.8bn gap to ours is NOT the missing countries. The 15 countries he marks missing (BMU, CPV, MUS, REU and other small islands) carry only $181M of our total. The mover is a broad per-country recalculation: no country matches to the dollar any more (the old table matched every row), all 232 comparable rows differ, and the differences concentrate where coastline is long relative to area – Russia +$6.6bn, Canada +$5.9bn, US +$5.1bn, Norway 5.9 percent, Chile 4.8 percent, ours higher almost everywhere. That is the signature of a border-cell or zonal-statistics change, not of prices, missing countries or currency. ⭐ The conservation check settles which side to suspect: the unmasked global sum of our per-cell carbon raster is 406,978,516,772 tC, worth $5,366,047,964,722 at the 2 percent rental – our country table captures it to 0.02 percent (the $1.1bn residue is cells with no country id), while his revised total sits $35.9bn BELOW the raster’s own global content. ⭐ Mechanism CONFIRMED (Yanxu, reply 2026-09-05): valid_mask = (lulc_block > 0) & (cz_block > 0) – the revision excludes every cell whose carbon-zone raster reads 0, where the old version valued them as their own group. So the density raster changed, not the country assignment; his pink-dot map of excluded cells is exactly where our comparison found the differences. ⚠⚠ What that discards is measured, not guessed: the zone-0 densities in the shared lookup are Spawn’s observed means on those very cells, stratified by land-cover class (forest 55.3 tC/ha fitted from 3.07M cells, grassland 8.97 from 3.5M). Exclusion also leaves partial-coverage countries looking complete – Russia’s figure silently omits part of Russia. ⚠ Data hygiene in his sheet: an unlabeled world-total row sits inside the country rows (a naive column sum doubles), six country names are mojibake (Cura√ßao for Curaçao), and Serbia and Kosovo collide on name.
replicated: Was: yes, the superseded vintage to the dollar. Now: no row matches his 2026-09-01 revision, for the zonal reason in reference, and which border treatment is right is the open question. ⚠ Same lineage on the density table and land-cover map either way, so agreement tests the port, not the science.
decided: -
number: Values the carbon stored in land ecosystems, priced at the rental social cost of carbon. Reproduces the superseded manuscript total of $5.365T to the dollar, after fixing a double-count that entered split countries once per sub-region (China six times, 23.5 percent overstatement). Priced at the rental social cost of carbon at 2 percent. The 3 percent sensitivity is a run of its own and gives $3.4627T against the update’s $3.43T. ⚠ The update’s terrestrial figures are $5.33T / $8.12T / $3.43T at 2 / 1 / 3 percent, verified against his per-country sheet; the $34.8bn gap to ours decomposes as $34.3bn of per-country recalculation (every row moved, coastline-heavy countries most), $181M of newly-missing small islands, and $0.3bn of countries dropped from the comparison by mojibake names.
need: ⭐ One of the two discount-rate questions is ANSWERED by the 2026-09-04 email: the 1 percent price is replicated following Rennert et al., who do not publish it directly. Still open: whether carbon prices are taken to grow. The r in the rental formula is the net rate, the discount rate minus the growth rate of carbon prices, so the 2 percent column assumes prices do not grow; the table carries a 0.8 percent net alternative giving $2.29 a tonne against $13.19. And now the substantive ask: what changed in his zonal statistics – every country moved and ours is higher almost everywhere, largest where coastline is long relative to area, so the two pipelines now disagree on border-cell treatment and one of them is right. ⚠ His email quotes the old combined climate-regulation total as $5.365T, which is also the old terrestrial-only figure we match to the dollar – the old combined column looks like it did not include coastal (the new sheet’s both tab, terrestrial plus coastal, verifies the new combined $5.3367T), worth one clarifying line when replying.
signed off: amber: examined, and at least one of the sixteen conditions is not yet verified. ⚠ 10 is OPEN for this module: no cold start from an empty project directory has been run – the density-raster build on the 10 arc-second grid is a cluster-scale job. Six services have closed it (erosion, ntfp, renewable_energy_provision, water_supply, extractive_energy, extractive_materials_provision); this is not one of them. ⚠ 11 is unverified: the base year is 2019 across every service, but the country list, the true-zero-against-missing rule and the shared parameters have not been checked service by service. ⚠ The two discount-rate decisions in need are open with the group. ## Coastal Carbon
subgroup: coastal
module: coastal_carbon
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes
method: Mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass area, times carbon density per habitat and pool, priced like terrestrial carbon. The quantity is habitat area measured here from the mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass extents.
total: $17.72bn seaward only. $58.75bn both sides.
code: Merged the author’s rework, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Checked the refactored code against the original on identical inputs.
grid: WGS84 geographic on the shared pyramid, cell area from ha_per_cell. ⚠ The grid was never the problem here. Its extent was: a 0/1 mask credited a habitat with every cell it touched, putting mangrove at 29.08 Mha against 14.69 Mha of polygon and salt marsh near three times its area. Mangrove and salt marsh now weight each cell by the share the habitat covers. ⚠ Seagrass does NOT, because its density is a polygon attribute, so it still sums polygon areas that overlap.
reference: The author’s reported numbers. ⚠ That agreement held while the extent was roughly doubled, so it never tested the extent. The coverage fix moves mangrove -48.8 percent and salt marsh -66.1 percent, and the EEZ-only total from $22.84bn to $17.72bn; he accepted the fix 2026-08-28. ⚠⚠ The reference MOVED (Yanxu, email 2026-09-04): his revision replaces the combined seagrass extent dataset with one covering 2019-2020, raises the assumed soil depth from 20 to 30 cm, and revises the zonal statistics, taking his total from $26.73bn to $6.60bn at 2 percent ($10.06bn at 1 percent, $4.26bn at 3 percent; all three verified against his per-country sheet, modified 2026-09-01). ⚠⚠ His revised areas look broken for the two raster habitats. His sheet carries mangrove at 0.37 Mha and salt marsh at 0.86 Mha globally – against the mangrove polygons’ own 14.69 Mha (and Global Mangrove Watch’s ~14.7): about 2.5 percent of the world’s mangrove survives his revision, Indonesia at 105,797 ha against a true ~3 Mha. His mangrove carbon density is plausible (216 tC/ha), so the area is what collapsed, and the value with it: mangrove $1.1bn, salt marsh $1.0bn, seagrass $4.6bn of the $6.60bn. Seagrass at 13.43 Mha is plausible (just under McKenzie’s 16-27 Mha range) – the new 2019-2020 dataset likely did resolve the overlap double-count. So the revision fixed seagrass and appears to have destroyed mangrove and salt marsh, which is what over-correcting a whole-cell rule to a stricter rule does to habitats narrower than a cell. Must be raised with Yanxu before anyone adopts $6.60bn.
replicated: Yes, against the superseded method, until we fixed the extent. ⚠ Every number on both sides is now pre-revision: his method changed 2026-09-04 and ours has not ingested it, so nothing currently replicates anything.
decided: Mangrove and salt marsh now weight each cell by the share of it the habitat covers, rather than crediting a whole cell to any extent that clips it. Mangrove extent falls 29.08 Mha to 14.60, which is the polygons’ own area, and the EEZ-only total moves $22.84bn to $17.72bn. ⚠ Yanxu has not been told. Seagrass is unchanged, because its density is a polygon attribute rather than a per-pixel value. ⚠⚠ Its overlap double-count is now measured: the 293,147 WCMC polygons sum to 54.46 Mha but dissolve to 30.02, so overlaps inflate the extent 1.8 times, and the dissolved figure lands inside the 16 to 27 Mha range the author’s own appendix cites from McKenzie. ⭐ His 2026-09-04 revision replaces that seagrass dataset with one covering 2019-2020, which plausibly resolves the overlap – the $20bn drop in his total is the right size and direction – but this is unconfirmed until the updated write-up and results arrive.
number: Values the carbon held in mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass. EEZ-only gives $17.72bn while including the landward pixels gives $58.75bn, both after our coverage fix and both against the superseded method. ⚠ His revised totals are $6.60bn / $10.06bn / $4.26bn at 2 / 1 / 3 percent, down from $26.73bn, and our library has not ingested the revision – the seagrass dataset, the 30 cm soil depth and the revised zonal statistics all have to come in before ours means anything again.
need: Count only habitat pixels seaward of the shoreline, or the landward side too (4.5 times the total)? ⚠ Settled with Yanxu Long, 2026-08-28. He accepts the extent fix (“this makes sense to me, I’ll double check”). Neither of the two rasters exists on his machine either, so the latitude step functions stay — and the appendix, global_climate_regulation_coastal_carbon_appendix.docx, documents them AS the method rather than as a fallback: salt marsh SOC is a four-bin latitude function based on Maxwell (36, 44, 50, 70 tC/ha), noting “a native raster from that source is not yet wired into the pipeline”, and the mangrove BGB default is called out as overestimating “along dry-tropical coasts such as Arabia and northern Australia”, which is the 42 percent of tropical mangrove measured here. ⚠ He is separately revising: reviewer comments, currency to 2019 international dollars, and disentangling zeros from missings. For their own paper he wants a newer base year and an annual time series with sea-level rise, so the GEP 2019 run and that paper will diverge.
signed off: amber: examined, and at least one of the sixteen conditions is not yet verified. ⚠ 10 is OPEN for this module: no cold start from an empty project directory has been run. Six services have closed it (erosion, ntfp, renewable_energy_provision, water_supply, extractive_energy, extractive_materials_provision); this is not one of them. ⚠ 11 is unverified: the base year is 2019 across every service, but the country list, the true-zero-against-missing rule and the shared parameters have not been checked service by service. ⚠ The seagrass overlap double-count in decided is measured but not fixed, held for Yanxu.

The table’s $540.75T is arithmetically the ocean’s ~41,000 GtC at the terrestrial rental price; the annual ocean carbon UPTAKE (~2.5 GtC per year) at the same price would instead be ~$33bn, four orders of magnitude smaller, so which quantity the service means decides everything.

Whether the service is the stock rental of the entire ocean inventory (including ~37,000 GtC of deep water that no policy touches) or the annual uptake flux. Whether $318.2T of High Seas value belongs in a by-country account. And whether one row should be allowed to be 98 percent of the account’s headline total.

subgroup: -
module: pollination
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes for the value raster, which the account’s number comes from. We built production times the world producer price we build ourselves times each crop’s dependence on animal pollination, over 153 crops. The sufficiency side weights that value by how much habitat sits near each field, and it belongs to the other caller rather than to this one: configure_sufficiency runs inside pollination_shock, which is a registered task with its own runner. A base-year account has no scenario for the weighting to vary against, so the GEP number is the value raster and the habitat weighting enters the scenario shock.
method: Each crop’s production raster times its world producer price times its pollination dependence ratio, summed over crops and priced at the GEP base year, then summed to countries. Coffee is blended by country from what it grows, because FAO files arabica and robusta under one item code with different dependence. The quantity is the CropGrids v1.08 production grid for 2020, a published gridded dataset.
total: ?meta:poll_raster without habitat sufficiency, ?meta:poll_with_sufficiency with it, both at 2019 prices from our own raster. Currency harmonized 2026-10-03: the price deflators now read the account’s shared CPI series through utilities.usd_deflation_factor instead of a private copy of the same FRED file — the price window is 2019-centred, so the factor is exactly 1.0 and the rerun returns the gep table identical to the cent. The same rerun carries the zonal measured-zeros fix: the published table is 250 rows with 193 positive, 4 measured zeros (Cayman Islands, Western Sahara, Iceland, Qatar — zones holding valid pixels whose value is exactly zero) and 53 NA, where all 57 non-positive rows were NA before.
code: Folded in from the author’s repo, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The value raster is now built by a task in the tree: pollination_value_raster reads the 158 CropGrids production rasters from base data and writes USD in the cell. Two fixes: The raster carried USD per square kilometre while the code that summed it assumed USD per cell. The price and dependence lookups were built by collapsing a table on a duplicated key, so the value kept was whichever row came last.
grid: WGS84 geographic on the shared pyramid. Cell areas come from hazelbean on the WGS84 ellipsoid, adopted 2026-08-26 in place of a 6371 km sphere that differed by -0.22 to +0.56 percent with latitude. Correct now. ⚠ The earlier $18.28bn was this same raster summed with no cell area at all, so the grid is exactly where this service went wrong before.
reference: No reference for the value, and two for the inputs, both pinned by tests as of 2026-09-01. Our pollination_1993_2024.parquet reproduces the author’s published csv over all 287,285 rows, every one of its 22 numeric columns agreeing to 1.4e-14, the only difference being a missing label reading as None out of parquet and nan out of csv. And our rebuilt value raster sits 0.93 percent above his staged one, correlation 0.995 over 2,941,471 shared cells. ⚠ The entry previously said the source raster was reproduced to 1.8e-08. That number was measured once by hand and the comparison behind it stopped running when the library began building its own raster, so it is replaced here by the two figures a test recomputes. ⚠ We build the raster ourselves, so the second is two pipelines meeting rather than one reproducing the other; the first checks our port and not the science.
replicated: The dependence panel exactly, to 1.4e-14 over 287,285 rows, and the raster to within 0.93 percent, both checked by a test on every run rather than measured once.
decided: Cell areas moved to the WGS84 ellipsoid from hazelbean, the convention the rest of the account uses, costing 0.1086 percent. Country aggregation moved to the centre rule, costing 0.1211 percent of the world total and moving 92 of 204 countries by more than 5 percent.
number: Values the crop output pollinators are responsible for. $387.67bn at 2019 prices over 193 countries, from the raster our own chain builds — FAO panel, yield-change ratios, Monfreda yields carried to the base year, CropGrids harvested area, our median price, the author’s dependence table with coffee blended per country. ⚠⚠ Changed on 2026-08-30 from $384.09bn, which was the author’s staged raster: the yield and production steps had no port until that day, so no run here could produce the value raster from source. Of the $3.40bn difference against his raster, $2.98bn is the coffee blend (FAO item 656 covers arabica at 0.25 and robusta at 0.65; his load_poll_dep keeps the first row, valuing every coffee country as pure arabica) and the rest is the per-cell versus density convention. Set pollination_blend_coffee_dependence to false and our pipeline returns his published pair exactly: $384.97bn unweighted and $161.45bn weighted, both to the cent, with the sufficiency raster identical to his in all 331,871,070 defined cells once the tile height is his 8192. Cell areas are WGS84 from hazelbean, the same convention the rest of the account uses through the ha_per_cell pyramid, which pollination alone did not: it was on a 6371 km sphere, differing by -0.223 to +0.557 percent with latitude, so the GEP total was summing services that measured a cell differently. Adopting it cost 0.1086 percent. Aggregated on the centre rule so a border cell goes to the country covering its centre rather than to whichever was rasterised last. That change cost 0.1211 percent of the world total and moved 92 of 204 countries by more than 5 percent, Iraq by 65.63. Vatican City, Gibraltar, Monaco and Macao drop out entirely, being smaller than a cell: $0.35M between them. From a raster we build (the original one was 2024). The previous $18.28bn was the same raster summed without cell area; area-weighted it gives $476.29bn. That figure is not an independent check: it comes from our own run of the source pipeline on 2026-07-25, which wrote both the raster and the summary beside it. What it does establish is that the source code treats the raster as a density, since its own summary area-weights what it wrote. The units are stated in that repo’s methods_overview.md, ‘global value raster (USD/km2)’. Fixing coffee’s dependence adds $3.76bn at 2024 prices. Our code reproduces the author’s raster to 1.8e-08. ⚠⚠ Computed both ways on 2026-08-28, one grid and one price year: production x price x dependence gives $388.47bn over the raster, and multiplying by 300 m habitat sufficiency built from lulc_esa_2019 gives $163.46bn, a ratio of 0.421. The $388.47 against the published figure is the raster sum against the country zonal sum, which drops cells outside any country. William Sidemo Holm’s 2019 equivalents are $385bn and $190bn, ratio 0.494 (revised 2026-08-28 when he switched price and yield windows from mean to median; his 2026-08-27 figures were $387bn and $191bn, the same ratio). So we agree closely unweighted and discount harder weighted. He confirms target_year and deflation_base_year are both 2019 in his config, which we verified at lines 118 and 128. The gap is not yet explained, and eight candidates are eliminated by measurement (2026-08-28). Not the value raster’s geography: his precomputed value raster under our sufficiency gives 0.4155, essentially ours. Not fill_non_ag — his runner calls run_pollination_sufficiency_300m without it, so both sides take the None default; this had been the prime suspect and is refuted. Not the constants: _RADIUS_METERS 2000.0, _THRESHOLD 0.30 and the _AG_CLASSES/_NAT_CLASSES sets are unchanged since his initial commit. Not the land-cover file: his config/default.yaml resolves lulc_esa_{target_year}.tif at target_year: 2019, the same map we read. Not the grids, all 0.05 degree 3600x7200 and 0.002778 degree 64800x129600. Not the aggregation: pixel-wise gives 0.4208 and an unweighted mean 0.7004, and his 0.4935 lies between them. Not the nodata convention: his valuation writes NaN as -9999, dropping cells we keep as zero, which moves ours only 0.4208 to 0.4291. Since his value raster under our sufficiency still gives 0.4155, his sufficiency raster must differ from ours. The target-year lead is also closed: commit 7f201c4 notes that before it “everything was set up for creating rasters with the target year 2020”, but he states his current figures come from the new code with both years at 2019, and independently ESA 2019 and 2020 differ by only 0.0405 percent of pixels (agricultural cover +0.044 percent), far too little to move a ratio 7 points. Twelve candidates eliminated, none remaining that we can test from outside. Also refuted: the differences do NOT compound — every combination of value-raster choice, per-cell versus density units, and nodata denominator lands between 0.4155 and 0.4291, a spread of 0.014 against a gap of 0.064. Per-cell versus density weighting alone moves 0.4208 to 0.4169, and sufficiency barely correlates with latitude (-0.005), mean 0.577 in every band. fill_non_ag can only push the wrong way: filling non-arable with 0.0 and scaling by agricultural area fraction lowers sufficiency, and ours is already below his. Our 300 m raster was checked directly and is correct — 96.04 percent NaN for non-arable, 1.02 percent genuine zeros (arable with no habitat in range), 2.93 percent positive, so arable totals 3.95 percent, matching the ESA agricultural share exactly, and the 5 km average really is arable-only. Aggregation level does not explain it either: country value times unweighted country-mean sufficiency gives 0.6495, overshooting, while value-weighted gives 0.4203. His 0.4935 is bracketed by our numbers but reproduced by none of them. ⚠⚠ Settled on 2026-08-28 by running HIS repository directly (scripts/pipelines/run_pollination_sufficiency.py --step sufficiency_300m on lulc_esa_2019.tif, his config, our machine): his own code gives $163.43bn, ratio 0.4207, against our port’s $163.46bn and 0.4208. The arable mask is identical cell for cell (1,657,059 defined cells in both on a 1-in-200-row sample) and mean sufficiency is 0.4511 his against 0.4494 ours; 78.4 percent of cells match exactly and the rest is tile-boundary noise that washes out in aggregate, since he tiles in 128 blocks and we use many more. His own sufficiency_5km step, on his own country_m49_cropgrids_grid.tif template, likewise gives 0.4207, matching a hand resample exactly, and all four pairings of the two value rasters with the two sufficiency rasters fall between 0.4155 and 0.4208. So our copy is faithful and the sufficiency chain is not the cause. ⚠ Scope: this covers his steps 1 and 2 only. His valuation_5km, mask_pa and attribution steps have never run here — valuation_5km wants poll_value_global_2019usd.tif and base_data holds only 2023 and 2024, so our own value raster is substituted at that point. The value raster of his we hold is the 2020 / 2024-USD one, not the 2019 raster behind his $385bn. ⚠⚠ RESOLVED on 2026-08-28 by running his full 2019 chain end to end — FAO yield change, Monfreda yield rasters, production, poll_value, then valuation_5km, all his code at his target_year: 2019. It returns $383.68bn unweighted and $189.732bn sufficiency-weighted, a ratio of 0.4945, against the $385bn and $190bn he reports. ⚠⚠ CORRECTED same day: the gap is neither the sufficiency code nor the value raster — it is his summing function. _sum_raster_tiled in run_pollination_sufficiency.py computes cell area once per 4096-row tile from the tile’s midpoint latitude; value_pollination_sufficiency_2019_5km.tif is 3600 rows, so it is ONE tile centred at -0.025 degrees and every cell on Earth is given 30.980 km2. method: How it works, in six steps. 1. InVEST SDR gives, for every pixel, how much soil erodes and how much stays. Which SDR rasters the account actually reads is a question about this run rather than about the method, and it is under run. 2. A threshold picks out what counts as severe erosion, 11 tonnes per hectare per year or 2 for small and low-lying countries. That is SES-11, the author’s baseline, and it is what our run is configured for: THRESH_HIGH 11.0 and THRESH_LOW 2.0, with nothing overriding them. The manuscript’s EPS-5 relaxes the threshold to 5 as a sensitivity analysis rather than an alternative baseline, letting more land in and taking the reported figure from $14.59bn to $29.1bn. 3. For each severe pixel, what share of the soil loss was stopped by the field’s own vegetation (on-farm), and what share by vegetation upslope catching water before it arrives (upstream). 4. The two are combined without counting twice: a field can be protected by both at once, so rather than adding them it asks, per pixel, the chance at least one of them saved it. On-farm protects 10.0 percent of production on average and upstream 10.8, and the combined share is 12.5 rather than 20.8, so the 8.4 point gap is production both mechanisms protect. 5. Losing soil dents a harvest rather than destroying it, so a per-crop yield elasticity turns soil saved into output saved. It is small: median 0.153, range 0.080 to 0.259, so of the 12.5 percent of production on protected land only about 15 percent of that is output genuinely at stake. 6. That output is priced at the FAOSTAT gross production value in constant 2019 USD, what the country’s crops are worth. GEP = shock share times gross production value, an identity holding to 8e-13 across 177 countries, which is a largest absolute disagreement of 4.5 hundred-thousandths of a dollar. ⚠ Two things look like errors and are not. The union in step 4 is per pixel while a country’s share is an average over pixels, so at country level combined is not 1-(1-onfarm)(1-upstream); averaging breaks the formula, which is arithmetic rather than a bug. Money is summed rather than averaged, so the dollars do reconcile exactly: on-farm $10.298bn plus the incremental upstream $3.661bn gives the combined $13.958bn. The formula in one line: soil loss prevented on cropland, on-farm and upslope combined as a union rather than a sum, turned into a crop production shock weighted by each crop’s production and its yield elasticity to erosion, times the country’s crop gross production value.

what a zero means here, and what an NA means: Condition 11’s clause 4 asks that a true zero be 0, missing data be NA, and the entry say which a country got and why. For this service: 0 means the estimated 2019 resource rent was negative and the account does not carry negative service values. 58 of 166 countries: their fishery’s landed value does not cover its costs once subsidy is subtracted, so the resource’s contribution is nil or worse. The rent is known, not missing – Norway -$698m, Vietnam -$697m, Sweden -$492m, Thailand -$415m, Poland -$249m, Cuba -$226m – and the account’s convention maps a negative service to zero. The floor is explicit in the code and pinned by test_negative_prediction_floors_at_zero_and_single_year_gives_nan, so it cannot drift into being an accident. France, Finland, Cuba, Algeria and Fiji publish 0 for this reason and not because their fisheries are unknown. NA means the rent could not be computed. 85 countries: a missing landed value or a missing cost leaves the rent undefined, and compute_econ_rent fills neither. A missing subsidy is the one exception and is treated as none, because a country with no recorded subsidy received none. ⚠ The 17 percent that the floor is worth is recorded below as a question for the account, not as a defect: the number implements a stated choice, the choice is the source’s too, and changing it is a convention decision rather than a correction.
need: ⚠⚠ Two findings from 2026-09-02, both of which change what the number means rather than what it is. 58 of 166 countries have a NEGATIVE estimated 2019 resource rent and are clipped to zero. They sum to -$5,050,794,564, which is 17 percent of the published $29.0bn: carrying them through would give $23.95bn instead. The largest are Norway -$698m, Vietnam -$697m, Sweden -$492m, Thailand -$415m, Poland -$249m, Cuba -$226m – fisheries whose landed value does not cover their costs, which is a real and well-documented result rather than a defect. France, Finland, Cuba, Algeria and Fiji all publish exactly 0 here and none of them has no fishery. ⚠ This is the concrete instance of the issues document’s own paper-level question, “No negative service values (forest fires, disease…)”. And the two halves of fisheries are valued by different methods, so the ratio between them is partly an artifact.
