So “agrees to -0.17 percent” is suggestive, not a verification – our figure is computed from FAO’s public data and our own GTAP share, independently of whatever produced theirs, and landing within $183m of it is evidence the two are the same quantity, not proof either is right. ⚠ 10 is open: no cold start, so the claim that a clone reproduces this rests on paths resolving rather than on a run. ⚠ 9 is open: two asks, neither sent – confirm the FishStatJ export excluded aquatic plants, and say what produced $110.68bn. 15 is met: base_data/global_invest/fisheries is organised by subgroup – commercial/, aquaculture/ – with the reference anchors flat where service_data_dir needs them, and C21 finds no duplicate in it. It found one on 2026-09-02, the Lynch workbook present twice because it is both the subsistence input and a reference anchor; it is one file now and the input path points at the anchor. C21 names 25 duplicates across eight other services, so this condition is newly unmet in most of the account rather than newly satisfied. 5 is met and is unusually strong here, which is worth saying because it is rare in this account: the inputs are FAO’s public release and our own GTAP base data, so this is not a port of somebody’s code checked against its own output. If it is wrong, it is wrong in a way somebody can find. ⚠ It was red until the task existed, deliberately: a figure computed beside the library is not a figure the library produces, and total stayed blank while that was true.
need: ⭐ Updated 2026-10-03, three asks from the delivery: which GTAP aggregation and FishStatJ vintage produced the cleaned CSV, and whether aquatic plants are in (‘all aquaculture species’ suggests yes, yet his China sits at 0.88 of our plants-excluded reading, so something else also moved); whether he adopts the revenue-share correction – his own x0.5 sensitivity points the same way; and the cleaned aquaculture script, which his email says is not yet on GitHub. The earlier state stands otherwise: Nothing external. All four inputs the source names were resolved on 2026-09-02 without asking anyone: aqua_prod_quant.csv and aqua_prod_value.csv are Aquaculture_Quantity.csv and Aquaculture_Value.csv inside FAO’s public Aquaculture_2025.1.0.zip (2.1 MB, and its MEASURE codes Q_tlw and V_USD_1000 are literally the source’s column names); fsh_endowment_gtap.xlsx is computed here from basedata.har as EVFP[NatRes, fsh, r] / EVFP[:, fsh, r]; and iso3_gtap141_mapping.xlsx is the account’s own ee_r264_correspondence.csv, which maps all 250 countries onto the 50 GTAP regions with none left over. None of the four existed anywhere in base_data beforehand – searched the whole tree, not just the fisheries folder.

title: GEP service library: status
text:
Crop Production

subgroup: commercial
module: crop_provision
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes, on the same footing as energy production rather than mining. FAOSTAT publishes the market value of the crop, not the part of it that belongs to nature, so no published figure is being relabelled. What is adopted is the CWoN land rental rate, and it is the entire attribution.
method: FAOSTAT gross production value (element 57, current USD) times the CWoN land rental rate, the share of crop value that accrues to land rather than to labour, capital or inputs. The rate is a per-country decade constant between 0.008 and 0.661, median 0.306 over 179 countries, applied by a backward as-of merge so each year takes the most recent decade that has started. The quantity comes from a CSV, FAOSTAT gross production value. Pairs carrying production and no current-USD value at the base year – FAOSTAT’s USD value stops wherever its own USD producer-price series stops – are filled from the values table the pollination chain stages (its production times that year’s USD producer price, the price falling back country to subregion to region to world), the rental rate applying to filled and read rows alike.
total: $814.3bn
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Two fixes: FAOSTAT still lists countries that no longer exist, the USSR and Yugoslavia among them, so production was being stranded on codes matching no present-day country; those now map to their successor states. The reporting year was also written into the code as a fixed number and now comes from the shared configuration.
grid: No raster. The service works on country tables (it reads only CSV and Excel), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-08-26 by checking every read in the module.
reference: The reference pipeline, cloned, run and reproduced. Its per-country 2019 output is staged in base_data and a test compares against it, where before this the agreement was asserted and nothing looked at it. $623,117,396,403 against $623,117,396,403 across 179 countries, largest per-country relative difference 3.4e-16. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests the port and cannot see an error the reference’s code also makes. Two rows differ by construction and the test collapses them first: FAOSTAT carries “Ethiopia PDR” and “Serbia and Montenegro” beside their successors under one M49 code each, the reference strands them at zero, and this library maps them to the successor.
replicated: The reference arithmetic yes, pinned by a test and published unfilled beside ours as crop_provision_gep_reference. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests our port rather than the science. The published figure departs from it deliberately: the price-gap fill adds value the reference’s source cannot carry.
decided: 2026-10-03, Chiara: fill FAOSTAT’s USD price gaps the way the pollination repo prices crops. One price chain for the account: crop_provision reads fao_values_1993_2024.csv, the values table pollination’s fao_median_prices task stages into base_data (William Sidemo Holm’s chain, which rebuilds USD prices from SLC and World Bank fx where FAOSTAT’s own USD series is discontinued, then values production at that year’s price with the country-to-subregion-to-region-to-world fallback), and adds no price arithmetic of its own. Each filled row says which level priced it in value_source; the fill is base-year only, the published year.
number: $814,321,561,732 across 174 countries, from our own run: $511,522,475,916 read from FAOSTAT and the rest through the price-gap fill, which values 5,233 pairs ($1.128T gross before the rental rate; 1,895 at the country’s own price, 2,708 subregion, 494 region, 136 world). India moves $12.9bn to $103.3bn – its rice, like most of its crops, carries 2019 production and no 2019 USD value – and 22 countries enter from nothing, the Democratic Republic of the Congo ($9.6bn) and Myanmar ($7.5bn) the largest. The 24 countries at exactly zero are small island and city states whose crops carry value but no CWoN rental rate, so nothing can be attributed; whether they should read as NA instead is the deck’s Q3. The fallback statistic is measured, not assumed: holding out each country-item pair with its own 2019 price and predicting it from the subregion’s other members, the median beats the mean value-weighted (|log error| 0.56 against 0.64, upward bias +0.25 against +0.41 in logs – both overprice large producers, the mean more), and 68 percent of the filled dollars ride on the country’s own price with no fallback involved ($206.6bn of $302.8bn post-rate). ⚠ The unfilled figure has been wrong twice and both times the cause was the FAO item list rather than the code. It was $678,413,996,115 until 2026-09-01, which is the reference at its earlier commit: 17 livestock items sat in the crop list, 16 of which our livestock service values too, so $43.6bn was counted twice across the account. Following the reference’s later commit gave $623,117,396,403, which is also what the reference itself produces today and is published beside ours as crop_provision_gep_reference. That figure is still too high, because the list carries three FAOSTAT group totals – Oilcrops Primary, Roots and Tubers Total, Sugar Crops Primary – as well as the individual crops those totals add up. Malaysia came out at 179% of its own crop production; 87 of 156 countries exceeded 100%. Keeping a group total only where no individual item is published leaves 1 of 155 above, median 0.877, and gives the figure above. ⚠ The GEP table registers $692.3bn, which no version of the reference produces.
need: Does the GEP total add crop production and pollination? Crop multiplies production value by the CWoN land rental rate, and pollination values the crop production attributable to wild pollinators, so both attribute part of the same output to nature. And how the CWoN land rental rate was derived. It is the whole of the attribution and moves the total proportionally.
signed off: amber: twelve of the fourteen conditions hold as of 2026-09-01, and 7 and 9 do not. 1, 2 and 3 are met: our code produces the figure, every step is a task in this library, and the figure is from the current code. 4 is met: no raster, so no cell area. 5 and 12 are met as of 2026-09-01, and the reproduction is now a check rather than a claim: the reference was cloned, run, its per-country output staged in base_data, pinned by a test, and the agreement claimed of the cold start rather than a warm directory. Before that the entry asserted agreement while also recording that the reference was not in the repo and nothing pinned it. ⚠ Same lineage still, so it tests the port and cannot see an error the reference makes too. 6 and 8 are met: the three gates pass, and the file set is the agreed four plus tests as of 2026-09-01, when a _quarto.yml that nothing had ever read was removed. ⚠ 7 is open: the GEP table registers $692.3bn, which no version of the reference produces at any commit, either item list, either FAOSTAT vintage, any year from 2015 to 2022, or either candidate base year; and the registry lists this service at base year 2020 against the account’s 2019, worth about $26bn. Both would change the figure. ⚠ 9 is open: neither has been put to the authors. 10 is met: projects/gep_crop_provision_coldstart_20260901_122846, run 2026-09-01, a fresh timestamped directory reusing nothing and seeded from input_template/, every input resolving inside the shared base_data. Reproducing the reference is claimed of that run, not of a warm one: the cold start returns $623,117,396,403 against the staged reference’s $623,117,396,403 over 176 countries to 3.4e-16, its subsistence reference column returns $1,832,260,428.28 against their published panel’s $1,832,260,428.28 over 66 countries to 2.3e-14, and the account’s own subsistence figure is $23,780,485,591. The two tests that check this scan every crop_provision run on the machine rather than one named directory, so a stale warm run cannot stand in for a fresh one – which is how they caught two superseded cold starts from earlier the same day, both since removed. 11 is met: the published table is 250 rows on the account’s list, with the countries the service has no value for recorded as NA rather than absent. 14 is met: H23 finds nothing in this service defined and never used. It found fifteen names across seven services when it was written on 2026-09-01, including pollination’s pixel_area_km2_spherical, the 6371 km sphere the account had already decided against. 13 is met: nothing in the pipeline or its verification reaches into anyone’s checkout. Every input and every reference output is staged in base_data, no path in es_parameters leaves it, and H22 checks that mechanically. The author’s repository could be deleted tomorrow and this would still run, still produce the figure and still verify itself. ## Crop Production
subgroup: subsistence
module: crop_provision
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes
method: Cropland area times the regional share of agricultural area in farms under two hectares (Lowder et al. 2021) times FAOSTAT’s value of agricultural production per hectare times the share of crop production value a household consumes rather than sells (FAO RuLIS national surveys), attributed by the CWoN land rental rate and deflated to the base year by each country’s own CPI. A surveyed country’s missing years are filled from a per-country regression on year, GDP per capita and commercial production; an unsurveyed country is filled from a global regression on cropland area.
total: $23.78bn
code: The reference pipeline ported stage for stage, so the library computes the figure rather than quoting it, and then departs from it in three places, each deliberate and each reported separately. FAOSTAT reports cropland in thousands of hectares against an intensity per single hectare and the Lowder share is a percentage, so each is read as its source labels it. Countries no survey reached take an imputed own-consumption share rather than an own-consumption level predicted from cropland area, so three of the four factors behind such a country are still its own. And the delivered table is put on the account’s country list by the house collapse. The reference’s own arithmetic runs through the identical stages in the same task and is published beside ours, which is what lets a reader check the port instead of taking it on trust.
grid: No raster. The component works on country tables (it reads only CSV), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-09-01 by checking every read in the task.
reference: The reference panel, reproduced. Running its arithmetic through our port gives $1,832,260,428.28 against its published $1,832,260,428.28 across 66 countries, largest per-country relative difference 2.3e-14. Each stage was checked separately on the way: 73 own-consumption rows to 1.3e-16, 63 interpolated rows to 1.9e-16, and the extrapolation choosing the same covariate and the same 49 observed / 1,339 predicted / 222 missing split. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests the port and cannot see an error the reference’s code also makes; where we found one, we publish our own arithmetic rather than theirs.
replicated: Yes, exactly, and the reproduction is published as its own column rather than asserted. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests our port rather than the science.
decided: The account’s figure is ours, not the reproduction, and on three counts. The units: FAOSTAT’s cropland is in thousands of hectares against an intensity per single hectare and the Lowder share is a percentage, so reading each as labelled is the method done correctly rather than a variant of it. And the imputation: what the survey measures is a share, a ratio of two quantities that move together and travel between countries, where the reference predicts the level from cropland area – which is the largest term in the formula that produced the level it is fitted to, so the fit is close to circular and the fitted rows outnumber the observed ones twenty-seven to one. Publishing either as the account’s number once we knew would have been repeating a mistake with our name on it. And the currency: the account reports 2019 US dollars and reads FAOSTAT current-year values as already being that, which holds for the Value of Production table but not for the production intensity, which FAOSTAT publishes only in international dollars. There is no current-US$ version of that element to read instead, so the estimate is converted – by the factor FAOSTAT’s own two publications of the same agricultural output imply, not an external table. It moves the figure 4.6%, from $24,930,567,445 to $23,780,485,591, and 48 of the 66 countries carry their own factor with the rest on a regional median.
number: $23,780,485,591 across 66 countries, in 2019 US dollars, and 72.3% of it rests on a country’s own observed survey rather than an imputed share. Two further figures are published beside it so each departure from the reference is separable: $18,322,604,283 is the reference’s own extrapolation with only the units corrected, and $1,832,260,428 is its arithmetic entirely, which reproduces its published panel. ⚠ The share imputation is not what drives the total: requiring anything from one to five surveys before a regional median is used, or forcing every unsurveyed country onto the global median, moves it only about 2%.
need: Three findings to put to the authors, none of which our figure now depends on: the factor of ten above; the delivered file, which joins the panel against the correspondence on a Natural Earth name column and carries 16 of its own 66 valued countries at $398,356,097; and eleven countries whose observed survey values leave the panel at the interpolation step, Ethiopia among them, because a row missing GDP per capita or commercial production is dropped and its observation goes with it. Separately, and for the account rather than the authors: whether subsistence is added to commercial at all, given RuLIS reports own consumption as a share of crop production value that FAOSTAT’s production figures already include. ⚠⚠ And the scope, which is the largest thing understating this figure. The reference restricts its panel to the World Bank low and lower-middle income classes, so 56 upper-middle-income countries are excluded by construction – China, Indonesia, Brazil, Thailand, Egypt, Mexico, South Africa. China matters most: Lowder gives East Asia and Pacific a 64.3% smallholder area share, the highest of any region. Our own method needs no survey to reach them, because three of its four factors are structural, so the cost of the restriction is measurable: adding upper-middle income takes 2019 from $24.93bn over 66 countries to $55.96bn over 109, and every income class gives $58.97bn over 154. We keep the restriction for now because changing the scope and the method at once would leave neither legible, but it is the reason the figure reads low and it is a question for the account rather than a defect.
signed off: amber: thirteen of the fourteen conditions hold as of 2026-09-01, and 9 does not. 1, 2 and 3 are met: our code produces the figure, every step from the eleven staged inputs to the published number is a task in this library and it reads nothing from the reference repository, and the figure is from the current code. 4 is met: no raster, so no cell area. 5 and 12 are met, and the check is real rather than nominal: the port was verified stage by stage against the reference’s own committed intermediates rather than only on the final total, their panel is staged in base_data, a test compares against it on every run present, and the agreement is claimed of the cold start. 6 and 8 are met: the three gates pass and it adds no file to the service. 7 is met as of 2026-09-01: it was open while the account’s figure was the reference’s arithmetic, because whether we published $1.83bn or $18.32bn changed the number; the account now publishes ours and the reference’s beside it, so nothing outstanding moves the figure. Whether subsistence is added to commercial remains open but is for the account to decide and does not change what the code computes. ⚠ 9 is open: the three findings have not been put to the authors, and the condition counts an unasked question as open. 10 is met: projects/gep_crop_provision_coldstart_20260901_122846, run 2026-09-01, a fresh timestamped directory reusing nothing and seeded from input_template/, every input resolving inside the shared base_data. Reproducing the reference is claimed of that run, not of a warm one: the cold start returns $623,117,396,403 against the staged reference’s $623,117,396,403 over 176 countries to 3.4e-16, its subsistence reference column returns $1,832,260,428.28 against their published panel’s $1,832,260,428.28 over 66 countries to 2.3e-14, and the account’s own subsistence figure is $23,780,485,591. The two tests that check this scan every crop_provision run on the machine rather than one named directory, so a stale warm run cannot stand in for a fresh one – which is how they caught two superseded cold starts from earlier the same day, both since removed. 11 is met: 250 rows on the account’s list, the 184 countries no estimate reached recorded as NA rather than absent. 14 is met: H23 finds nothing in this service defined and never used. It found fifteen names across seven services when it was written on 2026-09-01, including pollination’s pixel_area_km2_spherical, the 6371 km sphere the account had already decided against. 13 is met: nothing in the pipeline or its verification reaches into anyone’s checkout. Every input and every reference output is staged in base_data, no path in es_parameters leaves it, and H22 checks that mechanically. The author’s repository could be deleted tomorrow and this would still run, still produce the figure and still verify itself. ⚠ The second half of 13 is why the published figure is not the reproduction: our code departs from theirs on the units and on the imputation, and the entry says why in decided. ## Livestock Production
subgroup: commercial
module: livestock_provision
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes, and more so on one of the two value columns than the other. The service writes two, because two attributions of the same FAOSTAT gross production are on the table and the account has not chosen between them. livestock_provision_gep applies the CWoN land rental rate and gives $519bn; livestock_provision_gep_feed_share applies the share of animal intake that ecosystems grew and gives $1.37T. Neither FAOSTAT figure is a published ecosystem value, so nothing is relabelled. The rental-rate column adopts CWoN’s attribution whole, while the feed-share column derives its own, computing each country’s intake share from the GLEAM 3 dashboard rather than taking a published share.
method: FAOSTAT gross production value (element 57, current USD) over 65 livestock products, times an attribution factor: either the CWoN land rental rate or the GLEAM share of feed intake that ecosystems provided. The quantity comes from a CSV, FAOSTAT gross production value over 65 products.
total: $246bn on the rental rate. $653bn on the feed share. ⚠ It was $519bn until 2026-09-01, when the same group-total double count found in crop production was found here: the FAO item list carried “Livestock”, the total FAOSTAT computes by adding every animal product, alongside those products themselves. It put 106 of 152 countries above 100% of their own livestock output, median 1.397. Keeping the group total only where no individual product is published leaves a median of 0.985 and 15 countries above, none by more than 45%, and those carry items FAOSTAT files outside “Livestock” – beeswax, honey, silk cocoons. The feed-share attribution is written too and moves with it, by the same proportion.
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Plus a units fix. The feed share is now wired through the task layer, so a run writes the feed-share value beside the rental-rate one. Its method page was a copy of the crop provision text, describing crop items throughout; it has been rewritten for this service.
grid: No raster. The service works on country tables (it reads only CSV and Excel), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-08-26 by checking every read in the module.
reference: No reference output exists to obtain: Urgendalai/gep_livestock_provision commits two scripts with hardcoded D:/Netcapteems/ paths and no data. What it does commit is the feed-share formula, and that reproduces exactly – our feed_share against lambda.py recomputed from the same staged GLEAM table, 171 countries, largest difference 1.1e-16, pinned by a test. ⚠ Nothing checks the valuation half. ⚠ And the reference script reads FAOSTAT element 152, gross production value in constant 2014-2016 international dollars, where this service reads element 57, current US dollars. That is a different measure in a different currency, so the two would not agree even if an output existed.
replicated: The feed-share factor, exactly, and pinned. The valuation has nothing to match, because the reference commits no output.
decided: -
number: Values livestock output and attributes the part of it nature provided. The 65-product FAO list gives $2.29T of gross production; the two attribution factors give very different answers from it: the CWoN land rental rate gives $519bn over 178 countries, the GLEAM feed share gives $1.37T over 171, a factor of 2.6. Provisional until that choice is made. The feed share comes from GLEAM 3 intake harvested from FAO’s public dashboard for 231 countries, 205 matching a country in the account, giving a real share rather than a bound (median 0.73; Mongolia 0.998, India 0.911, Brazil 0.847, France 0.651, United States 0.567, China 0.513).
need: Which factor the account attributes livestock value with. The code computes both, and they differ by 2.6 times, $519bn on the CWoN land rental rate against $1.37T on the GLEAM feed share. The rental rate is the crop method’s factor. Also the compiled GLEAM extract (gleam3_dmi.xlsx) to validate our harvest against, the confirmation of which FAO products count as livestock, and one per-country output. And how the CWoN land rental rate was derived. It is the whole of the attribution and moves the total proportionally. ⚠ Which attribution is the GEP table using? It registers $1.488T, and no configuration we can run produces it: not either item list, either FAOSTAT vintage, with or without the group total, on either attribution. The nearest we have ever produced is $1,374,349,438,511, our own feed-share figure before 2026-09-01, which is 7.7% below it and rested on the double-counted gross, so reproducing it would not have been good news. But $1.488T is a feed-share-scale number rather than a rental-rate one, which suggests the table and this entry are reporting different attributions. That has to be settled before either figure is quoted.
signed off: amber: twelve of the fourteen conditions hold as of 2026-09-01, and 7 and 9 do not. 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 11 are met: our code produces both figures, every step is a task here, they are from the current code, there is no raster so no cell area, the three gates pass, the file set is the agreed one, and the published table is 250 rows with NA where no value exists. 5 and 12 are met: the feed-share factor reproduces lambda.py to 1.1e-16 across 171 countries and a test recomputes it; what the reproduction cannot test is stated, namely the valuation, for which no reference output exists. 10 is met: projects/gep_livestock_provision_coldstart_20260901_113704, run 2026-09-01, a fresh timestamped directory reusing nothing, returning $245,894,965,799 and $653,351,673,530 – identical to the warm run – with all six input references resolving inside the shared base_data. 13 is met: no path leaves base_data and nothing reads the reference repository, so it could be deleted tomorrow. ⚠ 7 is open and it is the one that matters: the account has not chosen between the rental rate and the feed share, and they differ by 2.7 times. 14 is met: H23 finds nothing in this service defined and never used. ⚠ 9 is open: three questions are unasked – which attribution the account wants, where the GEP table’s $1.488T comes from, and whether the group-total rule applied here matches what the authors intended. ## Coastal Protection
subgroup: -
module: coastal_protection
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: the mangrove half yes, the coral half no. That file holds a value per country and nothing underneath it.
method: Mangroves: protected hectares times value per hectare. Corals: a published annual benefit per country, carried to the base year by the shared US CPI factor. The quantity comes from CSVs, the CWoN mangrove workbook and the coral benefit table.
total: $36.28bn. Currency harmonized 2026-10-03: the coral half now rides the account’s one CPI series (utilities.usd_deflation_factor, 2011→2019 = 1.136623) instead of each country’s compounded World Bank GDP deflator — the coral values are USD, not local currency, so per-country local inflation was the wrong instrument.
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The mangrove value is run: we multiply protected area by value per hectare.
grid: No raster. The service works on country tables (it reads only CSV and Excel), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-08-26 by checking every read in the module.
reference: The published table for mangroves ($30.4bn), recomputed from hectares times value per hectare. Corals are carried through with no quantity or price behind them, so nothing there can be recomputed or checked.
replicated: Mangroves yes, recomputed from the published table. Corals are carried across rather than recomputed, so they are not a check on anything.
decided: -
number: $36.28bn ($36,282,030,656.66), and the total is the sum of them, of which 84 percent is ours and 16 percent is read through. Mangroves are ours, $30.4bn: hectares times value per hectare, matching the published table, unchanged to the cent by the currency harmonization. Corals are not, and the reason is what the file holds rather than whether we found any code. The mangrove table carries hectares and value per hectare beside its total, so the total can be recomputed from them and checked. The coral file has three columns: country, value, year. There is no quantity and no price, so there is nothing to recompute from. All we do is carry its $5.17bn at 2011 forward to 2019 with the shared US CPI factor, making it $5.88bn. The nine countries the World Bank deflator table lacked — which came out unvalued — now carry their value like everyone else, $85.7M in all, Taiwan the largest at $78.8M: the scalar needs no per-country coverage. Valued countries 97 → 106.
need: Whether code exists behind the coral-reef benefit table that we should be running.
examined for the issues table (2026-09-07): ⭐ The all-services sheet’s $34.03bn is ours minus 26 countries. Its 72 rows are exactly the countries with a coral-file row, and each matches our mangrove-plus-coral total (34 to the cent, residual $2,598 over the whole $34bn). The entire $2.69bn gap is the mangrove-only countries the column drops: a country with mangrove value and no coral row vanishes — Bangladesh $1.12bn, Suriname $0.55bn, Japan $0.36bn, New Zealand $0.19bn, and 22 smaller, $2,691,060,035 in all. The identity $36.72bn = $34.03bn + $2.69bn holds to the residual. A join artifact on the sheet’s side, not a method disagreement; the fix is one line — keep the mangrove value where the coral table has no row. ⚠ The to-the-cent agreement in this block was measured under the per-country WB deflator the sheet also used; since the 2026-10-03 CPI harmonization our coral values differ from the sheet’s by construction. Country coverage on our side is now 106 countries (the account total above), 97 under the old method.
signed off: amber: examined, and at least one of the sixteen conditions is not yet verified. ⚠ 10 is unmet here (no longer everywhere: erosion closed it on 2026-09-03, reproducing its published total to $11 in $18.24bn from an empty project directory). ⚠ 11 is unverified: the base year is 2019 across every service, but the country list, the true-zero-against-missing rule and the shared parameters have not been checked service by service 11 is met as of 2026-09-01: the published table is 250 rows on the account’s list, with the countries the service has no value for recorded as NA rather than absent. It carried 225 rows before, and the total is unchanged. ## Mining Production
subgroup: -
module: extractive_materials_provision
category: rescales a published rate
in the library: yes

How the number is built, in four steps.

What the old number asked. “What is all the output of farms that use water worth?” That is $1.06T – the value of irrigated farming: the land, the seed, the labour, the machinery, and the water. Not the water.
What the new number asks. “How much more does a hectare earn BECAUSE it is irrigated?” The premium is formed PER COUNTRY – that country’s irrigated value added over its irrigated area, less its rainfed value added over its rainfed area – and the median country premium at 2019 is $672 a hectare. ⚠ It is NOT $2,914 minus $1,793: those are the medians of the two per-hectare figures, and the difference of two medians is not the median of the differences.
Scale it up. Each country’s premium times its own irrigated area, summed over 173 countries and 342,393,869 hectares, is $701.4bn at the account’s 2019 year – an area-weighted average premium of $2,049 a hectare, well above the median because the large irrigators are also the high-premium ones. Rainfed land’s earnings are excluded on purpose: soil, climate and terrain would earn them with or without irrigation. ⭐ This is the step that fixes the old error. ⚠⚠ A handful of countries dominate it – on the latest-year variant India and China alone are 68% – so a total this concentrated stands or falls on those few, and they are where to check first. ⚠ Year matters more than expected: the same calculation on each country’s LATEST available year, median 2022, gives $886.0bn and $294.2bn. That is a different year’s answer, not a better one, and the account’s year is 2019.
Take nature’s share of it. The farmer still supplies labour and machinery. GTAP puts 33.2% of crop value added with the natural resource. Per country, clipped at zero – an account cannot report negative provisioning – the premium times 0.332 gives $248.0bn over 169 countries ($232.9bn without the clipping, a 6% difference).

⚠ The one caveat, carried in need: that 33.2% is land AND water together, because no dataset endows water separately. Step 3 is solidly water; step 4 is joint. The premium fixed the denominator, which was the actual bug, and the share is the remaining approximation.

Livestock takes FAOSTAT gross production, $2.29T, and attributes the part nature provided by one of two routes: CWoN’s land rental rate, or GLEAM’s share of feed intake that ecosystems provided (median 0.73; Mongolia 0.998, Brazil 0.847, United States 0.567). ⭐⭐ BUILT 2026-09-03, in the irrigation shape: the QUANTITY is measured and published, the price is an explicit parameter with no default. The method, in plain steps:

What is valued: nature delivering usable raw water – rivers, lakes and aquifers refilled by rain – to cities and industry. Unlike irrigation, nothing needs isolating: the product IS the water, so the quantity is the cubic metres taken.
The quantity: 2019 withdrawal from AQUASTAT (4251 municipal + 4252 industrial), 520.9 + 625.0 = 1,145.9 km3 over 183 countries; ⚠ minus desalinated production (4264, 23.3 km3), because a desalination plant manufactures water rather than a river providing it – and in Kuwait, Qatar and the Maldives desal EXCEEDS domestic withdrawal, so their ecosystem-provided domestic water is zero, floored rather than negative. What remains: 1,122.6 km3, published as domestic_withdrawal.csv.
The price: what a cubic metre of RAW water is worth – an abstraction charge or resource fee, NOT the water bill, which mostly pays for pipes and treatment. Nobody publishes a global table, so the price is IMPLIED BY IRRIGATION: the irrigation GEP over the agricultural withdrawal that produced it, $248.0bn / 2,911.7 km3 = $0.0852 per m3 – what a cubic metre earns in a field, which is what a city would have had to outbid. Squarely inside the range real abstraction charges occupy. An explicit water_use_raw_water_price_usd_per_m3 in es_parameters overrides it.
GEP = quantity x price: 1,122.6 km3 x $0.0852 = $95.6bn over 183 countries – against the $35.30T the old figure carried, which is the size of the category error. ⚠ Two exclusions named rather than modelled: water reclaimed from treated wastewater would re-price a cubic metre the ecosystem already provided at its first abstraction, and fossil groundwater is stock depletion rather than a renewable flow.

CWoN has no water rent; GTAP’s water-utilities sector wtr is folded into ser in the s26 aggregation we hold, so not even the delivered-water ceiling can be read from it. Component by component: IRRIGATION’S lambda is the 0.332 itself, the natural-resource share of crop value added applied to the premium; the open question about it is quality, not existence – it is land and water jointly, so it overstates water alone. DOMESTIC needs none, because a lambda’s job is to carve nature’s share out of a value that mixes nature with labour and capital, and domestic starts from the raw resource itself: cubic metres the ecosystem provided, desalination removed, with no human input inside that base to carve out. Its price is derived from the already-shared irrigation figure, so nature’s share arrives through the price – a lambda on top would discount twice. So $232.9bn is the natural-capital rent of what irrigation adds, not water’s rent alone, and it is an upper bound on the latter. If a joint figure is acceptable, this row is done and the share goes in es_parameters. If water must be separated, the thing to look for is a water analogue of GLEAM’s feed share – a MEASURED share of crop output attributable to irrigation water – and not a better land rent, because every land rent has this same problem. ⚠ Livestock faces the identical choice and publishes both answers rather than picking; that is the convention here, and water follows it. ⚠ Two smaller checks before the figure is used: the 45 countries of 173 whose premium comes out negative, all of them ones whose irrigated share of AREA exceeds their irrigated share of GVA; and whether the factor of 1000 in the old agriculture component was a units conversion. ⚠⚠ The irrigation component has the same defect, and the cleaner test shows it. Against FAO’s own gross production value for the same 86 countries, water_use_irrigation_gep is 38% of the entire gross output of their crops ($801,394,672,197 against $2,092,064,952,000), median 12% per country, and it exceeds all crop output in 7 of them – Oman 2.76x, Suriname 1.99x, Egypt 1.71x, Mozambique 1.68x, Bahrain 1.28x, Bangladesh 1.15x. Water is an INPUT to growing the crop; its value cannot be a third of the crop’s whole gross output and cannot exceed it at all. ⭐⭐ What the two figures actually ARE, exactly, from FAO’s own definition. CWUE is GVA_agriculture x (1 - rainfed share) / agricultural withdrawal, so multiplying it back by the withdrawal returns the gross value added of irrigated agriculture. The industrial and services indicators are GVA over withdrawal for their sectors, so the same holds. water_use_irrigation_gep is irrigated agriculture’s value added; water_use_domestic_gep is industry’s plus services’. That is why the first lands at 0.383 of crop gross output – value added over gross output in agriculture is typically 0.4 to 0.6. It behaves like value added because it is value added. (The seven countries above 1.0 are not a contradiction: FAO’s crop GPV excludes livestock where agricultural GVA includes it, so the comparator understates the denominator in livestock-heavy countries.) ⭐⭐ So these are DENOMINATORS, not answers, and the model needs replacing rather than adjusting. This is the same shape as aquaculture and forestry: a lambda is a share OF something, and the something here is sectoral value added. The account needs water’s share of it. Nobody publishes that – GTAP has no water endowment, and CWoN has no general water rent – so it has to be estimated or sourced, and that is the piece of work, not a coefficient to look up. For scale, at 2 / 5 / 10 / 15 percent the irrigation figure becomes $21.3bn / $53.1bn / $106.3bn / $159.4bn, against hydropower’s $146.1bn, which is the account’s other water number and the right order of magnitude to land near. ⭐⭐ The quantity that is water is the IRRIGATION PREMIUM, and naming it is what makes this buildable. A rent is what is left of value added after labour and capital are paid, and in crop agriculture that residual is attributed to LAND. Rainfed cropland earns it too – soil, climate, terrain, location. So applying a land rent share to irrigated value added credits water with things water did not do, and it would double-count the moment the account ever prices agricultural land as its own service. What irrigation adds is the difference: rent(irrigated hectare) - rent(rainfed hectare), times irrigated area. Two sources measure the land rent and agree, which is worth having but is NOT the answer. Among Congo pixels with a positive net return: FML 20 on ESA 50 is 63.3 percent kept, FML 20 on ESA 30 is 72.2, FML 20 on ESA 11 is 22.2, and FML 11 on ESA 50 – 6.75 million pixels, the largest pair – is 1.8 percent, so about 122,000 pixels are kept and 6.6 million dropped from an identical class combination. 20.3 percent of pixels sit in pairs that are neither mostly kept nor mostly dropped. how CWoN and FAOSTAT combine, read from CWoN’s own do-file: They are not two sources to reconcile. forest_timber_depletion.do imports for_faostat_forestry_production_trade.csv – CWoN’s own 254 MB FAOSTAT forestry extract – builds revenue from it, and then applies a rental ratio: tot_rev = FAOSTAT roundwood production x price; ratio = a country-specific adjustment where one exists, otherwise a regional default: AFR 0.41, EAP 0.26, ECA 0.26, EU 0.17, LAC 0.24, MNA 0.22, NA 0.11, SA 0.10; and tot_rent = tot_rev x ratio. ⚠ Which is the same shape as ours. the FAOSTAT bound, published as a third column 2026-09-02: timber_roundwood_gross_value is each country’s roundwood production priced at its own industrial-roundwood export unit value, and the world value where FAOSTAT reports none. It is a bound, not a third estimate: a land factor share is a fraction of the gross value of the wood it comes from, so a country whose timber GEP exceeds its own gross roundwood value is saying something impossible. Pricing each country by its own export value matters and was the second attempt. At one world price ($111/m3) the bound flagged six countries per method, most of them tropical hardwood exporters whose timber is several times that – the exceedances were a price error the bound had manufactured. At own prices, which run $24 to $1,193/m3, it flags four for the spatial estimate (KGZ, MUS, NCL, SYR) and three for CWoN (BLR, MYS, SYC), and all but one sit at 1.0 to 1.5x, which is the noise of using an export unit value as a domestic price. ⚠⚠ The exception is Malaysia, and it is CWoN’s. CWoN puts Malaysia’s forest rent at $6,302,838,837 against a gross roundwood value of $2,461,578,578 at Malaysia’s own export price – 2.6x. A rent cannot be 2.6 times the gross value of the wood, and Malaysia is CWoN’s fourth largest country. ⚠ Stated precisely, because the ratio explains part of it and not the gap: FAOSTAT gives Malaysia 17,208,164 m3 of roundwood and an export unit value of $143/m3 on its own 2019 exports. At CWoN’s EAP regional ratio of 0.26, a rent of $6.30bn implies revenue of $24.2bn and therefore a price of about $1,409/m3 – roughly ten times Malaysia’s own export price. No plausible ratio removes the gap: a smaller ratio implies a higher price still. So the question is not the rental share but the price CWoN puts on Malaysian roundwood, and it is a question for CWoN rather than a demonstrated error.

decided: ⚠⚠ The units question is settled as of 2026-09-02, and summing flat is correct. It could not be settled from inside the pipeline – the raster carries no unit metadata and the committed output was produced by summing the same raster the same way – so it was settled against the market, from FAOSTAT’s own bulk release, now staged and pinned by a test. World industrial roundwood production in 2019 was 1,985,026,611 m3, and the world export unit value was $111.01/m3, so the gross value of all industrial roundwood produced on earth was about $220.4bn. The pipeline’s flat sum of $88.74bn is 40.3 percent of that – high for a land factor share but possible. Reading the raster as dollars per hectare gives $708.47bn, which is 321.5 percent of gross. A land share cannot exceed the gross value it is a share of, so the per-hectare reading is not merely implausible, it is impossible, and the flat sum is the only reading the roundwood market supports. ⚠ Which also means condition 11’s clause 3 does not bite here: no density is being converted to a total, so no cell area is needed and the absence of area weighting is correct rather than an omission.
