That matters because the account adds the services together, so the share attributable to nature should mean the same thing across them. ⚠ Switching is not a configuration change: no CWoN timber rent is staged anywhere in base_data. The CWoN files we hold cover crop, livestock, fisheries, renewable energy, extractive energy and non-wood forest products, and ntfp/cwon_nwfp_value_per_ha.csv is non-wood, a different quantity. CWoN 2024 does carry timber, as a land asset category beside agricultural land, forest recreation, non-wood forest products and forest water services, so the rent exists and the gap is that we do not hold the file. The two approaches are also closer than the source difference suggests: SNA and SEEA-CF count forest timber as an asset only where it can be logged commercially at a profit, which is the same restriction as the missing forest-management mask.
signed off: amber as of 2026-09-02, and two conditions are open: 9, the ask, and 11. 1 is met on the decision that the value raster is an input, which condition 2 allows explicitly. Our code produces the country figure from it, and produces the CWoN and FAOSTAT columns beside it. 10 is met: projects/gep_timber_provision_coldstart_20260902_160627. 12 is met: the committed anchor is staged and test_every_timber_run_reproduces_the_committed_anchor compares what every run wrote against it. 4 is met, and was the hard one: the grid is the house 10-arc-second WGS84 pyramid, identical to ha_per_cell_10sec.tif, and the units question that made cell area unanswerable is settled against FAOSTAT. 15 is met: C21 finds no duplicate here. ⚠ 11 is unmet, and the input forecloses it. The published table has 84 exact zeros and no NAs, and the zeros cannot be told apart: the delivered raster writes 0 for not managed, for net return at or below zero, and its nodata is 0 as well. Clause 4 asks that a true zero and missing data be distinguishable, and by the time the file reaches us they are the same number. This is now a limitation of an accepted input rather than a gap in our code, and it cannot be closed without a raster that carries a real nodata value. ⚠ 9 is open: which multiplier the account adopts, the GTAP land factor share or the CWoN rental ratio, with the Malaysia check as evidence against the second. ## Floods
subgroup: -
module: flood
category: process model run here
in the library: yes
run: Four of its six tasks, across three project directories. ⚠ An earlier version of this entry said two, which was wrong: it read one project directory and generalised, when gep_flood_flow, gep_flood_valuation and gep_flood_gep each hold a different task. task_compute_service_flow, task_compute_flood_damages, task_compute_flood_gep and task_generate_maps_and_figures have all run here. The two that have not are task_prepare_flood_inputs and task_build_sda – which are exactly the two the author’s RUN.md tells a reader to skip by copying in the staged Sections B and C, because rebuilding them turns a 3-hour run into an 11-hour one. So the unrun pair is the pair his own instructions say not to run, not a gap nobody noticed. ⚠ Neither has ever executed from a fresh project seeded from the template: two cold starts on 2026-09-01 both died in task_prepare_flood_inputs on a blank parameter.
ours: the damage yes; the ecosystem share not fully. ⚠⚠ The counterfactual amplification rasters are staged rather than recomputed: _open_amp reads them and, when they are absent, names counterfactual/build_amplification_rasters.py — a script that is not in this repository. The builder exists only in the author’s copy on MSI, as code/global_invest/flood/counterfactual/build_amplification_routed.py. Until it is folded in, our GEP rests on 37 staged layers (about 100 GB) that our code can read and not rebuild, which is the same standing as erosion reading his USLE rasters. ⚠⚠ The whole tree ran here on 2026-08-30 and 2026-08-31 (MSI jobs 17529966 and 17589055), so flood is no longer among the services we hold and have not run, where stormwater and air filtration still sit. The MSI setup that needed doing is done: the run writes to /projects/standard/jajohns/shared/gep_flood with its machine-specific inputs in that project’s input/. ⚠ gep_calculation still reads his per-country export as an interim, so the account carries his $11.40bn rather than one we derived; 17589055 is the first run that could replace it.
method: Flood depth by return period, through JRC depth-damage curves, times asset value per pixel, integrated into an expected annual damage. Five lettered sections, one task each.


A, inputs. Download the JRC depth rasters (metres of standing water at each pixel for the 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500-year floods) and warp them onto the LULC reference grid, so no later step re-warps. Build the LULC-to-SDA mapping.
B, SDA. Delineate the service-demanding areas, the assets exposed to flooding. A pixel qualifies when standing water exceeds flood_depth_threshold_m, 0.1 m, AND its ESA class is one the mapping counts: 190 built-up, 10/11/12/20/30/40 cropland, 130 pasture. Each country is windowed out of the global grid, and flood_all_touched is false, so a border pixel belongs to the country covering its centre, the same centre rule erosion uses. This is the expensive section: the grid is 112,582 x 74,596, about 8.4 billion pixels, and every country is cut from it once per return period, so 250 x 6 = 1,500 passes write 3,000 rasters.
C, service flow. Reproject the precomputed upstream SPA ratio onto each SDA grid and keep it where there is demand, flow = where(sda_mask, spa_ratio, 0). ⚠ The service-providing area is NOT delineated here. From the author’s appendix it is land whose cover retains rainfall that would otherwise run off, curve-number potential retention thresholded to a binary mask, and the ratio is the share of each demanding cell’s upstream catchment that is service-providing. That is why the file we read is continuous between 0 and 1, mean 0.22, while the mask behind it is binary. Built per continent, mosaicked by mosaic_counterfactual.py. ⚠ The appendix is explicit that this supports no marginal statement: the SPA covers 48 to 77 percent of drained land by continent, and the threshold producing that is a statistical convention rather than a physical criterion.
D, valuation, in four substeps. 4A converts the canonical JRC EUR2010 table into USD2019 curves. 4B computes damage per pixel per return period. There is no asset-value raster, and this is where the money enters: jrc_max_damage_values_long_with_iso3.csv gives a maximum damage in EUR per m2 for each country crossed with land type, what a square metre is worth when the water destroys it outright, and the JRC curves give a fraction between 0 and 1 per region, land type and depth. damage_per_m2 = max_damage_eur_m2 * fraction, so the per-pixel value is per-country, per-land-type EUR/m2 scaled by how deep the water is, never a mapped asset stock. Below 0.1 m a pixel is not flooded; the curves run to flood_depthbin_max, 6.0 m. 4C integrates across return periods into an expected annual damage per country. 4D consolidates the per-country files into the global table.
E, maps. The figures.
The GEP is produced by none of these: it is ead_bare - ead_current, the difference between damage in a counterfactual degraded world and damage today, computed by task_compute_flood_gep in a separate tree. ⚠ The source scripts numbered the valuation section 4 with no steps 1 to 3, and its outputs used to carry step4x names; they are named for what they hold now, with the correspondence to his scripts in flood/reference/output_provenance.csv.


total: $112.78bn
which number is which: Five figures appear in this entry and they are five different quantities, so read this first. $112.78bn is ours: expected annual flood damage that occurs, recomputed here, and it is what the total row means. $110.59bn is the source pipeline’s own summary of that same quantity, which is why reproducing it settles the port. $887.828bn is undefended expected annual damage, a larger quantity because it is before flood protection, and it is the figure the author publishes and the one our runs are checked against. $11.40bn is the GEP, the damage ecosystems prevent, ead_bare - ead_current, and it is the only one of the five the account carries; it is still his figure rather than one we derived. $17.601bn is tonight’s superseded run, kept only because it is how the damage-table defect was found. ⚠ The first three are damage, the fourth is the service, and an entry that lists them without saying so invites someone to compare two of them.
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Every step of the flood calculation was rewritten as a function.
grid: Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) at 537.23 m, which is neither the shared pyramid nor equal-area. The damage pass used to give every cell one constant 288,615 m2, the equator value, while true ground area falls as cos squared of latitude to 14.43 ha at 45 degrees and 1.93 ha at 75; weighting by country latitude moves the total about -28 percent. Fixed in code on 2026-08-26 (6dadedf): each row’s latitude is transformed to WGS84 and the cell area computed from it, so a cell now carries its own ground area. ⚠⚠ Corrected 2026-09-02, and the correction runs the other way: the published numbers do NOT carry the equator constant, and this entry said they did. The author’s own flood_tasks.py carries VAL_LATITUDE_CORRECT_AREA = True at line 1124, reads it from p.flood_latitude_correct_area, and applies mercator_area_scale in the same damage-pass block ours does – ours is his code with that module constant made a parameter. So both sides scale by cos squared of latitude and the outputs on both sides are corrected. This was found by asking why our run agrees with his committed table to the cent at high latitude, where the correction is 2x at 45 degrees, 4x at 60 and 8.55x at 70: Sweden, Norway, Finland, Russia and Canada all match to $0.00, which is impossible if one side corrects and the other does not. The agreement is the evidence the correction is on, not evidence it is missing. What 6dadedf did on 2026-08-26 was restore parity with him after the fold-in, not diverge from him. The SDA layer is built from ESA-CCI, natively EPSG:4326 at 0.002777778, which IS the pyramid. ⚠ Corrected 2026-08-31: Section A does not reproject it out. flood_lulc_path reads lulc_esa_2019_int_reproj.tif, EPSG:3857 at 537.23 m, a copy reprojected before it was staged, and Section A warps the JRC depth rasters ONTO that grid. So the pyramid is left upstream of this repository, in one input, and everything downstream inherits it because the LULC file defines the reference grid.
reference: The author’s own committed table, flood_gep_for_merge_v2_2024hazard.csv, the one he names as the file to join against the other services. Staged in base_data with his full 21-column account and both of our run’s variants, and pinned by a test as of 2026-09-01. It agrees to the cent, country by country: 250 of 250 join, largest absolute per-country difference $0.000000, totals $11,403,596,548.37 against his $11,403,596,548.35. ⚠ One country differs and the test names it rather than hiding it in a tolerance: Iceland is NaN in his table and 2.1 cents in ours, which is the whole of the 162-against-163 positive-country count. ⚠⚠ Same lineage: the module is his pipeline with our path handling and ProjectFlow wiring, so this agreement was close to guaranteed. It is a build test – it catches our refactor breaking his arithmetic and says nothing about whether the arithmetic is right.
replicated: Yes, and now on the number that matters rather than only its input. Our run gives $11,403,596,548 against his published $11.40bn, 0.032%. ⚠ Same lineage: the module is his pipeline with our path handling and ProjectFlow wiring, so reproducing him was close to guaranteed and this is a build test rather than an independent replication. Both his delivered variant and the waterkept variant are staged in base_data so the comparison is re-runnable.
decided: A cell now carries its own ground area rather than the equator’s. The JRC curves are a USD per square metre of real asset and the pass gave every cell one constant 288,615 m2, which is right only at the equator on EPSG:3857. ⚠ Not yet rerun, and held: his $11.4bn GEP is a different quantity from what we compute.
number: $11,403,596,548 across 250 rows, positive in 163, from our own end-to-end run on MSI including the counterfactuals (job 17648214, 6h50m, completed 2026-08-31). Against the author’s published $11.40bn that is 0.032%, which is his rounding to one decimal. gep = ead_bare - ead_current holds to 1.2e-07 across all 250 rows. The damage side reproduces too: ead $887,827,659,820, ead_nc $194,256,309,530, ead_ncplus $551,051,565,602. ⚠ The nc and ncplus columns are populated for 37 countries only; they are a separate diagnostic and the GEP identity does not use them. ⚠⚠ The water treatment moves the headline more than anything else found in this account. The run writes four variants and gep_flood_bare is $6.29bn on 4rp, $7.34bn on v1_2016, $11.40bn on v2_2024_waterremoved – the delivered one – and $24.54bn on v2_2024_waterkept. Keeping permanent water more than doubles the figure, and which variant the account intends is not written down anywhere we have found.
need: ⚠ Largely closed on 2026-08-28. The repository is public, cloned, and folded into the library: the module is now his full pipeline rather than a reader, vendored so nothing imports the source repo, paths resolved from flood_root_dir in es_parameters, and the harmonization gate clean. gep_calculation reads his own per-country export, $11.40bn over 162 countries, into the shared table — so the account’s number does not depend on us running anything. ⚠⚠ If that ever changes, read the rerun warning in the method page first. Seven MERIT flow-direction packages went missing at various points in his own work and every absence was silent: accumulation over a missing network writes nodata, amplification clips to 1.0, and the valuation reads 1.0 as no change here rather than no data here. Japan, Korea, Portugal and Kazakhstan returned zero service against $49bn of exposure, Nigeria, Chad, Cameroon, Niger and the CAR another $4bn, and nothing appeared in any log. Recovering them raised GEP 18.5 percent and then a further 16. His check catches regressions but not a package never downloaded, which was the original failure. The MSI setup is done: the run writes to /projects/standard/jajohns/shared/gep_flood with its machine-specific inputs in that project’s input/. Still open on the science: the real upstream service-provision ratio raster, since the drive copy is byte-identical to the binary mask beside it. ⚠⚠ What a cold start actually costs, measured 2026-09-01. Sixteen flood parameters ship blank in the template. A genuine cold start has to run the two tasks that never have – task_prepare_flood_inputs and task_build_sda – which need those rows filled and their files reachable. His input tree is 129 GB, and 117 GB of that is the counterfactual and counterfactual_mosaic amplification rasters that _open_amp reads and silently falls back from. Two cold starts on 2026-09-01 died on the first of the four missing tasks, one parameter at a time: flood_lulc_path, then flood_depth_aligned_path. Staging the LULC fixed the first and the second is the same shape, so the remaining thirteen will behave the same way. This is a staging decision rather than a bug, and it is why condition 10 is open here in a way it was not for crop or livestock. ⚠ The 17 other p.flood_* attributes that are absent from the template are set by tasks, not read from configuration, so they are not a gap.
signed off: amber as of 2026-09-01, and 10 is a recorded limitation rather than an unfinished task. 2, 12, 13 and 14 are met: it reads the account’s own country layer, the author’s committed table is staged and pinned to the cent, nothing points into his repository – the single mention is a _source_url row, so it could be deleted tomorrow and nothing here would break – and no name in the service is defined and never used. 4, 6 and 8 are met: the grid is stated (EPSG:3857 at 537.23 m, neither the shared pyramid nor equal-area, and that is stated too), the three gates pass, and the file set is the agreed one. 5 is met and is a warning: the module is his pipeline with our path handling and ProjectFlow wiring, so reproducing him was close to guaranteed and the entry says so. ⚠ 10 is a stated limitation. A cold start needs the four tasks that have never run, which need fifteen blank parameters filled and 129 GB staged, 117 GB of it the counterfactual amplification rasters. Decided 2026-09-01 to record it rather than stage it. ⚠ 1 is partial for the same reason: the amplification rasters are an input we have chosen not to recompute rather than one we cannot produce – a distinction the entry got wrong until 2026-09-01. counterfactual_mosaic/ is 37 derived global amplification rasters and counterfactual/ is MERIT Hydro tiles and flow direction, which are public; his RUN.md says they are built from rainfall and flow direction rather than from the hazard maps. So reproducing them is the two-week routing run his RUN.md describes, not a missing input. What our code demonstrably produces today is the valuation and GEP chain on his staged Sections B and C. 9 is met as of 2026-09-02: a reply went to the author reporting that our run reproduces his committed table exactly, and nothing of ours is now waiting on him. The three threads that had been open are each closed by a different route, which the condition allows and which is recorded here rather than left to be inferred. The global_invest.utilities question he asked on 2026-08-28 stopped existing when his repository was slated for deletion, so it was deliberately not asked. The water variant was deliberately not asked either, for the reason condition 7 gives: he has reported about $11.4bn consistently, so the delivered variant is settled by his own reporting rather than by our question. And the two changes of ours that were untold — step 4D taking region_wb from the country table rather than the boundary, and the two ISO3 detectors sharing one column set — are told. 7 is met as of 2026-09-01: the water variant looked open until it was noticed he has reported about $11.4bn consistently, in the 2026-08-27 email and in his committed table, so the delivered variant is settled by his own reporting. The $24.54bn waterkept figure is pinned by a test so it cannot drift, but it is not a question for him.
decided: The country boundary is the account’s own layer as of 2026-09-01, cartographic/ee/ee_r250.gpkg, not the author’s staged country_boundary_r250_with_iso3.gpkg. What had blocked the switch was step4D taking region_wb off the geometry: the account’s layer carries iso3 id, label and name and no region, so the export failed on it. Step4D takes the region from the shared country table now, and the layer resolves 250 rows with pick_iso3_column returning iso3_r250_label. ⚠ Against the r264 correspondence that detector returns adm0_a3, Natural Earth’s code rather than the account’s, and 264 rows for 250 countries – so the r250 layer is the one to point at and a test pins all three facts. The parameter now carries that path in the template rather than being left blank for each machine to answer differently, which is how it came to be the author’s file.

title: GEP service library: status
text:
NTFP (non-timber forest products)

subgroup: -
module: ntfp
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: the reachable area yes, the rate no. The accessible forest is computed here, on the source module’s own grid: ESA land cover at its native 300 m in Mollweide, screened by a five-year mean NDVI and by a 10 km dissolved buffer of the road and river geometries. The rate applied to it is CWoN’s published value per hectare, which is the half we do not produce.
method: CWoN’s non-wood forest product value per hectare, applied to the forest within 10 km of a road or a river that also carries a five-year mean NDVI of at least 0.2. The country total therefore sits below CWoN’s own, because the value notionally earned on forest nobody can reach is dropped rather than redistributed. The quantity is reachable forest area computed here from the land cover, the road and river geometries and the NDVI; the rate comes from a CSV. The screen, plainly, is two filters on which forest hectares get valued. (1) ACCESSIBILITY: only forest within 10 km of a road or river counts, because non-timber products – mushrooms, rattan, nuts, medicinal plants – have to be walked out; the reach is grown in metres on the account grid from the road and river lines. (2) VEGETATION: the cell’s five-year mean NDVI must reach 0.2, so land the map classes as forest but which carries no live green canopy – burned, degraded, sparse – yields nothing. Both filters and both thresholds are the source module’s own, pinned by tests.
total: $13.85bn over 196 countries, computed on the account’s own grid on MSI, 2026-09-03. The capped variant, the superseded Mollweide figure and the per-country cap amounts are in decided and number.
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The valuation is tested. The accessibility stage decides which forest people can reach: a 10 km buffer around every road and river, on an equal-area grid. Every step follows the source module’s own choices, and a test pins the country stage to the aggregation that module performs.
grid: The account’s own: WGS84 at 10 arcsec, the grid ha_per_cell_10sec.tif defines, with cell area READ per cell rather than assumed. The 10 km reach is grown in metres per latitude band, so the metric distance the old Mollweide grid existed to provide is exact here too, and a test pins it (15 columns at 60N against 7 at the equator). The rasters are POG-able by construction; they are accessibility intermediates rather than results, which is the recorded C22 answer – no per-cell value map is produced, the value is a table. ⚠ The stale Mollweide-era rasters this field used to flag are deleted (2026-09-03).
reference: CWoN publishes forest_nontimber_annual_nwfp.dta, which is the same service and is now compared against directly. In 2019 it is $28,877,638,160 over 149 valued countries, against our $13.85bn over 196. On the 149 both value, ours is $13,179,901,744 and theirs $28,877,638,160, a ratio of 0.456; we add $672,652,004 across 55 countries their gap-fill drops. ⚠ The gap is the area, not the rate: they multiply by total forest area and we multiply by the forest people can reach, and dividing their value by our rate returns 3.79 billion hectares against our 1.44 billion on the same countries, a ratio of 0.377. The source author has no committed outputs, so this is a comparison against the rate’s publisher rather than a replication of anyone’s run.
replicated: No, and there is nothing here to replicate: the source author has no committed outputs. What is compared against is the RATE’s publisher rather than the source module — CWoN’s own $28.88bn for the same service — and ours is 0.464 of it because we price the reachable forest and they price all of it. $13.85bn rests on our run alone.
decided: ⭐ Two of the row’s three questions are OURS to decide, and the house precedents decide them – neither goes to the group. (1) CWoN’s divide-by-five is NOT applied; the headline is the uncapped $13.85bn, with the capped $12.76bn beside it. The precedent is hydropower: its reference blanks 17 countries for no recorded reason, and this library refused to blank them, because reproducing an unexplained edit fits our number to the reference instead of deriving it, and a discrepancy silently reproduced can never surface. The divide-by-five is the same object – a hand edit whose basis its own author did not record (the GDP-share cap it stands in for is computed in their do-file and dropped unread). Both figures are published, so adopting the cap later is one line, not a rerun. (2) The accessibility screen STAYS. It is not a deviation to justify; it is the module’s method and the reason a spatial model exists at all – CWoN’s number needs no code, it is a column in a published table. Forest nobody can reach yields products nobody collects, so pricing it would value transactions that do not happen. CWoN’s $28.88bn stands beside ours as the no-screen bound, and the gap between them IS the screen, measured: 1.44bn reachable hectares against 3.79bn priced. (3) The denominator question is ANSWERED OURSELVES, and the headline is $13.85bn (decided 2026-09-03). Two independent checks agree. EMPIRICAL, on data we hold: if the rate were a country total spread over ALL forest, countries where little forest is reachable would show diluted rates – regressing log rate on log accessible share across 188 countries gives a slope of 0.059 where dilution predicts about +1 (correlation 0.12), and the least-accessible tercile’s median rate ($11.68/ha at 10% reachable) equals the most-accessible tercile’s ($12.89/ha at 100%). No dilution. CONSTRUCTIVE, from the IUCN/PROFOR technical report (public): the values are grid-cell-level meta-regression predictions, with road density and distance to urban centres as covariates, aggregated by country – a per-hectare value by construction. So the per-used-hectare reading holds, the screen is the consistent construction, and CWoN’s all-area multiplication is the overcount. ⚠ The denominator caveat this paragraph used to carry is resolved in (3) above: the rate carries no accessibility dilution, so the screen does not double-subtract.
number: The service has carried three totals, and each difference has one cause. $22.40bn (the group’s earlier figure) -> $14.07bn: the BUFFER, not the value. The source workflow’s own file (ntfp2.py) burns roads and rivers onto a 0.18-degree grid – cells about 20 km wide – then thresholds distance at 0.09 degrees, with its own NOTE admitting ‘approximate degrees for buffering’. Any 20 km block a road touches becomes reachable in full, so the reach is built from 20 km blocks instead of 10 km ribbons, and accessible forest inflates by roughly 60%. Replacing that with a true 10 km buffer around the actual line geometries – the method as the script’s own description states it – gives $14.07bn. $14.07bn -> $13.85bn (-1.6%): the grid, Mollweide 300 m to the account’s WGS84 10 arcsec, with cell area read from ha_per_cell rather than held constant. Ours vs CWoN’s $28.88bn: the SCREEN – same rate, they multiply by all forest, we by the 1.44bn reachable hectares. Their two code defects explain none of that gap; both push their total down.
lambda: ⭐ None is applied, and none should be – the rate is already the ecosystem’s share by CWoN’s own construction. The check is internal to CWoN: for TIMBER they build the rent explicitly, gross production value times a rental ratio (0.376), because market timber revenue pays labour and capital too. For NWFP their do-file applies NO ratio: the IUCN per-hectare value is multiplied by forest area and capitalized directly into natural wealth. They treat it as the ecosystem-service value itself – the meta-analysis values behind it are meant as nature’s contribution, not the gross takings of collectors. Applying GTAP’s forestry share on top would discount the same thing twice. ⚠ The property this rests on – that the IUCN values are NET of collection labour and costs – cannot be verified from the package, because the workbook (nontimber_ecosystem_services_iucn.xlsx) is not shipped with it. The denominator half is answered in decided (3); what remains is a FOOTNOTE-level confirmation, not a blocker: the IUCN/PROFOR methods convert estimates to dollars per hectare per year without stating whether the 49 underlying studies report net or gross values. If the values turned out to be gross collection value, the forestry lambda (0.380 of revenue) would apply and $13.85bn would become about $5.26bn – so the question is worth a sentence to the CWoN team, not a guess.
need: ⚠⚠ Both of the questions this row used to carry are now answered from CWoN’s own reproducibility package, which ships Do/forest_nontimber.do alongside the outputs. Neither needs an author. Is there a model behind the rate? No. The per-hectare values are read straight out of an IUCN 2020 workbook, nontimber_ecosystem_services_iucn.xlsx, one sheet per service, and our rate table is its NWFP sheet – the series name in our file is the string the do-file matches on, character for character. Countries the workbook does not cover were meant to take their World Bank region’s average, and the line that would do it is replace \var’ = `var’ if mi(`var’), which replaces a missing value with itself and does nothing. The working version sits a few lines below inside a comment block. A country is therefore labelledRegional averageand then dropped by thedrop if tot_ES == .that follows, which is why CWoN publishes 217 rows and values only 149 of them. **What is the edit for the Central African Republic, DR Congo and Mozambique?**replace nwfp_ES = nwfp_ES/5 if countrycode==“COD” | countrycode==“MOZ” | countrycode==“CAF”. It is CWoN's own cap, and the three countries are named in the code with no reason given -- unlike the water cap, which is written to hold the flow under one percent of GDP, and the recreation cap, which is a share of tourism receipts. The line above it computesnwfp_ES_gdp = (nwfp_ES*tot_area)/gdpand that variable is then dropped without ever being read, so the divide-by-five looks like a hand-applied stand-in for a GDP-share cap that was worked out and never wired up. ⚠ Our rate table is the un-capped one. Whether to adopt the cap is decided above, indecided`: not applied, both figures published.
signed off: amber, and the distance to green is now entirely LIBRARY-wide rather than anything about this service. Service-specific conditions are met: the number is the account grid’s own ($13.85bn, MSI 2026-09-03, every raster proving it holds data as built), 11 and 16 are met (the grid is the pyramid, area is read from ha_per_cell, the rasters are recorded intermediates), the headline is decided, the cap is deliberately refused with the variant published, the lambda question is answered, and no blocking asks remain – the net-of-costs footnote is a confirmation, not a condition. What keeps it amber: ⚠ 10, unmet here – though no longer everywhere: erosion closed it on 2026-09-03, and this service’s own cold start is queued (erosion closed it on 2026-09-03; this service’s own cold start is queued as MSI job 17939275) – and a sliver of 15, one unreferenced sidecar in the input folder. ## Stormwater
subgroup: -
module: stormwater
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: not yet. InVEST stormwater is installed and its run sits outside the task tree.
method: Runoff the land cover holds back instead of sending to drainage, in cubic metres, priced at the cost of replacing the same capacity (currently a placeholder of 1). The quantity comes from an InVEST retention raster produced by a run outside this tree.
total: 185.85bn m3 retained, superseded. ⚠ That figure is the staged per-country CSV, built before the ground-area fix of 2026-08-27; the corrected volume measured on the full raster is 122.30bn m3, and the run has not been repeated. No dollar total either way: the price is a placeholder of 1, so a dollar figure would be the volume relabelled.
code: Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The step that totals retained water inside each country is in the repo.
grid: EPSG:3857 at 537.23 m, which is NOT equal-area, and it matters. The volumes come from InVEST, which builds them as precipitation times ONE pixel area taken off the transform (pixel_area = abs(pixel_size[0] * pixel_size[1]) in natcap.invest.stormwater). On this grid that constant is 288,615 m2, the area a cell covers at the equator, so every cell further out is credited with more water than its ground can hold: 1.7 times at 40 degrees. Fixed here on 2026-08-27: the zonal sum weights each row by the cosine squared of its latitude, which is what ha_per_cell does for the geographic grids the rest of the library uses. Measured on the full raster, the retained volume falls from 185.87 to 122.30 billion cubic metres, -34.2 percent. ⚠ The staged per-country CSV still carries the old figure, so the run has to be repeated before any published number changes. The grid is projected only because InVEST requires one; nothing else here needs it.
reference: None. No author run exists to compare against. There is also no dollar total: the price is a placeholder of 1, so a valuation would be the 185.85bn m3 relabelled.
replicated: Nothing to match: no author run exists, and there is no dollar total yet because the price is a placeholder.
decided: Ground area. The zonal sum now weights each row by the cosine squared of its latitude, so a cell carries its own ground area rather than the equator’s. InVEST builds the volumes on one constant pixel area and has to, because it needs a projected grid; this run is EPSG:3857, where that constant holds only at the equator. Measured on the full raster the retained volume falls 185.87 to 122.30 billion cubic metres, -34.2 percent. ⚠ Not yet rerun, so the staged per-country CSV still carries the old figure.
number: 185.85 billion cubic metres retained across 104 countries, ⚠ superseded by the ground-area fix under decided, which takes it to 122.30 billion pending a rerun. No author run exists to compare against, and no dollar total: at the placeholder price of 1 the value would just be the volume again.
need: A source for the price per cubic metre. ⚠ The method is no longer the open part: the authors’ appendix, staged at stormwater/input/peak_flow_mitigation_appendix.docx, specifies the avoided cost of treating and pumping the water that would otherwise reach the works, framed around combined sewer overflows, and works an example at $2.75/m3. Our runs use a placeholder of 1.0, so what is missing is a defensible per-country rate rather than a decision about approach. ⚠ Also an urban mask, or the InVEST run restricted to urban extents. The service is defined on urban areas, the retention run we were given covers all land, and we hold no mask to restrict it, so the volume is larger than the service. ⚠ The same appendix confirms the quantity formula is V_R = lambda x (1 - RC) x P x A with A the pixel area, which is the term the 2026-08-27 ground-area fix corrects.
signed off: amber: examined, and at least one of the sixteen conditions is not yet verified. ⚠ 10 is unmet here (no longer everywhere: erosion closed it on 2026-09-03, reproducing its published total to $11 in $18.24bn from an empty project directory). ⚠ 11 is unverified: the base year is 2019 across every service, but the country list, the true-zero-against-missing rule and the shared parameters have not been checked service by service ## Groundwater Recharge
subgroup: regulating
module: groundwater_recharge
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: the valuation yes, the recharge no. The avoided-pumping arithmetic is computed here; the country mean recharge depths are the owner’s InVEST Seasonal Water Yield output, read from the staged table and taken as given.
method: Recharge valued as the pumping energy it saves: recharge keeps the water table higher, so every cubic metre withdrawn is lifted a shorter distance. Value = gamma x tariff / (eta x 3.6e6) x mean recharge depth x groundwater withdrawal – the lift cost at the country’s electricity price, times the year’s head increment, times the year’s AQUASTAT withdrawal.
total: $6.80M in 2019 USD; $7.21M at the owner’s 2021 tariffs, which is the sheet’s figure
code: Built 2026-09-06 on the library template: functions open nothing, tasks own the IO, four unit tests pin the physics constant, the missing-input rule and the anchor, name aliases spell out every AQUASTAT and price-table join so no country drops silently.
grid: No raster read here. The recharge depths come from a raster model run elsewhere; what this module reads are country tables.
reference: ⭐ The all-services sheet’s column, REPRODUCED IN FULL: all 108 valued countries match to the cent, total $7,211,275.96 against the sheet’s $7,211,275.95. The staged committed ground_water_gep.csv (2025-10) is an older input vintage and agrees for 21 of 109 countries; the sheet is the current construction and ours is it, end to end. ⚠ Same lineage on the recharge depths, so the agreement tests the valuation, not the hydrology.
replicated: Yes, the sheet’s column, to the cent, every country.
decided: Built despite the exclusion note (Chiara, 2026-09-06), so the group decides scope with the number and the method on the table rather than in the abstract. ⚠ The tiny magnitude is the METHOD’S OWN, not an error: valuing one year’s recharge as a one-year marginal head increment prices the lift at a fraction of a cent per cubic metre. And the construction WEAKENS the double-count argument the exclusion rests on – avoided pumping energy is an energy saving, not the water’s end-product value, so it does not obviously overlap purification or the irrigation premium.
number: Values the pumping energy recharge saves: $7,211,275.96 across 109 countries (India $2.6M, USA $0.6M, Indonesia $1.2M). Five orders below neighbouring services by construction. The Jasechko groundwater-depth data staged by the owner suggests the natural extension: valuing the STOCK of avoided depth rather than one year’s increment would scale the row by the ratio of water-table depth to annual recharge, typically two to three orders of magnitude.
need: The scope decision, now sharper than include-or-exclude: (a) out on the double-count reasoning – then the sheet’s column should go; (b) in as marginal pumping savings – then $7.21M stands and the account owns its smallness; (c) in as the stock of avoided depth – a different, larger construction the owner’s staged data could support. Condition 10 is minutes once blessed.
signed off: amber: built and run 2026-09-06, the sheet’s column reproduced to the cent in every country, but the scope decision is the group’s. ⭐ Condition 10 CLOSED 2026-10-02: a cold start from an empty project directory reproduces $7,211,275.96 to the cent at the owner construction. Currency harmonized 2026-10-03: the published table now deflates the 2021 tariffs to 2019 USD through the account’s one CPI series ($6,803,550.52); the sheet remains the owner construction, reproducible by setting the deflation year to 2021 ## Fuelwood

subgroup: -
module: health_hypertension (physical) and health_depression (mental)
category: raster arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes, both strands (2026-09-09)
ours: yes for the constructions (built 2026-09-09 from the appendices’ named sources); the dose-response effect sizes, cost tables and the InVEST mental-health formulation are the owners’ parameters, taken as given with sources beside them.
method: PHYSICAL (hypertension, Tajibaeva-Bo-Kula appendix 2026-08): per urban pixel, WHO prevalence times the NDVI-driven risk reduction (Bu 2024 / Zhao 2022 odds ratio per 0.1 NDVI, converted at the country’s prevalence) times the urban population aged 30-79, priced at the country’s published treatment cost – 20 countries carry a cost study, by construction. MENTAL (depression, Yingjie Li appendix 2025-11, the InVEST urban mental health model): per urban pixel, observed depression cases times the prevented-cases factor exp(-10 ln RR x NDVI) - 1 (Liu 2023 odds ratio 0.931 per 0.1 NDVI, converted the same way), priced at the societal cost per case (Christensen 2020, ⚠ USD PPP, mostly 2018) – 32 countries carry a cost study. Both strands share the same three rasters: WorldPop 2019 1 km, the GHS-SMOD urban mask, and a MODIS 2019 annual-mean NDVI built via Google Earth Engine (the appendices use 300 m Copernicus and 30 m Landsat; the 1 km grid is the named deviation).
total: physical $148.71bn over 20 countries ($247.44bn over 187 with costs transferred where no study exists); mental $96.15bn in market 2019 USD over 32 countries at the method’s stated scope – the owner’s PPP-2018 costs converted by country price levels and the account’s one CPI series ($97.96bn before conversion).
code: Both modules built 2026-09-09 on the library template: functions open nothing, tasks own the IO, the raster work is one blockwise pass per strand, eight unit tests pin the odds-to-risk conversion, the dose-response conventions and the missing-input rule. The id rasterization was promoted to utilities and recreation now shares it. Nothing existed to port: the drive holds no pipeline for either strand.
grid: WGS84 throughout on WorldPop’s own 1 km grid; the urban mask warped nearest onto it, the NDVI bilinear. No metric operation, so no conversion question arises.
reference: PHYSICAL: the appendix’s Table 6, $104,664,962,067 over 19 countries. ⚠⚠ The drive’s committed health_hypertension_gep.csv is that table MISALIGNED – values sorted by country name pasted against labels sorted alphabetically, so 7 of 19 countries carry a neighbour’s value (Nigeria shows Poland’s $6.86bn); verified exactly, total unchanged. The all-services sheet’s column ($106.65bn over 13) is a third, earlier vintage matching neither. MENTAL: the author’s high resolution file, $159,602,811 over 32 countries, which IS the sheet’s column to the cent; a low resolution variant carries $167.3M; the committed per-country CSV is an unfilled template stub.
replicated: PHYSICAL: the level and rank, not the file – our run lands 42 percent above the appendix with log-correlation 0.989 over the 19 shared countries (Nigeria and Zimbabwe within 6 percent; the gap concentrates where NDVI resolution and the wider SMOD urban mask bite: China 1.61, Greece 1.72, Kenya 3.7). Ghana, which they priced but never valued, comes out at $36.6M. MENTAL: deliberately not an anchor – our full-scope run is 370 times the author’s file at the median country (USA 835, Germany 405), ⭐ which MEASURES the scope question: their run covers roughly a quarter of a percent of the urban population its own cost countries hold, i.e. a city sample, undocumented which.
decided: Built both strands at the methods’ stated scopes with every parameter in es_parameters (Chiara, 2026-09-09), so the group decides with numbers on the table: the physical strand’s coverage question (20 countries is the price data, not the method), and the mental strand’s scope question (city sample or national urban populations – the answer moves the row from $0.16bn to $98bn).
number: Values what urban greenspace saves in illness: $148,706,081,307 of avoided hypertension treatment (China $69.7bn, USA $66.3bn – the per-case costs of $3,394 and $9,529 dominate) and $97,960,172,780 of prevented depression at societal cost over the 32 cost countries (USA $51.1bn, UK $10.3bn, Australia $9.8bn; 64.5M prevented cases). ⚠ The two strands overlap conceptually (same greenness, comorbid outcomes) and the mental costs are USD PPP – neither should be added to the other or to the account without those two decisions.
need: For the physical authors: the committed CSV’s sort misalignment (re-export Table 6); which vintage the sheet’s $106.65bn is; and whether our cost transfer matches their planned extrapolation – the extended column prices every country by the ln-ln fit of cost on GDP per capita over their 20 studies (R2 0.32, Duan smearing, observed costs kept), giving $247.44bn over 187 countries. For Yingjie Li: the run’s spatial extent (our measured 370x gap says a city sample); which of the two variants is blessed; PPP against the account’s 2019 USD. For the group: whether the zero-vegetation counterfactual (physical) and the all-built counterfactual (mental) are the accounting the GEP wants, and how the two strands avoid double counting each other.
signed off: amber, both strands: built, run and tested 2026-09-09, the physical strand rank-anchored on the appendix (0.989) but 42 percent above its level on named deviations, the mental strand deliberately unanchored until the author’s scope is known. ⭐ Condition 10 CLOSED for both strands 2026-10-02: cold starts reproduce $148,706,081,306.76 (and the extended $247bn column’s fit statistics) and $97,960,172,780.38 with 64,530,894 prevented cases, all to the cent ## Pests
subgroup: -
module: pest_control
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes for the construction (built 2026-09-08 from the appendix’s named sources); the effect sizes, yield ratios and price premium are the owner’s parameters, taken as given with their sources beside them.
method: Organic agriculture only, by design: a proportional yield benefit from biological control (Boldorini et al. 2024, the one meta-analysis their systematic search surfaced; effect sizes for cereals, for vegetables-with-oilseeds-and-pulses and for fruit-and-stimulants, every other FAO group zero), times organic production (FiBL organic area times FAOSTAT conventional yield times an organic-to-conventional yield ratio re-estimated from the Ponisio et al. 2015 pairs), times an organic producer price (FAOSTAT conventional price times an organic-to-conventional price ratio from USDA GATS trade unit values). ⚠ Lambda is 1 by design – the full value is attributed to nature, unlike most other rows. Conventional agriculture is excluded on the stated ground that a marginal biocontrol benefit under synthetic pesticides is not quantifiable (Dainese et al. 2019). The owner’s estimate is a Monte Carlo mean; the appendix (2026-08-21 vintage, Sidemo-Holm, Miller, Sylla) says 1,000 iterations in one paragraph and 10,000 in the next.
total: $10.34bn with the appendix’s 38 percent organic price premium; $7.49bn without it (the value is linear in the premium).
code: Built 2026-09-08 on the library template: functions open nothing, tasks own the IO, five unit tests pin the benefit convention, the missing-input rule and the crop map’s integrity, the published table carries all 250 countries. The drive’s own GEP_biocontrol.R (January 2025) is the author’s work-in-progress prototype with his own desktop paths, nine months older than the committed output and predating the appendix’s method; the pipeline that produced the committed file is not on the drive.
grid: No raster anywhere in the construction; country-by-crop tables throughout.
reference: The committed pest_control_gep.csv (2025-10-20): $6,250,523,049 over 132 valued countries on the 250-row account list. ⭐ The all-services sheet’s Pest control column IS this file to the dollar. It is a Monte Carlo mean from the missing pipeline, so the module anchors on coverage and rank (log-correlation 0.934, every committed country valued), not to the cent.
replicated: The level and shape, not the file: our run at premium 1.0 gives $7.49bn against the committed $6.25bn with log-correlation 0.934 and no committed country missed – so the committed file sits at the no-premium level of the same construction. Deviations named in the run log: FiBL aggregate rows with no FAOSTAT analogue excluded (11.3 percent of area, where the owner’s matching claims under 0.1 percent removed), and 223 yields and 671 prices filled with global item medians where the owner imputes with mixed models.
decided: The construction (2026-09-08): the appendix’s method deterministically (the Monte Carlo mean of a product of independent draws is the product of the means), parameters in es_parameters with sources beside them, the premium defaulting to the appendix’s 1.38.
number: Values the extra yield natural enemies provide on organic cropland at the organic producer price: $10,338,294,391 published at 2019 over 138 countries with the appendix’s premium, $7,491,517,675 without it. Largest: China $3.9bn, France $1.1bn, USA $0.9bn, Italy $0.7bn – organic vineyards, orchards and vegetables, since only organic area carries value. ⚠ Viet Nam is the one real anomaly against the committed file: their $291M is roughly nine times anything the staged FiBL 2019 areas support under any reading of the method.
examined for the issues table (2026-09-08): the committed file explains the sheet exactly ($6,250,523,049 both). ⭐ The level question is one parameter: the committed total matches this construction WITHOUT the organic price premium the appendix describes (median country ratio 1.14 at premium 1.0, clustering at 1.4-1.6 at premium 1.38), and the output predates the appendix by ten months – so the committed run likely predates the premium step.
need: Three asks. Whether the committed $6.25bn includes the organic price premium (the level says no; the appendix says the method has one). What produced Viet Nam’s $291M. And the final pipeline with its inputs from William Sidemo-Holm (the Ponisio meta-regression, the imputation models, the run script), so the anchor can tighten past rank agreement. Plus the group’s view on lambda equal 1 while the neighbouring crop rows carry a human-input adjustment.
signed off: amber: built and run, five tests green, but the two level questions (premium, Viet Nam) are the owner’s to answer and the committed reference cannot be reproduced past rank agreement without the missing pipeline. ⭐ Condition 10 CLOSED 2026-10-02: a cold start from an empty project directory reproduces $10,338,294,391.30 to the cent, the premium-1.0 reading identical ## Moisture Recycling (Regional Hydrology)
subgroup: regulating
module: moisture_recycling
category: table arithmetic
in the library: yes
run: yes
ours: yes
method: The WAM2layers country-to-country sink-fraction matrix (Bakels and Wang-Erlandsson, drive submission MREcosystemService) says what fraction of each country’s 2019 precipitation evaporated from each other country’s land. Each destination’s irrigation and domestic water GEP is scaled by its terrestrial-origin share and distributed over source countries with the matrix, so the service credits the countries whose land sent the rain. ⚠⚠ A RE-ATTRIBUTION of the water-supply row, never an addition: source-side and sink-side totals agree by construction and the task raises if they differ.
total: $127.7bn
code: Built 2026-09-05 on the library template: functions open nothing, tasks own the IO, seven unit tests pin the orientation convention and the conservation, the published table carries all 250 countries.
grid: No raster. The matrix is a 225-country table and the water values are country tables; nothing multiplies a density by a cell area.
reference: For the VALUE, nothing: the all-services table’s Rainfall pattern Regulation column is empty (zero countries), and the drive submission’s appendix (Bakels and Wang-Erlandsson) is a methodology plan whose monetary section is exploratory – our construction implements its “combine with the water provision value” direction, the rare row where the library figure exists before any reference figure. For the QUANTITY, the owner’s countries_overview workbook (staged 2026-10-03) is the independent check: our terrestrial-origin shares match its recycled-moisture fractions at correlation 0.992 over 213 countries; see replicated.
replicated: No reference VALUE exists anywhere. ⭐ The QUANTITY side gained independent corroboration 2026-10-03: the owner’s countries_overview workbook (added to the drive 2026-09-10, after our build) carries per-country recycled-moisture fractions, and our matrix’s terrestrial-origin shares match them at correlation 0.992 over 213 countries, mean absolute difference 0.04 (max 0.12). The TRANSPOSED reading correlates at only 0.41, so the comparison also confirms the matrix orientation our build chose. The residual is NOT the lake split (tested: adding their lake fraction changes nothing) – most plausibly an aggregation-vintage difference between their overview and the November 2025 matrices we stage; one line to the owner settles it.
decided: The construction (2026-09-05): re-attribute the water row’s irrigation plus domestic GEP (the account’s own $248.0bn plus $95.6bn) with the sink-fraction matrix; ecosystem share held at 1.0 in es_parameters pending the transpiration decision; the water table read as a staged snapshot of the 2026-09 water_supply run. Coverage: 12 destinations below the 0.5 degree tracking grid ($42.6M unattributed) and 28 account countries absent from the matrix ($1.1M) – both named in the run log. The submission’s companion fields are staged beside the matrix and deliberately unread by the valuation: countries_source.csv and countries_sink.csv (mm volumes) and countries_source_fraction.csv (where each country’s own evaporation rains out), kept for the scenario and variability work the appendix plans.
number: Values the rain a country’s land sends to its own and other countries’ water use: $127,682,011,050 published at 2019 (the attribution computes $127.96bn; $279M of it sits in the matrix’s three small-island aggregates, CSID, IOSID and PSID, which no account country can carry – logged by the run), of which $52.3bn serves the source country itself and $75.3bn crosses a border as exported rain. The withdrawal-weighted terrestrial share works out to 37 percent of the water value, consistent with the literature’s 40-50 percent of land rain having a terrestrial source. Largest sources: India $25.5bn, China $20.6bn, Russia $6.5bn (mostly exported).
need: Three group decisions. The transpiration share (1.0 counts all terrestrial evaporation as ecosystem-mediated; the literature’s transpiration fraction would roughly halve the row). The accounting rule: publish as a decomposition of water supply or as a row carrying only the $75.3bn transboundary part, but never added whole to water supply. And whether hydropower’s water value should also be re-attributed (rain feeds the rivers too); the current construction re-attributes irrigation and domestic only.
signed off: amber: built and run, conservation asserted in the task, but the three decisions in need are the group’s and no reference exists to compare against. ⭐ Condition 10 CLOSED 2026-10-02: a cold start reproduces the published $127,682,011,050.38 with every one of the 250 rows identical – and caught a dormant defect doing it: the map-writing merge lacked the region id after the 250-row refactor, invisible warm because skip-existing never re-ran it; fixed the house way (the collapse frame merged in before the write) ## Nature View Amenity

title: Where the es_parameters values come from
text:
Provenance for the rows in global_invest/input_template/es_parameters.csv. It lives here rather than in the CSV because that file holds values a run reads, and a note is not a value: every one of these was being hydrated onto the ProjectFlow object as an attribute nothing read. The *_source_url and *_source_archive_member rows stay in the CSV, because a URL and an archive member name are values you can act on.


erosion_fao_gpv_iso3 — the author’s processed FAOSTAT table, from the drive’s erosion folder
erosion_yield_bridge — alpha is the flat erosion-to-yield coefficient a GTAP sector falls back to when none of its crops has a coefficient (the 8% damage_area method hardcodes 0.08 and does not read it); yield_coefficient_fallback is what Method B uses for a crop with no coefficient of its own. They are the same 0.08 today and the code comment says they are the same bridge, but they answer different questions, so they are two rows rather than one. 19 of 46 crops take the fallback and 5 have no entry at all.
erosion_sdr_params — one calibration for both the static GEP and the dynamic shock path. They used to differ, with sdr_max and ic_0_param transposed between them; these are the dynamic values, the conventional Borselli pair.
erosion_threshold — threshold_high 11.0 t/ha/yr is the SES-11 severe-erosion threshold the account is named for, and threshold_low 2.0 the tolerable one. They decide which pixels count as severe, so they are the two rows most worth checking against the methodology before a run.
erosion_yield_reduction — 0.08 is the fallback yield response used when a crop has no row in the elasticity table. 19 of 46 crops take it, and 5 crops have no entry at all, so it is doing more work than a fallback should.
erosion_gdp_csv — World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, GDP in current US dollars, filtered to 2019. Staged rather than fetched per run because the World Bank revises it, which would move the erosion valuation without recording why.



fire_panel — the district panel, from the drive Wildfires folder



air_filtration_workbook — the committed workbook, from the drive air filtration folder
air_filtration_vsl — value of a statistical life per country, the price half of the air-quality valuation. Rebuilt from the workbook the group circulated; sandstorm prevention reads the same column.



flood_return_periods — the six on disk under floodplain_depth_v2_nowater/aligned_to_lulc, which is the reported 2024 hazard set with permanent water removed.
flood_input_reference — machine-specific, so these ship blank: base_data carries no global_invest/flood tree. On MSI they are under /projects/standard/jajohns/shared/flood_gep/inputs/. Three are not where a tidy layout would put them: the reported depths are floodplain_depth_v2_nowater/, the SPA ratio is in counterfactual_mosaic/, and the CN table is in counterfactual/ while the amplification rasters are in counterfactual_mosaic/.
flood_amplification_pattern — the staged files are global_amplification__rp.tif. The f0p3 and f0p5 variants beside them are alternative depth exponents; the unsuffixed file is the default.
flood_country_dir — blank means each task writes its per-country tree into its own cur_dir. A machine holding an earlier run points these at it to reuse Section B rather than rebuild it.
flood_optional_tables — protection_path and protection_evidence_path are optional companions: blank means the table is not supplied, and the readers branch on None. When an evidence table IS given and has no ISO3 column the run stops, because which countries count as documented decides how much damage is truncated.
flood_skip_damage_tables — flood_tasks reads this with TWO different defaults – False at the run_valuation_chain call site and True at the GEP one – so the behaviour depended on which ran. The damage tables are prebuilt inputs and the inputs directory is not writable, so building them raises PermissionError; the deleted set_flood_paths set True. Setting it here makes both call sites agree
flood_divergent_defaults — apply_service_flow and report_protection_split are TRUE here and FALSE as getattr defaults in configure_valuation. The deleted set_flood_paths set both True, so the run behaviour was True while the code default said otherwise. Deleting it without moving these would have silently turned off the ecosystem attribution that produces ead_attributed_to_spa_usd2019
flood_valuation_settings — the Section D switches, moved out of configure_valuation on 2026-08-29 where they were getattr defaults in code. Code set before hydration WINS over the CSV – hydrate_es_parameters skips an attribute that is already set – so defaults living in code silently shadowed anything put here
flood_settings — the settings the module reads. iso3_list all means every country in the boundary layer; iso3_n 0 means all remaining; an MSI array runner overwrites start and n from SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
flood_gep_for_merge — the author export gep_calculation falls back to when the counterfactual chain has not run here: iso3_r250_label and gep_const2019_usd, $11.40bn over 162 non-zero countries, v2 2024 hazard. Produced by his scripts/export_gep_for_merge.py from step4e_flood_gep_USD2019.csv; that script is not carried here because the output is a base_data input like any other author artifact



local_climate_regulation_city_savings — the chain’s own per-country city-month valuations, one file per country: avoided kilowatt-hours, national price and their product



ntfp_roads_vector — the global roads layer the source module buffers, staged from its submission folder. The accessibility polygon is built from these geometries rather than from a rasterised road length, which is what the source does.
ntfp_countries_vector — the boundary polygons the source module takes its zonal statistics over. Burned onto the analysis grid rather than reprojected from an id raster, so a cell is assigned to the country whose polygon covers its centre.
ntfp_ndvi_mean — five-year mean NDVI from MODIS MOD13Q1 Collection 6.1 at 250 m over 2015 to 2019, quality masked and exported from Google Earth Engine. int16 storing NDVI times 10000, nodata -9999. Screens bare and sparse cells out of the land-cover forest mask.
ntfp_value_per_ha — derived from the public CWoN 2024 reproducibility package: the non-wood forest product annual value (forest_nontimber_annual_nwfp.dta) over the matching forest area (forest_nontimber_total_area.dta), per country and year. Note the areas differ in definition: CWoN prices over ITS forest area while the quantity we multiply is accessible forest from the ESA land cover, which is the source method’s own construction



cwon_crop_coefficients — the CWoN land rental-rate coefficients, from the drive



cwon_crop_coefficients — the CWoN land rental-rate coefficients, from the drive
gleam_dmi — GLEAM 3 dry-matter intake per country, harvested from FAO’s public dashboard by the recipe in howto_harvest_gleam_intake.md. Carries all eight feed categories: the four the ruminant tables omit are served on the chicken and pig tables instead.



pollination_crop_benefits_repo — the source author’s pipeline. The GEP value raster is his output, not a construction of ours: CropGrids harvested area times a Monfreda within-country yield pattern times FAO calibration. The raster is staged into base_data by hand when a base year he has not published is needed; docs/runbook_pollination_value_raster.md has the six commands. Deliberately not automated: running his pipeline from ours would make this the only task in the library that executes another repository code
pollination_fx — World Bank PA.NUS.FCRF, official exchange rate in local currency per US dollar, period average, fetched 2026-08-25. 7,149 rows over 214 countries and 1990 to 2024. Pinned rather than fetched per run because the World Bank revises the series, which would move the pollination total by whatever had changed since.
pollination_value_raster_dir — the precomputed baseline pollination-value raster the shock path resamples, poll_value_global_usd.tif. Output of the source pipeline run once over Monfreda yields, CropGrids area, FAO producer prices and pollination-dependence ratios. Reused rather than rebuilt, so it has no URL and a person stages it.
pollination_crosswalk_m49_iso3 — FAO M49 area codes to ISO3.
pollination_fao_classification — the FAO item classification.
pollination_crosswalk_fao_cropgrids — FAO items to CropGrids crop names.



coastal_protection_coral_reef — annual expected coastal-protection benefit of coral reefs, per country. Supplied by the author rather than computed here, which is why coastal protection is only half ours.
coastal_protection_gdp_deflator — GDP inflation deflator, for putting the mangrove and coral figures in one price year. The drive folder spells it gdp_inflation_delator, sic; staged under the corrected name.



landslide_elevation — elevation in metres, the slope input to the stability model. Read from the shared SEALS static regressors rather than a landslide copy, so the two models see one terrain.
landslide_lulc_path_template — the ESA land cover per year, formatted with the year. A template rather than a path because the task iterates data_processing_range.

title: Where the es_parameters values come from
text:
erosion_fao_gpv_iso3 — the author’s processed FAOSTAT table, from the drive’s erosion folder
erosion_yield_bridge — alpha is the flat erosion-to-yield coefficient a GTAP sector falls back to when none of its crops has a coefficient (the 8% damage_area method hardcodes 0.08 and does not read it); yield_coefficient_fallback is what Method B uses for a crop with no coefficient of its own. They are the same 0.08 today and the code comment says they are the same bridge, but they answer different questions, so they are two rows rather than one. 19 of 46 crops take the fallback and 5 have no entry at all.
erosion_sdr_params — one calibration for both the static GEP and the dynamic shock path. They used to differ, with sdr_max and ic_0_param transposed between them; these are the dynamic values, the conventional Borselli pair.
erosion_threshold — threshold_high 11.0 t/ha/yr is the SES-11 severe-erosion threshold the account is named for, and threshold_low 2.0 the tolerable one. They decide which pixels count as severe, so they are the two rows most worth checking against the methodology before a run.
erosion_yield_reduction — 0.08 is the fallback yield response used when a crop has no row in the elasticity table. 19 of 46 crops take it, and 5 crops have no entry at all, so it is doing more work than a fallback should.
erosion_gdp_csv — World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, GDP in current US dollars, filtered to 2019. Staged rather than fetched per run because the World Bank revises it, which would move the erosion valuation without recording why.

title: PhD APEC 8601: Natural Resource Economics
text:
Canvas link: https://canvas.umn.edu/courses/412194
Course repository: https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/apec_8601_2024


This course has two main objectives:

To acquaint you with the major issues and seminal literature in natural resource economics. We will cover issues related to the use of renewable resources such as fisheries, aquifers, and timber, and non-renewable resources such as oil and minerals. We will also cover issues related to the conservation of biodiversity and provision of ecosystem services, climate change, and sustainability. We will analyze the issue of efficient use of resources over time and under what conditions market equilibrium achieves an efficient outcome, intergenerational equity and discounting, common property resources, imperfect competition, spatial modeling, uncertainty, and irreversible decisions. We will also consider new research on global integrated assessment modeling and creation of earth-economy models.
To increase your ability to do economic research. We will do a set of activities to increase your ability to think critically and formulate specific researchable questions, as well as improving your modeling and analytical skills.




APEC 8000-8004 or equivalent (graduate level microeconomic theory). It is possible to take microeconomic theory concurrently. If you haven’t had such classes (or are taking them concurrently) please talk to me about what you will need to do to keep up. We will adjust the course based on how familiar students are with the techniques of dynamic optimization (optimal control theory and dynamic programming).

title: Justin Andrew Johnson
text:
Teaching Philosophy
My philosophy for teaching economics is that it should be an interactive experience that exposes students to the core principles of decision making and economic growth, builds students’ competence with quantitative and computational methods, and prepares them for future research or jobs. I believe students learn best when they address directly the ways in which economics is connected to underlying moral questions about how a society should be organized. This allows the student to build a better sense of how economics can illuminate policy debates or decision making with analysis techniques and quantitative methods. I then build on this understanding to increase students’ mastery of the mathematical, theoretical and computational skills necessary to enable future use of economic models.
The reason I emphasize interactive experience is that I find relating abstract economic concepts to specific policy questions or real-life experiences dramatically increases the intuitive (and then eventually, methodological) skills a student can obtain. An example of this I used in the past is conducting game-theory based exercises in class in which students compete to have the highest semester-running score through a series of games. After each version of the game we play, I engage the students in a discussion of why they played the strategy they did and award extra points for describing how their strategy is based on the economic theory. I find that these discussions cement previously discussed lecture material very well. Another interactive method I use is conducting mock-negotiations or debates. For example, in a course I taught on the economics of climate change, each student represented a country and we held an international climate negotiation. Students immediately connected with this approach and were motivated enough to use relatively sophisticated integrated assessment models to support their negotiations with economic analysis. Both of these examples also used new communication and web technologies to improve interactivity and feedback.

title: GTAP-InVEST User Guide
text: This is the User Guide for GTAP-InVEST, a new earth-economy model introduced in “Investing in nature can improve equity and economic returns” (Johnson et al. 2023, PNAS). The content here originally derived from the supplemental information document included with PNAS article. However, development on the model is progressing rapidly, so please refer to this document, which will remain up-to-date. For additional details, please see the GTAP-InVEST Github repository (github.com/jandrewjohnson/gtap_invest). All code and results of the model are available and licensed under a permissive open-source license. Full results may be downloaded at justinandrewjohnson.com/gtap_invest/results.

title: GTAP-InVEST User Guide
text:
2. Contents

Narrative chapters

Model summary — overview of how GTAP, SEALS, and InVEST are coupled.
Scenarios — scenario design and shock construction.
GTAP details — economic model formulation and database choices.
InVEST details — ecosystem service models used downstream of SEALS.
Ecosystem service impacts — how ES feedbacks enter the second GTAP run.



GTAP Database reference
The current GTAP-Invest pipeline uses the GTAP 12 Data Base (released 2025), aggregated for analysis. Older v11 references are kept for archival comparison.

GTAP v12 regions (163) — current
GTAP v12 sectors (65) — current
GTAP v12 model variables — sets, parameters, value flows, prices, shocks, welfare
GTAP v11 regions (160) — legacy
GTAP v11 sectors (65) — legacy
GTAP v11 model variables — legacy



GTAP-Invest aggregation (v12_s26_r50)
The GTAP-Invest pipeline runs on an aggregated form of the full database — 50 regions and 26 sectors — so simulations are tractable and aligned with the resolution at which SEALS land-use change and InVEST ecosystem services can be coupled to the economic model.

title: GTAP Database reference
text:
This section documents the native classifications of the GTAP Data Base — the full region and sector lists at the resolution Purdue ships, plus the set/variable/parameter definitions of the GTAP v7 model that operates on them. Use it when you need to know what a code like xea or gro actually covers, or which set a variable is indexed over.
This is the unaggregated reference. For the smaller aggregation actually used in GTAP-Invest simulations (50 regions × 26 sectors), see GTAP-Invest aggregation (s26_r50).


The v12 Data Base (released 2024) is the default for new GTAP-Invest runs.

v12 regions (163) — region codes, names, and the countries that compose each “Rest of” aggregate. Three new African countries split out from xac/xec relative to v11.
v12 sectors (65) — the 65 GTAP sectors with descriptions. Codes are unchanged from v11.
v12 model variables — sets, subsets, exogenous/endogenous variables, and parameters of the GTAP v7 model. These are properties of the model, not the database, and are identical between v11 and v12 — only the dimensions they’re indexed over change.




Kept for reproducibility of older GTAP-Invest results. Prefer v12 for new work.
