title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Faithful-port notes
Two behaviours are reproduced rather than corrected, so the port stays comparable against the anchor.
The source pivots the regression table with a mean aggregator over every value column, including the character significance stars. R’s mean() on character returns NA, so every wide significance column, and therefore every *_signif_level in the output, is 0 by construction. The p-value columns beside them are real.
Beta selection is by regression-type id, which in the source is data.table’s .GRP, the first-appearance order of the triple in the input CSV. A reordered input would silently reassign the betas, so build_regression_type_ids asserts the expected triples and raises before any beta is read.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
Taken as given
The AR(1) regressions themselves, which are run upstream and consumed here as a committed results table. The committed per-country output reproduces to the float, which the test suite pins.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Fire Protection
text:
What is open
Which of the three variants is the account’s fire protection value. Baseline and nature-versus-human cause both total negative globally, so the choice sets both the number and its interpretation. fire_protection_gep defaults to the nature-versus-human cause difference provisionally.
The ADM2 burned-area panel is not staged, and its own README says it lives on the drive. Until it arrives, the 2018 burned areas and the damage rates are read from the frozen reference output, with a loud log line each time, so the beta science and everything downstream still run and verify on any machine.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year crop-productivity shock for the eight crop sectors (PDR, WHT, GRO, V_F, OSD, C_B, PFB, OCR), so the economic model responds to the soil protection each scenario’s land cover actually provides rather than to a frozen table.
Land cover enters soil loss only through the cover-management factor, so scenario differences in this module are land-driven by construction.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year crop-productivity shock for the eight crop sectors (PDR, WHT, GRO, V_F, OSD, C_B, PFB, OCR), so the economic model responds to the soil protection each scenario’s land cover actually provides rather than to a frozen table.
Land cover enters soil loss only through the cover-management factor, so scenario differences in this module are land-driven by construction.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Method
The biophysics is InVEST’s Sediment Delivery Ratio model, run per scenario and anchor year. It yields two rasters that everything downstream is built from: USLE, the soil loss under actual land cover, and RKLS, the loss the same pixel would suffer bare. Their difference is the erosion the land cover prevents.
Turning that into an economic shock needs a coefficient linking erosion to yield. No method avoids this, so it is the key calibration for erosion regardless of which variant is used.
We report two formulations side by side, because they answer different questions and neither is strictly better.

A, “damage_area” (the conservative reading, the 8% approach)
Only severe erosion is assumed to harm yield. A pixel is severe where USLE exceeds 11 t/ha/yr. Cropland is SEALS7 class 2, measured as the full-resolution cropland fraction of each cell. For each zone,
\[\text{level}_A = -100 \times 0.08 \times p_{crop}, \qquad p_{crop} = \frac{\text{severe cropland area}}{\text{total cropland area}}\]
This is thresholded, binary, on-farm only, and weighted by cropland area. Because land cover carries no crop detail, method A is necessarily uniform across sectors; it cannot tell wheat land from vegetable land. It runs as erosion_method = 'damage_area' (erosion_damage_pipeline.py), and its shock is the scenario’s level minus the base scenario’s level in 2023, not the contemporaneous difference described below.


B, “service” (the comprehensive reading)
All erosion prevention counts, everywhere on cropland, and off-site protection is included. The prevention share combines the on-farm fraction \(1 - \text{USLE}/\text{RKLS}\) with an upstream term obtained by D8 flow-accumulating prevented and potential mass, so vegetation upslope is credited for the sediment it stops reaching land below.
Two properties matter. The zone average is magnitude-weighted: it aggregates tonnes, not percentages, as prevented over potential production-weighted mass. Without this, a pixel preventing 90 % of almost no erosion would count as much as one preventing 40 % of a great deal. And the coefficient is per crop, so a crop’s own erosion sensitivity is applied to its own prevention share before production-weighting across crops.
\[\text{level}_B = 100 \sum_c w_c \, \alpha_c \, \frac{\text{prevented}_c}{\text{potential}_c} \Big/ \sum_c w_c\]
Because crops are mapped to GTAP sectors, B reports a different shock per sector: a zone eroding mainly under cereals sends that signal to GRO rather than spreading it across all eight.


Sign conventions
A measures damage borne and is negative; B measures protection delivered and is positive. This does not affect the shock, because the two differ by a constant that cancels when the baseline is subtracted.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
From level to shock
Each level is already a percentage of crop productivity, so the shock is the absolute difference against the contemporaneous baseline (the nature-off counterfactual in the same year) not a relative change. That difference is zero at the base year and interpolated linearly between the 5-year anchors, then applied as a factor-productivity term (afeall).

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Crop coefficients
The per-crop coefficients come from a table of erosion-to-yield sensitivities keyed by FAO item names, joined to IFPRI SPAM crop groups. The join is one-to-many in places, since SPAM’s 46 groups are coarser than FAO’s item list, so a few resolutions are representative substitutions rather than exact matches (all citrus through oranges, all temperate fruit through apples, pigeon pea through dry peas). Four SPAM aggregates have no FAO counterpart and inherit their sector’s mean; for other cereals that gives 0.30, matching every named cereal in the table.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Static fallback
When a service is not listed in dynamic_es, the same seam grafts a static task that reads the frozen per-scenario dependency table instead. That table carries a single 2050 endpoint computed on older land cover, so intermediate years are a synthetic ramp rather than real per-year values, which is why the dynamic path exists.

title: Erosion-control ecosystem-service shock
text:
Compute
The SDR model is multi-hour and memory-heavy per global map, so resolution follows the run modality: a 6.45 km analysis grid locally, native SEALS resolution on a cluster. run_erosion.py runs the calculation standalone, which is the practical way to iterate on it without invoking the economic model.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text: This section outlines how we value coastal protection as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. Coastal habitats reduce the energy of waves and storm surge before it reaches the shore, so property and infrastructure behind them suffer less damage than they would on a bare coast. The service is therefore valued as avoided storm and flood damage, and it is reported for two habitats: mangroves and coral reefs. Both are attributed to the country whose coast they protect, and the two components are added to give one national coastal protection value.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Quantity
Neither component is modelled from habitat extent inside this module. Both arrive as published per-country tables in which the physical protection modelling has already been done upstream, so the quantity stage here is the read and the aggregation onto the country list rather than a biophysical calculation.
Mangroves. The mangrove component is the World Bank Changing Wealth of Nations mangrove table, staged as data_mangroves_2019.xlsx. It carries, per country, the mangrove area in hectares, a protection value per hectare, and the annual protection value that is their product, all for 2019 and all in current US dollars. The model reads the annual value column. Because the table is keyed on the r264 country label, a country that the correspondence splits into sub-regions arrives as several rows, and those rows are summed so that each country ends up with exactly one value.
Coral reefs. The coral component is the annual expected flood protection benefit table staged as coral_reefs_annual_expected_benefit_nfamara.xlsx, which gives one annual benefit per country in 2011 US dollars. This table is keyed on country name rather than country code, so it is joined to the correspondence on the name and then reduced to one row per country before the currency conversion below.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Price
No price is applied in this module. Both source tables are already monetary, which means the quantity and price stages are fused upstream and the attribution factor is one:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{coastal protection}} = Q \cdot P \cdot \lambda = \text{avoided damage} \times 1 \times 1
\]
The only monetary adjustment made here is a currency year alignment. The mangrove table is already in the base year’s dollars and needs none. The coral table is in 2011 US dollars, so every value is multiplied by one scalar: the US CPI annual-mean ratio between 2019 and 2011 (FRED’s CPIAUCSL, the same series every temporal dollar conversion in the account uses), which is 1.1366 on the staged data. The values are dollars, not local currency, so one US factor carries every country; a per-country inflation rate would answer a different question.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Valuation
The two components are joined on country and year, a country present in only one table contributes that component alone, and the national value is their sum:
\[
\text{GEP}_{\text{coastal protection},c} = V^{\text{mangrove}}_{c,2019} + V^{\text{coral}}_{c,2011} \cdot D_{2011 \rightarrow 2019}
\]
where \(V^{\text{mangrove}}_{c,2019}\) is the country’s annual mangrove protection value in 2019 dollars, \(V^{\text{coral}}_{c,2011}\) is its annual coral reef protection benefit in 2011 dollars, and \(D_{2011 \rightarrow 2019}\) is the US CPI factor between those years. The result is written as one row per country for the base year 2019, with the two components kept as separate columns beside the total so that either can be inspected on its own.
On the currently staged input data this gives a global total of \(36.28\) billion in 2019 US dollars, of which \(30.40\) billion is the mangrove component and \(5.88\) billion is the coral reef component.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Coastal Protection
text:
Known limitations
Two properties of the calculation are worth stating because they affect coverage rather than arithmetic, and neither is silent once you know to look for it.
The coral table is joined on country name, not on a code. A name that the correspondence spells differently would drop the country without failing, so the join is a place to check first when a coastal country is missing.
Because the module consumes pre-valued national tables, it cannot separate the physical extent of a habitat from the value assigned to it. A change in either the mapped habitat area or the damage function behind these tables enters here only as a changed national total.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text: Non-timber forest products cover what forests yield other than wood. The account values them per hectare of forest people can actually reach. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is value per accessible hectare.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Quantity
Hectares of accessible forest. Forest is the ESA CCI class range 50 to 90 inclusive. Accessible means inside a 10 km buffer around roads and rivers. The source repository, geo_ntfp, implements that intersection two ways, a vector-buffer calculation and a distance-raster calculation, and commits no output from either. The library therefore runs both variants and presents both, following the pattern fire protection uses for its variants.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Price
The CWoN 2024 non-wood forest product value per hectare per country, in current USD, read at the GEP base year.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Valuation
ntfp_gep_by_country filters the value series to the base year, joins it onto the accessible-area table by country label, and multiplies:
\[
\text{NTFP GEP} = \text{accessible forest (ha)} \times \text{NWFP value (USD/ha)}
\]
The function is in place and unit-tested.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the ntfp service:

ntfp_roads_region1_path, the GRIP4 Region 1 vector geodatabase, with a _source_url row pointing at the public PBL download.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Output
gep_by_country_base_year.csv in the gep_calculation task directory, holding the country label, the accessible forest hectares, the value per hectare and ntfp_gep. It is not yet produced.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Method constants

NTFP_ACCESS_BUFFER_M = 10_000, the accessibility buffer around roads and rivers.
ESA_FOREST_CLASS_MIN = 50 and ESA_FOREST_CLASS_MAX = 90, the inclusive ESA CCI forest class range.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
Taken as given
The CWoN NWFP value-per-hectare series.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Non-Timber Forest Products
text:
What is open
The accessibility raster stage is being ported and is not yet built, so gep_calculation raises NotImplementedError naming exactly what is missing rather than emitting a partial number.
The committed roads file is unusable, because only the sidecar files were committed and the .shp itself never was. The accessibility stage therefore runs on a public global roads dataset, and the original roads file remains a replication ask.
The CWoN value-per-hectare table has no es_parameters.csv row yet, so the price side of the valuation has no recorded path.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year pollination productivity shock for the crop sectors (V_F, OSD), so the economic model responds to the pollinator habitat each scenario actually produces rather than to a frozen table.
The science is William Sidemo-Holm’s crop_benefits package, imported unchanged. This module only drives it per scenario on our maps and aggregates the result to GTAP regions.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Turn the pipeline’s own 300 m SEALS land-use maps into a per-region, per-year pollination productivity shock for the crop sectors (V_F, OSD), so the economic model responds to the pollinator habitat each scenario actually produces rather than to a frozen table.
The science is William Sidemo-Holm’s crop_benefits package, imported unchanged. This module only drives it per scenario on our maps and aggregates the result to GTAP regions.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Method
For each scenario, at each SEALS anchor year:

Sufficiency (300 m). For every cropland pixel, count natural-habitat pixels within a ~2 km latitude-adjusted elliptical kernel and normalise against a 30 % habitat threshold, giving a 0–1 sufficiency index (≥30 % habitat nearby → 1; 15 % → 0.5; none → 0). SEALS7 classes: cropland = 2, natural habitat = {3, 4, 5}. The ellipse (rather than a circle) keeps the foraging radius ~2 km on the ground as longitude degrees shorten away from the equator.
Stable cropland. Sufficiency is computed only on pixels that are cropland in both the baseline and the scenario map. This isolates the change in pollinator support on continuously farmed land and excludes land that converted into or out of cropland, matching the original PNAS/InVEST pollination_shock() treatment. Each scenario therefore produces its own paired baseline raster as well as its own scenario raster.
Aggregate to 5 km. Average the 300 m index onto the CropGrids 5 km grid (over stable-ag sub-pixels only), the resolution at which crop production and value are known.
Value. Multiply 5 km sufficiency by the fixed global pollination-value raster (poll_value_global_<base_year>usd.tif, pollination-dependent crop value). The value raster is the same in every scenario, so all scenario variation enters through sufficiency.
Difference. Scenario value minus paired-baseline value, on the 5 km grid.
Regional shock. Area-weighted zonal aggregation to GTAP r50 × AEZ18 zones: (Σ difference × area) / (Σ baseline value × area) × 100, i.e. the percentage change in supported pollination value per zone.
Nature effect. Subtract the corresponding value for the baseline_ignore_dependencies scenario, so the shock isolates the nature signal rather than the shared climate/land trend.
Annual series. The per-anchor-year shocks are interpolated piecewise-linearly (numpy.interp) to annual values, anchored at 0 in the base year (all scenarios share the base-year land, so the shock is zero there by construction). Computing at every SEALS anchor year (rather than only at the horizon) lets the series follow non-linear land trajectories instead of assuming a single straight ramp.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Output
pollination_interpolated.csv with columns ENDW, ACTS, REG, scenario, year, shock_pct, shock_pct_contemp, shock_pct_fixedbase, written into the shared ES-shock directory (p.es_shock_dir). The downstream build_combined_afeall_cc_es step consumes it unchanged and is agnostic to whether the shock was computed dynamically (as here) or, for other services, read from a precomputed table.

title: Pollination ecosystem-service shock
text:
Inputs







Input
Source




Scenario LULC (300 m, SEALS7)
pipeline’s stitched SEALS maps, one per scenario × anchor year


Baseline LULC (300 m, SEALS7)
pipeline’s SEALS7 base-year map


poll_value_global_<base_year>usd.tif
crop_benefits precomputed baseline value raster


ee_r50_aez18_correspondence.gpkg
GTAP r50 × AEZ18 region boundaries



The FAO / CropGrids / Monfreda stages are not run on the shock side: they build the baseline value raster, which is fixed across scenarios, so the finished raster is used directly here.
They are run on the GEP side, where the account needs the value raster for a base year rather than a scenario. That chain is ours, in pollination_tasks.py, and it is the author’s method rather than a second one:

FAO panel. Filter the FAOSTAT production bulk to Yield and Production over 1993–2024 for the crop items in the FAO classification (run_fao_production).
Yield-change ratios. Median FAO yield in a window at the base year over a window at 2000, per country and crop, with subregion, region and world medians alongside for the countries FAO does not report (fao_yield_change).
Yield rasters. Monfreda’s 2000 yields aligned to the CropGrids grid, gaps filled from the nearest valid cell in the same country, then each country rescaled so its area-weighted mean matches the FAO number for the base year (pollination_yield_rasters).
Production rasters. Yield times CropGrids harvested area, written as tonnes per square kilometre (pollination_production_rasters).
Value raster. Production times the world producer price we build ourselves times each crop’s dependence on animal pollination, with coffee blended per country from what it grows.

Checked against the author’s own 2019 rasters on 2026-08-30: the FAO panel matches his row for row, and global production over 157 crops is 9,008.3 million tonnes on both sides.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation
text: Nature-based recreation is valued on a capital-account basis: realized visits to high-quality natural sites, priced at what each traveler spends to make them. The headline sums the ground travel of residents and of tourists to the sites, following the source’s own combined total. The accommodation tourists stay in and the international air travel that brings them to the country are valued as separate additive components and published beside the total, exactly as the source reports them. The base year is 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation
text:
Quantity
Sites. Six SEALS7 land-cover class shares plus the accessible protected-area share combine into a 0-3 environment class; urban share and distance-to-road combine into a 1-5 accessibility class; the two cross into a 1-9 site rank, of which rank 9 is a high-quality site. Contiguous high-quality pixels dissolve into discrete sites by 8-connected labelling, so one large park is one destination rather than many independent site pixels.
Trips. Each population pixel carries an annual trip budget: population times a participation level, split over distance bands within a fixed 50 km cutoff by a closed-form exponential decay. Participation and decay rate come per country from the demand-parameter table (his documented calibration: one worldwide group). A band’s fixed budget divides evenly across the sites its ring reaches; a band with no reachable site, and all demand beyond the cutoff, is tracked as unmet rather than discarded. Residents travel from their home pixels (WorldPop) with the full annual rate; tourists travel from their accommodation, each person-night carrying the rate’s daily share (a/365), built by allocating each country’s UNWTO overnight stays over its national hotel stock, with the nearest reported year standing in where 2019 is unreported and a country with no overnights data in any year kept missing rather than zero. The workbook’s Units column reads Thousands, so the panel’s numbers are read as thousands of person-nights, the same convention the arrivals sheet already gets.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation
text:
Price
Ground travel: realized visits price the round trip to their band’s midpoint distance at the origin country’s fuel cost: the 2019 per-litre gasoline price times the IEA GFEI fuel economy of 7.1 litres per hundred kilometres (the staged table’s own cost-per-km column applies that economy per kilometre, one hundred times too high, so the price column is read instead). A country without fuel-price data keeps its visits and gets a missing value, never free travel. Accommodation: overnight stays times the hotel price per person per night from the author’s hybrid price surface; a price gap is missing, not free, and each country’s price-coverage share is published beside the value. Air travel: arrivals by origin region times the staged region-to-region round-trip 2019 airfare matrix (the author’s hub-pair scrape deflated by the jet-fuel producer price index; this module reads it as a staged input and makes no network request).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation
text:
Valuation
\[
\text{GEP}_i = V^{\text{daily}}_i + V^{\text{tourist}}_i
\]
the source’s combined total, plain addition, so a country whose fuel-cost or overnights gap makes either ground channel unknown has a missing total rather than a partial one presented as complete. Accommodation and air travel are published beside the total as separate additive columns with their coverage shares, as the source’s own country table reports them. One row per country on the r250 list.
A tourist person-night carries the daily share of the annual participation rate, a/365 or about 0.28 visits per night at zero distance. This is the author’s correction of the delivered construction, which priced each night at the full annual rate of 102.5 visits. The demand parameters are his documented calibration, one worldwide group (a 102.50 annual visits per capita, decay 0.167 per km) from the England, Tel Aviv and Beijing surveys; country-specific groups are the outstanding task his methods page names.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation
text:
Implementation notes
The flow engine windows by country where the source windows by parameter group; the maths is pixel-local within the 50 km cutoff and country ids partition each group’s pixels, so the two give the same flows, pinned by a test that computes both formulations on one toy grid. The source also computes a distance-to-site transform its engine never reads; that step is not ported.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Recreation
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the recreation service key: the six land-cover share rasters, the protected-area share, distance-to-road, the road-length reference grid, WorldPop, the fuel-cost table, the UNWTO all-data workbook, the hotel-points vector, the demand-parameter table, the hotel-price surface, the region crosswalk and the staged airfare matrix, each with a source row beside it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text: Air filtration is valued as avoided mortality. Vegetation captures dry pollutants, fewer people die, and those deaths are priced at a value of statistical life. One workbook on the consortium drive carries two channels, so this module writes two service columns. Deposition is the air filtration service. Dust, meaning windblown-dust suppression, is the sandstorm prevention service, which has its own row on the account sheet and no module of its own. The base year is 2019 and the price convention recorded in es_config.csv is VSL (avoided mortality).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Quantity
Avoided deaths per country per channel, the workbook’s Dep_Deaths and Dust_Deaths columns.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Price
The workbook’s VSL column. Where a country has its own VSL the workbook marks VSL_Source as country. Where it does not, the row is marked global_avg and carries the mean of the country-source VSLs. verify_global_average_fill asserts that rule at rtol 1e-9 and raises if the workbook stops following it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Valuation
air_quality_benefits recomputes both products from the workbook’s own columns:
\[\text{air filtration GEP} = \text{Dep\_Deaths} \times \text{VSL}, \qquad
\text{sandstorm prevention GEP} = \text{Dust\_Deaths} \times \text{VSL}\]
The tests hold that recomputation to the workbook’s own benefit columns. The deposition total, $17.81bn, is the manuscript’s air-filtration number.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Joining to countries
air_quality_gep_by_country joins the workbook onto the r250 ids by position, because both the workbook and the reference order are the r250 geopackage in row order and the workbook’s FID is the geopackage feature id. The join refuses to proceed unless the row counts match and at least AIR_FILTRATION_MIN_NAME_MATCHES names are identical. 199 of 250 names are identical, and the rest differ only in sovereign versus territory naming of the same rows.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Inputs
From es_parameters.csv, scoped to the air_filtration service:

air_filtration_workbook_path, the committed per-country workbook, with a _source_note row recording that it comes from the drive’s air filtration folder rather than a public URL.

reference/r250_gpkg_order.csv ships inside the module and supplies the row order the positional join checks against.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Output
gep_calculation writes gep_by_country_base_year.csv into its own task directory, holding the r250 identifiers and attributes, year, air_filtration_gep and sandstorm_prevention_gep. Both totals are logged.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Method constants

AIR_FILTRATION_VSL_USA = 9_900_000, the US anchor VSL the documented method starts from.
AIR_FILTRATION_MIN_NAME_MATCHES = 190, the sanity floor under the positional join.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
Taken as given
The science behind the avoided-death columns, a coupled set of process-based emissions models, Global InMAP and health impacts as the appendix describes it, is not rebuildable here and is adopted as published. The valuation layer on top of it is rebuilt and verified against the workbook exactly.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Air Filtration
text:
What is open
The VSL build behind the workbook. The folder’s vsl.R and its raw CSVs document a US-anchored, GDP- and life-years-adjusted method, and gdp_adjusted_vsl ports that method for transparency, scaling the US VSL per life-year lost by GDP and applying it to each country’s own life expectancy minus median age. Run against the committed raw data it does not reproduce the workbook’s VSL column, which points to a different data vintage. That vintage gap is a named ask.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Mental Health (Depression)
text:
Urban greenspace is valued as the depression cases it prevents. Paving over a city’s nature would raise its residents’ depression risk; the cases that rise represents are the cases today’s greenness prevents, priced at the societal cost of one case. The base year is 2019.
⚠ Coverage is the 32 countries with a societal-cost estimate (Christensen et al. 2020), by construction. Those costs arrive in international (PPP) dollars of mostly 2018 and are converted to market 2019 USD by the shared price-level and CPI series, with the owner’s PPP reading kept beside the result. The counterfactual converts all urban nature to built land, following the InVEST urban mental health model.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Mental Health (Depression)
text:
Quantity
Per urban pixel on WorldPop’s 1 km grid: observed depression cases (WHO prevalence times population) times the prevented-cases factor \(e^{-10 \ln(\text{RR}) \, \text{NDVI}} - 1\), the InVEST model’s dose-response at the pixel’s annual NDVI, summed per country over the urban settlement mask. The risk ratio comes from the Liu et al. 2023 meta-analytic odds ratio (health_depression_odds_ratio) converted at the country’s own prevalence (Zhang and Yu 1998).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Mental Health (Depression)
text:
Price
The societal cost of one depression case – healthcare plus productivity losses – from the owner’s staged Christensen et al. 2020 extract. The extract reports international (PPP) dollars, so each country’s cost is multiplied by its price-level ratio (market GDP over PPP GDP, the account’s shared series) and then by the US CPI factor from the cost year to 2019, giving market 2019 USD.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Mental Health (Depression)
text:
Valuation
\[
\text{GEP}_i = c_i \; x_i \sum_{j \in \text{urban}} n_j \left(e^{-10 \ln(\text{RR}_i)\,\text{NDVI}_j} - 1\right)
\]
with \(c_i\) the cost per case, \(x_i\) the prevalence and \(n_j\) the pixel population. The author’s high-resolution results file is carried beside the result as the comparison point; its spatial scope is an open question, so the run log reports the gap rather than anchoring.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Mental Health (Depression)
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the health_depression service key. The three rasters (population, NDVI, urban mask) are the hypertension strand’s staged files, shared deliberately; the disease tables (prevalence, costs, odds ratio, the author’s reference) are this service’s own, each with a source row beside it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text: Extractive materials provision covers mineral extraction. The account values it from two World Bank series, the share of a country’s GDP that mineral rents represent and the GDP itself, with an attribution factor applied to the resulting rent. The base year is 2019.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Quantity
GDP in current USD, the World Bank series NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, read from the path recorded in es_config.csv as gep_quantity_input_path.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Price
Mineral rents as a percentage of GDP, the World Bank series NY.GDP.MINR.RT.ZS, read from the path recorded in es_config.csv as gep_attribution_input_path.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Attribution
A factor of 0.49 is applied to the rent. MINERAL_RENT_GEP_FACTOR holds it in the tasks module.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Valuation
mineral_rent_gep is the whole product:
\[
\text{GEP} = \frac{\text{mineral rent (\% of GDP)}}{100} \times \text{GDP (current USD)} \times 0.49
\]
The task reads each wide World Bank CSV and passes the frame to world_bank_wide_to_long, which melts the year columns into long form keyed on Country Code and drops the descriptive columns by not naming them. The two long tables are merged on Country Code and year and deduplicated on that pair. collapse_countries_to_r250 reduces the r264 correspondence to one canonical row per country before the join, so a country that r264 splits is not repeated. The base-year table is the rows where year equals p.gep_base_year. group_countries aggregates the value column by year for the time series.
Country references are published at 30 arcsecond simplification for this service, rather than the 300 arcsecond default the other modules use.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Inputs
Both data paths come from es_config.csv rather than es_parameters.csv. The extractive_materials_provision row names gep_quantity_input_path for the GDP series and gep_attribution_input_path for the mineral rent share, along with gep_regions_input_path as cartographic/ee/ee_r264_correspondence.gpkg and gep_regions_id_col as ee_r264_id. The service has no es_parameters.csv rows.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Outputs
gep_calculation writes four tables into its own task directory:

gep_by_country_year_mineral.csv, the merged long table with the valuation column.
gep_by_country_year.csv, the same table carried forward.
gep_by_country_base_year.csv, the 2019 rows, plus a matching .gpkg for mapping.
gep_by_year.csv and an .xlsx alongside it, the annual totals.

The valuation column is extractive_materials_provision_gep, mirrored into a Value column for the annual aggregation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Method constants
MINERAL_RENT_GEP_FACTOR = 0.49, applied to mineral rents times GDP in the valuation.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
Taken as given
Both World Bank series are used as published.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Extractive Materials Provision
text:
What is open
The attribution factor’s provenance is undocumented as of 2026-08-16. There is no source for 0.49 in the code, in the drive submission, or in its raw_data notes, and it is an open question for the service owner. The staged reference output embeds the factor, so it should not change without an owner-blessed source.
gep_by_country_year.csv and gep_by_country_year_mineral.csv are the same table written twice. The valuation produces one row per country and year, so there is nothing for the second table to add until the service gains a per-mineral breakdown.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Moisture Recycling (Rainfall Pattern Regulation)
text:
Moisture recycling values the rain that a country’s land sends elsewhere. Terrestrial evaporation supplies roughly 40 to 50 percent of the rain that falls over land, so part of every country’s usable water was made by ecosystems upstream of it, often across a border. The account values water where it is withdrawn; this service re-attributes the terrestrially-sourced share of that value to the countries whose evaporation became the rain. The base year is 2019.
⚠ The published total is a re-attribution of a subset of the water-supply row, never an addition to it. The source-side total equals the sink-side total by construction, and the task raises if they differ.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Moisture Recycling (Rainfall Pattern Regulation)
text:
Quantity
The WAM2layers country-to-country sink-fraction matrix (Bakels and Wang-Erlandsson): cell \([i, j]\) is the fraction of column-country \(j\)’s 2019 precipitation that evaporated from row-country \(i\)’s land. A column sums to \(j\)’s terrestrial-origin share, below one because the remainder comes from the ocean. Read from the path recorded in es_parameters.csv as moisture_recycling_sink_fraction_input_path. Twelve destinations sit below the 0.5 degree tracking grid and carry all-NaN columns; their water value goes unattributed and the task names them and it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Moisture Recycling (Rainfall Pattern Regulation)
text:
Price
None of its own. The value being re-attributed is the water-supply account’s irrigation premium GEP and domestic GEP by country, read as a staged snapshot from moisture_recycling_water_gep_input_path with the component columns listed in moisture_recycling_water_gep_component_cols.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Moisture Recycling (Rainfall Pattern Regulation)
text:
Attribution
moisture_recycling_ecosystem_share scales the terrestrial evaporation credited to ecosystems. It is 1 in es_parameters.csv, counting all terrestrial evaporation; the transpiration-share decision that would lower it is open with the group.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Moisture Recycling (Rainfall Pattern Regulation)
text:
Valuation
reattributed_water_value is the whole product:
\[
\text{GEP}_i = s \sum_j M_{ij} \, V_j
\]
where \(M\) is the sink-fraction matrix, \(V_j\) is destination \(j\)’s irrigation plus domestic water GEP, and \(s\) is the ecosystem share. The diagonal term is published as the own part (a country’s moisture serving its own water use) and the rest as the export part. The destination-side view, \(V_j\) times \(j\)’s terrestrial-origin share, is published beside it as moisture_recycling_sink_side_value: the same money read from the other end, which is what makes the nesting under water supply visible per country.
collapse_countries_to_r250 reduces the r264 correspondence to one canonical row per country before the join, and the published table carries every account country, NA where the matrix has no row.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Moisture Recycling (Rainfall Pattern Regulation)
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the moisture_recycling service key: the sink-fraction matrix, the water-supply snapshot it re-attributes, the component column list, and the ecosystem share, each with a source row beside it.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Physical Health (Hypertension)
text:
Urban greenspace is valued as the hypertension treatment cost it avoids. Greener urban surroundings lower the odds of hypertension, so each city’s greenness translates into avoided cases among its adults, priced at the country’s published cost of treating one case. The base year is 2019.
⚠ Coverage is limited to the countries with a refereed treatment-cost study (20, appendix Table A1), by construction; every other country carries NA with the absence named. The counterfactual is a zero-vegetation city, which does much of the work in the magnitude.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Physical Health (Hypertension)
text:
Quantity
Per urban pixel on WorldPop’s 1 km grid: population times annual NDVI (clamped at zero below), summed per country over pixels inside the urban settlement mask (health_hypertension_urban_smod_min). That sum, in 0.1-NDVI increments, times the WHO hypertension prevalence among adults 30-79, times one minus the risk ratio, times the 30-79 population share, is the country’s avoided cases. The risk ratio comes from the meta-analytic odds ratio (health_hypertension_odds_ratio) converted at the country’s own prevalence as the baseline (Grant 2014).

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Physical Health (Hypertension)
text:
Price
The country’s per-person hypertension treatment cost in 2019 USD, one refereed study per country (appendix Table A1), read from the staged table.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Physical Health (Hypertension)
text:
Valuation
\[
\text{GEP}_i = c_i \; x_i \, \frac{\sum_{j \in \text{urban}} \text{NDVI}_j \, n_j}{0.1} \left(1 - \text{RR}_i\right) s_i
\]
with \(c_i\) the treatment cost, \(x_i\) the prevalence, \(\text{RR}_i\) the converted risk ratio, \(s_i\) the 30-79 population share and \(n_j\) the pixel population. The appendix’s own Table 6 is carried beside the result as the comparison anchor; because the authors’ pixel-level choices are not fully pinned, agreement is judged at the level-and-rank grade.

title: Overview of Ecosystem Service: Physical Health (Hypertension)
text:
Inputs
All paths and parameters come from es_parameters.csv under the health_hypertension service key: the WorldPop mosaic, the annual NDVI, the GHS-SMOD urban mask and its threshold, the WHO prevalence, the 30-79 shares, the cost table, the odds ratio and the appendix reference, each with a source row beside it.

title: Hazelbean
text:
Hazelbean is the shared base library of the Earth-Economy Devstack. Every model in the stack — SEALS, GTAP-InVEST, GTAPPy, global_invest — imports it, and it supplies two distinct things:

Geospatial and analytical utilities built on GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, Cython, pygeoprocessing, taskgraph, natcap.invest and geopandas, for common tasks in sustainability science, ecosystem service assessment, integrated modelling, natural capital accounting and CGE modelling.
ProjectFlow, the task-tree engine that gives every model its project directory layout, skip-if-already-computed re-runs, automatic base-data download, and parallel iteration.



pip install hazelbean
For the developer install from a clone — and the C/C++ compiler needed to build the Cython extensions — see Installation.
Test that it imports. This also triggers compilation of the Cython files if they are not already built:
import hazelbean as hb






page
what it covers




Learning path
a guided route through the library, from first import to a full workflow


Tutorial examples

Troubleshooting
common environment, compilation and runtime problems

Project complexity

Conventions

Geospatial processing — raster read/write and processing, vector operations over shapefiles and GeoPackages, Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) creation and validation, and Performance Optimized GeoTIFFs (POG) for speed.
Larger-than-memory computation — hb.raster_calculator() streams a computation chunk by chunk across cores, so a global raster never has to load at once.
Path resolution and data acquisition — p.get_path() resolves a relative ref_path against the project input directory, then base data, then a cloud bucket, downloading whatever is missing. One base_data directory serves every project on a machine.
ProjectFlow — projects, task trees, existence-checked tasks, run_mode reuse policy, and parallel iterators. See ProjectFlow.



Hazelbean is developed at github.com/jandrewjohnson/hazelbean_dev. Its release history is in the repository’s CHANGELOG.md, and is summarized on the Release Notes page.

title: Base Data
text:
The Earth-Economy Devstack maintains a single shared, curated data store — base_data — that all projects in the stack draw from. Rather than each project bundling (or losing track of) its own copies of common inputs, code references data by a ref path (a path relative to the base_data root) and ProjectFlow’s get_path() resolves it: locally if present, from a shared data root if one is mounted, and otherwise by downloading it from our cloud storage automatically. The full resolution order is defined in Conventions.
Two properties make base_data more than a pile of files:

It is automatically downloadable. Any project that references data by ref path “just works” on a fresh machine — clone the repo, run it, and get_path() fetches what is missing. This is the backbone of our replicability story.
All rasters are Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (POGs). Every raster spans the globe on one of a fixed set of nested resolutions with bit-identical geotransforms, which enables downloading a subset of a single raster, exact and very fast zonal statistics, and accurate area-per-cell calculations without ever using projected data.



Top-level directories group data by theme or by the tool that consumes them — for example cartographic (administrative and other boundary vectors, e.g. GADM), pyramids (the canonical ha_per_cell_<res>sec.tif grids the POG system is built on), lulc (land-use/land-cover time series such as ESA CCI and their simplified reclassifications), gtappy (GTAP aggregation mappings and correspondences), luh2 and iams (coarse projection sources), plus crops, soil, seals, global_invest, gtap_invest, and invest_sample_data.
Within these, files follow the EE Spec naming and organization rules in Conventions, so a ref path is predictable from what the data is.



Lab members can contribute their project’s input data so their work runs seamlessly for everyone else — see Contributing Base Data for the submissions workflow, and POGs for the raster format contributions are cleaned into.
Changes to the store itself are tracked in the Base Data release notes.

title: GTAP Aggregation: building an aggregated database with GTAPAgg2
text:
The GTAP database ships fully disaggregated — in GTAP 10A, 141 regions × 65 sectors × 8 endowments. Almost nothing is run at that resolution. GTAPAgg2 is the tool that collapses it to whatever regional, sectoral and factor aggregation a study needs, and the aggregated database it emits is what GTAPPy runs against.
The aggregation is named, versioned and treated as an input, following the v11-s26-r50 style described in Conventions: database version, sector count, region count. GTAPPy iterates over a list of these, so producing them is a prerequisite rather than a one-off.
This page walks through producing the fully disaggregated (1:1) case, because it is the one that trips people up — it is the same procedure as any other aggregation, just with an identity mapping. Any real aggregation is the same clicks with a different scheme.


Everything happens from one window. The right-hand panel always reports what is currently loaded — release, product, data year, the source .agg file, and the current mapping counts — so it is the first thing to read when something looks wrong:



The GTAPAgg2 main menu. The right panel reports the currently loaded aggregation


The panel above reads “141 old regions map to 10 new regions, 65 old sectors map to 10 new sectors, 8 old factors map to 5 new factors” — that is the shipped Default.agg, a 10×10 aggregation. It is a useful thing to run first, because it solves in seconds, but it is not what we want here.
Note the source path it reports (...\GTAP10A\GTAP\2004\Default.agg) — the product is plain GTAP and the year is 2004. If you want AEZ land detail or a more recent base year, fix that under Choose source data before touching the mapping.



Work down the menu:
View/change regional aggregation and View/change sectoral aggregation — set both to 1:1, so all 141 regions map to 141 new regions and all 65 sectors to 65 new sectors.
View/change factor aggregation — this one does not default to the identity. It arrives as 8 endowments mapped to 5, so it has to be set to 8:8 explicitly:



Factor aggregation set 8:8, with ETRAE values determining mobility


The right-hand column is the part that matters economically. ETRAE is the elasticity of transformation between uses: a finite negative value makes a factor sluggish (Land at −1.0, NatlRes at −0.001, i.e. nearly fixed in place), while mobile makes it perfectly mobile across sectors. Here everything except Land and Natural Resources is set mobile — the labour categories, capital, and tech_aspros are all free to move.






NoteAEZ land and factor aggregation



When using the AEZ product, land is specified separately for each agro-ecological zone, which interacts awkwardly with factor aggregation. As of these notes that was an open issue Erwin was working on, and the workaround was to fall back to the standard (non-AEZ) GTAP package for the 1:1 build. Check the current state of the AEZ package before assuming this still applies.


An alternative to all of the above is Read aggregation scheme from file, which loads a .agg you already have — the shipped Default.agg is the 10×10 one described above.



Save aggregation scheme to file writes the .agg into AggStore. Name it for what it is, not for the project that first needed it:



Saving the scheme as gtp65_141_all.agg in AggStore


The .agg file is plain text. Once you have seen one, the fastest way to produce a systematic family of aggregations is to write them with a text editor (or from Python) rather than clicking through the GUI each time — which is how the aggregations GTAPPy iterates over are actually maintained.



Create aggregated database does the work and reports what it produced:



The aggregated database, written as a zip archive into AggStore


The output is a zip in AggStore named for the aggregation — here GTAP10A_GTAP_2014_65x141.zip — containing the pieces the model reads:







file
contents




basedata.har
the flows database


baserate.har
implied tax rates


baseview.har
general summary


default.prm
behavioural parameters (elasticities)


sets.har
set definitions


co2.har, gsdvole.har, gtapsam.har
emissions, energy volumes, SAM


metadata.har
metadata


gtp65_141_all.agg
the aggregation mapping used to build it


gtapv7.zip
the v7-format version of the same database



That last entry is the one to pay attention to. GTAPAgg2 emits the database in two formats: one for the GTAP v6.2 model code and one for v7.0, the latter nested inside gtapv7.zip. GTAPPy uses v7. Extracting the outer zip and pointing at its contents is a standard mistake that produces a database the v7 model will not read.
So the aggregated database you want ends up somewhere like:
C:\GTPAg2\AggStore\GTAP10A_GTAP_2014_65x141\gtapv7
That directory is what gets copied into a model version directory in Run GTAP, and what a GTAPPy run file points at as its data directory for that aggregation label.

title: Installation of Hazelbean in Julia
text:
Warning



This page is a work in progress.





On windows, Install Julia (which includes juliaup, the official Julia installer/manager) from the Microsoft Store: https://www.microsoft.com/store/apps/9NJNWW8PVKMN

For full installation instructions here: https://julialang.org/install/


Run the Julia application you just installed.

An easy way is to do this is press the start button and type Julia.
This will call juliaup, which is a nice tool that will get you the latest version of the actual Julia code.


After juliaup is called, each subsequent time you call Julia, it will enter a Julia REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop, basically a command line instance of Julia)





Julia can have different environments (configurations of packages). Managing environments is notoriously challenging, but it is important.
When you called juliaup above, it created a default system environment, stored in your Users directory


This is the default system Julia installation. It’s tempting to use only this, but that can quickly get confusing and cause dependency nightmares.
Better is to have specific environments tied to specific project and Git repo.





A good Julia git repository will have two critical files at its project root: Project.toml and Manifest.toml. Together, these will tell your Julia how to install the exact versions of all packages needed. After you clone a repo with these files, navigate to that directory in the Command Prompt/Terminal and run:
julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
This will launch Julia, set the project to the current directory, and then install all of the packages in Project.toml and Manifest.toml.



If you’re making your own environment or need to add additional packages, you can add them via Julia’s package manager. To do so:

Launch Julia REPL for this project with julia –project=.
In Julia REPL, type ] to enter the Package manager.
Install additional packages by name with something like this:

add ArchGDAL DataFrames JuMP CSV Plots Statistics GLM Optim JSON HTTP
When run in a project folder, this Add command will write/update the Manifest and Project files.

title: Installing New Repos
text:
Assuming you have already setup your python environment and installed VS Code, the first step is to clone all of the relevant repositories into the exact-right location. Throughout this documentation, we refer to “EE Spec”, or Earth-Economy Specification. This is simply the common conventions for things like naming files and organizing them so that it works for all participants; the full set is written up on the Conventions page. The EE Spec organization is to clone the earth_economy_devstack repository, available at https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/earth_economy_devstack, into your Users directory in a subdirectory called Files. The PC version is shown below.

To clone here, you can use the command line, navigate to the Files directory and use git clone https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/earth_economy_devstack . Alternatively you could use VS Code’s Command Pallate <ctrl-shift-s> Git Clone command and navigate to this repo. This repository configures VS Code to work well with the other EE repos and, for instance, defines launch-configurations that will always use the latest from github.



Next, create a folder for each of the five core repositories in the Files directory, as in the picture above.

hazelbean
seals
gtappy
gtap_invest
global_invest

Inside each of these folders, you will clone the corresponding repositories:

https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/hazelbean_dev
https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/seals
https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/gtappy_dev
https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/gtap_invest_dev
https://github.com/NatCapTEEMs/global_invest_dev

If successful, you will have a new folder with _dev postpended, indicating that it is the repository itself (and is the dev, i.e., not yet public, version of it). For GTAPPy it should look like this:

SEALS is the exception: it is public, so the repository is named seals rather than seals_dev and clones to Files/seals/seals. The nesting (a folder named for the model, containing the repository) is the same either way, and it is what lets a project directory sit next to the repository rather than inside it.
All code will be stored in the repository directory. All files that you will generate when running the libraries, conversely, will be in a different projects directory as above (This will be discussed more in the ProjectFlow section). You do not create that directory by hand: ProjectFlow derives it from the repository layout, placing a run’s outputs at Files/<model>/projects/<project_name>/. See ProjectFlow for how that resolution works and Run templates for what a run file that uses it looks like.


The five above are what the workspace file loads and what the libraries import from each other. Several further repositories build on them, and are cloned the same way (a folder named for the model, containing the repo) only when you need them:



repository
what it is




https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/gtap_invest_viz
visualization and reporting for GTAP-InVEST outputs


https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/linneabean_dev
linneabean


https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/seals_cgebox_dev
the SEALS ↔︎ CGEBox coupling



Individual studies get their own repository too, cloned into a wrapper directory under the model they extend — Files/gtap_invest/projects/ngfs/ngfs_pnas/ and Files/seals/projects/nff_global/ are the pattern. A project repository holds one study’s run file, its scenario and parameter CSVs, and any tasks specific to it; everything reusable stays in the libraries above. Adding one to your workspace is the same clone-into-a-named-folder step.

title: Installing New Repos
text:
Assuming you have already setup your python environment and installed VS Code, the first step is to clone all of the relevant repositories into the exact-right location. Throughout this documentation, we refer to “EE Spec”, or Earth-Economy Specification. This is simply the common conventions for things like naming files and organizing them so that it works for all participants; the full set is written up on the Conventions page. The EE Spec organization is to clone the earth_economy_devstack repository, available at https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/earth_economy_devstack, into your Users directory in a subdirectory called Files. The PC version is shown below.

To clone here, you can use the command line, navigate to the Files directory and use git clone https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/earth_economy_devstack . Alternatively you could use VS Code’s Command Pallate <ctrl-shift-s> Git Clone command and navigate to this repo. This repository configures VS Code to work well with the other EE repos and, for instance, defines launch-configurations that will always use the latest from github.

title: Release Notes
text:
Release history for the Earth-Economy Devstack itself — hazelbean, ProjectFlow, the conventions, and the shared examples.
Each product keeps its own release notes: SEALS · GTAP-InVEST · Hazelbean · GTAPPy · Base Data.



Changed versioning to match the GTAP-InVEST project to which its development was associated. In this, we had:

1.0 WWF, 141 regions, no AEZs
2.0 ECN, 36 regions, 18 aez, endogenous LUC
3.0 PNAS, 36 regions, 18 aez, endogenous LUC, new policies
4.0 CWON, 50 regions, 18 aez, endogenous LUC, GTAP v11 data, recursive dynamic

New feature: 2-stage downscaling is now default (rather than implemented in the GTAP-InVEST code). Users can optionally give either (but at least one) coarse_projections_input_path or regional_projections input path. The two different downscaling scales are referred to as regional, where we assume a vector-file of regions that have corresponding LUC for different classes, or coarse, where we assume a raster file of LUC classes.
Added documentation of different sceanrio_definition.csv paramters:

scenario_label: User-defined string to identify the scenario. Will be referenced (NYI) by automatic plotting calls according to baseline_reference_label or comparison_counterfactual_labels
scenario_type: One of [‘baseline’, ‘bau’, ‘policy’].

Baseline scenarios aren’t downscaled (because they have been observed), but they still need a line in the scenarios file to define which model defined them and in what year they have data.
BAU scenarios are downscaled, relative either to the baseline sceanrio or the previous year if not the first year. Technically bau scenarios are no different than policy scenarios except insofar as they have different interpretation about if e.g. a policy is effective relative to BAU.
Policy scenarios are downscaled, relative to the baseline scenario or the previous year if not the first year and might be compared to BAU (NYI)

aoi: One of [‘global’, , or canonical_path to a gpkg vector file]
exogenous_label: String representing some set of exogenous drivers, typically defined by the SSP database for population, TFP growth, GDP, etc. By convention, if its an SSP, format it as e.g. ssp3
climate_label: String representing the RCP in use. Format as e.g. rcp45
model_label: String representing the model used to generate the scenario. Format as e.g. luh2-message.
counterfactual_label: String representing some counterfactual. For example, in the latest release, we have a new test file that has 3 counterfactuals:

bau: defined just by the luh2 results
bau_shift: shift the luh2 results by the values in regional_projections_path
just_shift: downscale only the shift using a proportional coarse downscaling

years: space-delimited list of years that will be downscaled.
baseline_reference_label: scenario_label to which dowscaled scenarios might be compared (NYI)
base_years: space-delimited list of years that are in the observed data. If not calabrating the algorithm, these will just be a single year (which will be identical to key_base_year), but when calibrating, these are the years that define the training set. For future applications, these years could also be the validation/backcasting years
key_base_year: The final base year from which the model transitions from “oberved” to “projected” data.
comparison_counterfactual_labels: scenario_label to which policy scenarios might be compared (e.g., the bau), NYI.
coarse_projections_input_path: canonical path to a file that contains the coarse gridcells of how much each changing class will change. Typically this is a netcdf file with a layer for each year and each proportional LULC class as a variable, but there is great variation on HOW these are defined. This, the task tree must define a task that is capable of converting this file into the next step, which is geotiffs per class.
lulc_src_label: There are two different correspondences currently idntified. The first is a correspondence between src and simplification labels. Currently implemented, src is usually ‘esa’
lulc_simplification_label: Simplification label is what it gets simplified into, currently implemented to be ‘seals7’. IN PROCESS OF DEPRECATING. Use just the correspondence’s src and dst id column headers to define these.
lulc_correspondence_path: Path to a correspondence file. Defines lulc src and lulc dst labels.
coarse_src_label: IN PROCESS OF DEPRECATING.
coarse_simplification_label: IN PROCESS OF DEPRECATING.
coarse_correspondence_path: Path to a correspondence of the coarse_gridded to lulc dst
lc_class_varname: attempt at making netcdf work for all possible organizations. not sure if we should keep this.
dimensions: attempt at making netcdf work for all possible organizations. not sure if we should keep this.
time_dim_adjustment: attempt at making netcdf work for all possible organizations. not sure if we should keep this.
calibration_parameters_source: file path to a csv file that contains the calibration parameters. Could also be directory i think for when there are zone-specific ones.
base_year_lulc_path: path to LULC used for the key_base_year.
regional_projections_input_path: path to a region_id and region_label mapped to different class changes.

In simplifying lulc_src_label etc, we have clarified a few terms:

correspondence: a one to many mapping with no extra information. Contains src_id, dst_id, src_label, dst_label at minimum No additional information is stored in this file. The src and dst labels are defined in the file columns. So for instance in esa_seals7_correspondnece.csv, the file name could have been anything, but the actual src_label and dst_label strings themselves are defined in the columns esa_id and seals7_id.
structured_mapping: contains multiple one to many relationships, but also requires that the first src listed is unique. Note that if you groupby, you have to drop the previously disaggregate label (or perhaps nyi list it in a curled-up dimension with cat-ears?).
unstructured_mapping: like structured_mapping but doesn’t require that the first src listed is unique. If you take a structured_mapping and groupby on it, it will necessarily result in an unstructured_mapping.

NOTE: The proposed changes to correspondences etc. haven’t been incorporated into the GTAP-InVEST code yet. do it.

Earlier ProjectFlow-era entries (v0.4.0, v0.5.0) have moved to the Hazelbean release notes.

title: Running GTAP by hand
text:
GTAPPy generates CMF files and calls GEMPACK so you do not have to do this manually. It is still worth doing once. The manual route is where the model version directory comes from in the first place, it is the fastest way to check that a new database or a new shock is sane before wiring it into a task tree, and when a GTAPPy run fails it fails at one of the steps below.


RunGTAP organises work into versions — a directory holding model code, data, shock files and experiment definitions. What we want is a v7 version containing our own aggregated database rather than the toy one RunGTAP ships with. The quickest way to get one is, somewhat inelegantly, to have RunGTAP build it and then swap the data underneath:

Under Version → Change, select NCORS3x3 — the shipped 3×3 v7 version.
Under Version → New, run the wizard with Same aggregation as current version and Simply copying everything, naming the result v7all (RunGTAP version names are capped at 8 characters):



Creating v7all from NCORS3x3 by straight copy


This creates c:\runGTAP375\v7all. Now replace the data files in it with the fully disaggregated database produced in Building an aggregated database — the contents of the gtapv7 directory, not the outer zip.



The new version also inherits .shk files from the 3×3 original (tinc.shk and friends). Those are dimensioned for the old aggregation and are wrong for the database you just dropped in.
Tools → Run Test Simulation rewrites them to match the current aggregation. This is also the full end-to-end test that the version works at all — if the database, sets and model code are inconsistent, this is where you find out.
To confirm it worked, look at Results → Macros, or open the solution in ViewSOL via View → Results Using ViewSOL. The distinction matters: RunGTAP’s own results view shows only the subset of variables in its mapping, whereas ViewSOL loads the whole .sl4 file. Checking pgdp is a quick tell — under the default test shock, prices come out up about 10%. From ViewSOL, File → open in ViewHAR gives more still, including dimensional sorting.




A non-trivial shock usually needs sets the base model does not define — you rarely want to shock all commodities, you want to shock the agricultural ones.
Sets live in the CMFSTART file, which is the version’s runtime configuration: it sets solver options and names the files to use, and it is where the closure’s sets get defined. Reach it through RunGTAP → View → Sets, enable advanced editing, then Sets → View Set Library.
Clicking COMM and copying its elements in TABLO format gives you the full commodity set as text, which you then pare down to the ones you want:



Set definitions in CMFSTART, edited in TABmate


The pattern in that file is worth reading carefully, because it is exactly what GTAPPy emits programmatically:
xset agcom #key_ag_comm# (pdr, wht, gro, v_f, osd, c_b, pfb, ocr, ctl, oap, rmk, wol);
xset agcom_sm #smaller_set# (pdr, wht, gro);

xsubset agcom is subset of acts;
xsubset agcom_sm is subset of acts;
xsubset agcom_sm is subset of agcom;

xset xagcom_sm = agcom - agcom_sm;
Three things are going on. xset declares a set by listing its elements. xsubset asserts containment, which GEMPACK checks and which is what lets the set be used where a subset of ACTS or COMM is expected — omit these and the solve fails with a set-mismatch error rather than a helpful message. And the last line defines the complement, xagcom_sm, by set subtraction: having the complement available is what lets you shock one group while holding the rest fixed, or apply opposite shocks to the two halves.
Here agcom is the full agricultural commodity list and agcom_sm a three-element subset used for quick tests.



With the sets defined, the Shocks tab takes shock statements over them:



A uniform 10% productivity shock over agcom_sm on the Shocks tab


Shock aoall(agcom_sm, reg) = uniform 10;
Then set the solution method to Gragg 2-4-6, save the experiment, and solve.






TipWhen the solver will not converge



From Tom: if Gragg does not work, use Euler with many steps — 20 to 50. It is slower but far more forgiving of a badly behaved database.




The shock statement above is the simplest of several forms:
Uniform. One value applied across the whole set:
Shock aoall(agcom_sm, reg) = uniform 20;
From file. Values read per element, which is how any spatially or sectorally heterogeneous scenario is applied — a yield shock from a SEALS run, a population path, a GDP trajectory. Zero means no shock, so the file covers the full set:
Shock pop(REG) = SELECT FROM FILE <filename> HEADER "<4-letter header>";
Anything in the exogenous list can be shocked this way.
Swap. Exchange an exogenous variable for an endogenous one, which changes what the model is solving for rather than perturbing it. Swapping aoreg with GDP lets you drive the model with a GDP path and back out the productivity that implies — the standard move for calibrating to an exogenous growth scenario.
Parameter replacement — not a shock. Elasticities live in gtapparm, so changing one means writing a new .prm file. This is an input change, not a perturbation, and the difference has a real consequence: with a new base database and its matching .prm and no shock, the model reproduces that database exactly. A supply-response elasticity (as in the PNAS work) is the exception — that one does change the outcome.




For production, RunGTAP is replaced by a sequence of batch files. This is the sequence GTAPPy automates, and the names are worth knowing because they appear in logs:

testsim.bat — the test simulation, as above, run first.
rungtapv7.bat — the actual simulations.
simresults.bat — post-processing. It takes the .sl4 solution files, converts each to a .sol HAR file, combines them into one file, and splits that to CSV.

Two levels of aggregation come out of the post-processing: RMAC is full dimension, RMCA is aggregated according to the chosen reporting simplification. AggMap.har defines that reporting aggregation; Allres.cmf runs it, calling allres.tab to clean the results.
Adding a new scenario therefore means touching more than the shock file: allres.tab needs the new scenario added at the top, and Allres.EXP — along with the per-scenario .EXP files — needs the correct exogenous variables listed (e.g. tpdall). Forgetting the .EXP side is a common cause of a scenario that runs but produces nothing in the summary tables.


One idiom worth recording, from working through import taxes with Erwin. A tax applied to both domestic and imported goods needs an added equation that makes the components sum:
E_tpm (all, c, COMM)(all, r, REG) tmp(c, r) = tpmall + tpreg + tpall;
And mind the distinction between shocking a rate and shocking a power: “the beef tax rate increases 50%” is not the same statement as “the power of the tariff increases 50%”, and the two give materially different answers.
