And mind the distinction between shocking a rate and shocking a power: “the beef tax rate increases 50%” is not the same statement as “the power of the tariff increases 50%”, and the two give materially different answers.

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
Pogs are Pyramidal COGs. COGs are Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs which are super awesome and allow for, among other things, downloading only a small subset of a huge file. A COG is still a regular GeoTIFF that any GIS can open, but its internal layout (tiling, internal overviews, header placement) is arranged so that a remote reader can grab just the tiles and zoom level it needs via HTTP range requests.
Pogs extend the concept to guarantee global pyramidal alignment: every POG covers the whole globe on one of a fixed set of supported resolutions, with a geotransform that is bit-for-bit identical across all files at that resolution. Because the grids nest exactly, any two POGs can be combined across resolutions with pure array indexing — no reprojection, no resampling, no half-pixel shifts — which is what makes fast exact zonal statistics and cross-resolution modeling in the devstack possible.



Solves zonal statistics inaccuracy once and for all (and is about 10-100x faster than QGIS/ArcGIS)
Solves the hectare at different latitudes problem once and for all and greatly enhances accuracy (Never, never, NERVER use projected data again!)

The function for making a pog is in Hazelbean at make_path_pog. Point it at any GeoTIFF and declare what the values are:
import hazelbean as hb

# Rewrite the file in place as a POG
hb.make_path_pog('cropland_share.tif', variable_class='intensive')

# Or write to a new file and control the details
hb.make_path_pog(
    'cropland_ha.tif',
    output_raster_path='cropland_ha_pog.tif',
    variable_class='extensive',  # hectares: summed at every coarser rung
    output_data_type=None,       # optional; defaults to the input's data type (integer extensive -> Int64)
    output_arcseconds=None,      # optional; see below
    observed_area_path=None,     # 'derive' when the input's nodata means "not observed"; see below
    compression='DEFLATE',       # default
    blocksize=512,               # default
)
variable_class is one of four, and it fixes both how the overviews aggregate and how nodata is carried:









Class
Examples
Overviews
Nodata (declared value / cells holding it)




extensive
hectares, tonnes, counts
sum of the children, in double precision; integer types are promoted to Int64 so the top rung cannot overflow
the per-type value / none: empty cells hold 0


intensive
proportions, densities, yields per ha
area-weighted mean: the block sum of value × hectares divided by the block sum of hectares, written into the overview directly. intensive_weighting='none' declares the plain mean instead, a fast approximation with no exactness claim
the per-type value / none: empty cells hold 0


categorical
land-use classes, zone ids
mode, for display only; model with per-class intensive proportion POGs
the per-type value / none: empty cells hold the none class (categorical_none_value, default 0)


covariate
elevation, temperature, slope
unweighted mean over valid children, no exactness claim
the per-type value / missing cells



The per-type value is -9999 for signed integers and floats and the type maximum for unsigned integers (255 for Byte).
An input that declares no class (no POG_VARIABLE_CLASS in its metadata, no variable_class argument) is taken as categorical if its data type is an integer and covariate otherwise, with a log line saying so. Those are the two classes that promise nothing, so a guess never manufactures an exactness claim, but declare the class: averaging hectares or summing proportions silently corrupts every coarser rung.
If the input is not already on the canonical grid, make_path_pog places it there. The steps, in order: snap the cell size to the nearest rung (or take output_arcseconds); if the input is point-registered with samples on canonical grid lines (SRTM, NASADEM, the Copernicus DEM), apply the registration shift instead of resampling (below); otherwise resample once onto the rung’s grid (a copy when already aligned; sum for extensive; nearest for categorical and integer data; bilinear for floats; the class aggregation when the target is coarser); apply any ndv_above / ndv_below censoring and value_reclassification_dict; apply the nodata rule of the class; then compute exact statistics, build the overviews by the class rule, and write through GDAL’s COG driver. If the input already validates as a POG, it does nothing.
Nodata and observed area. Every POG declares the per-type nodata value, so tools that expect a declaration (and code that copies one from a match raster) find it. In extensive, intensive and categorical POGs no cell holds it, so sums, means and zonal statistics never have to tell a missing observation from a true zero; a raster whose real values include the per-type value needs a wider type, and make_path_pog refuses it. When the input’s nodata means not observed rather than empty, pass observed_area_path='derive': make_path_pog writes <output stem>_observed_area.tif beside the output, an extensive POG of the hectares observed in each cell, derived from the nodata mask, and records it in POG_OBSERVED_AREA. An intensive raster is then weighted by the observed area rather than by ha_per_cell (POG_DENOMINATOR names it). The coverage of a zone is then itself a zonal statistic, the zone’s sum of observed area over its area. Pass a path instead of 'derive' to attach an observed-area POG you already have.
Registration shift. SRTM, NASADEM and ASTER GDEM are point-registered, with samples on whole arcseconds, half a cell off the canonical area-registered grid. Rather than resampling them, make_path_pog reads each sample as the canonical cell whose north-west corner it occupies: the geotransform moves half a cell east and half a cell south, the values are copied unchanged, the duplicated edge row and column of a 3601 × 3601 tile are dropped, and POG_REGISTRATION_SHIFT=+0.5,-0.5 is recorded. Slope, flow direction and every other derivative of the field are unchanged to the bit; the shift (15 m at 1 arcsecond) is inside the products’ own horizontal accuracy. Pass allow_registration_shift=False to resample instead.



make_path_pog detects the input’s resolution and snaps it to the nearest rung within a tight tolerance. The target grid is synthesized from the ladder tables (hb.write_pyramid_frame_raster, a sparse raster), so no match raster needs to exist at any rung.
That automatic detection only works when the input is already close to a rung. When it isn’t (say, 0.3-degree cells), or when you deliberately want a different rung than the input’s, pass output_arcseconds:
# An input far from any rung: choose the target explicitly
hb.make_path_pog('weird_resolution.tif', 'now_a_pog.tif', output_arcseconds=1800, variable_class='covariate')

# Deliberate cross-rung conversion: 10 s cropland hectares become 900 s cropland hectares
hb.make_path_pog('crop_ha_10sec.tif', 'crop_ha_900sec.tif', output_arcseconds=900, variable_class='extensive')
When the requested rung is coarser than the input, the conversion aggregates by the class rule. If the input sits aligned on a rung that divides the target (10 s into 900 s, say), the aggregation is exact: block sums for extensive, area-weighted block means for intensive, with nodata children left out and, under observed_area_path='derive', the observed hectares under each coarse cell carried along. Otherwise it is one GDAL resample, sum for extensive, average for intensive and covariate, mode for categorical: a single documented entry, the only resampling that product will undergo on the lattice. Without output_arcseconds, an input far from every rung raises an error that names its CRS and cell size and suggests the rung to pass.
The EE Spec convention still holds: compute in proportions or per-hectare intensities and multiply by the canonical ha_per_cell of the rung as the last step. hb.write_ha_per_cell_pog(path, arcseconds) writes that raster for any rung, and hb.ha_per_cell_rows(arcseconds, first_row, n_rows) gives the same numbers for a block of rows. It is the single definition: rows are addressed by their global index (row 0 touches 90°N), and row k’s top edge is the exact rational (324000 − k × arcseconds)/3600 degrees rounded to a double once, so a row has the same bits in a global POG, a tile, a column file or an aggregation, however the raster is split. Row areas are differences of one cumulative function at those edges, so the areas of the children of a coarse cell sum to its area, which is what makes area-weighted aggregation exact.
You can verify the result (and see exactly which criterion fails, if one does) with:
hb.is_path_pog('my_raster_pog.tif', verbose=True)



The pyramids paper (Colesanti Senni and Johnson, in prep.) defines the spec in full; this page is its operational summary. A POG is a GeoTIFF that passes both checks below (this is literally what hb.is_path_pog tests — is_path_global_pyramid and is_path_cog).
1. It is a global pyramid:

Global extent, exact geotransform. The raster spans the whole globe, (-180, res, 0, 90, 0, -res), matching the canonical geotransform for its rung bit for bit. The canonical cell size of a rung of a arcseconds is the double nearest the reduced fraction a/3600 degrees (for 300 s, the double nearest 1/12, 0.08333333333333333); a value that is merely close is a different grid. The CRS is EPSG:4326 and the file is area-registered (AREA_OR_POINT=Area or absent).
A rung of the ladder. The ladder has main rungs and side rungs. A main rung stands in an exact integer ratio to every other main rung, so the main set is closed under divisibility and every path of block sums between two main rungs gives the same result; successive main ratios are 3, 3, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 2, 3, 3, 2. A side rung is a rational cell that divides at least one main rung but not all of them; it joins the main ladder at the finest main rung it divides. Both are asserted when hazelbean is imported, and ratios are tested as reduced fractions, never as floats. Fractional rungs are named as reduced fractions, 3-10sec for 3/10 arcsecond:

Main rungs from 1/9 s to one degree sit where WGS84 product families live: the USGS 3DEP 1/9” and 1/3” DEMs, SRTM, NASADEM, Copernicus GLO-30 and FABDEM at 1 s, 3DEP 2” (Alaska) at 2 s, ESA CCI at 10 s, WorldClim and GPW at 30 s, WorldClim 2.5’ at 150 s, MapSPAM and EarthStat at 300 s, LUH2 and GTAP-AEZ at 900 s, and the half- and one-degree climate grids. Above one degree they nest toward the 180-degree top rung, a 2 × 1 grid: the two faces of the equirectangular map. 5° is HadCRUT and NOAA GlobalTemp, 10° is the zoning and tile edge, and 30°, 90° and 180° are structural. The top rung is the aspect ratio of the map itself, so the ladder is body-independent: the one body-specific parameter is the area stack that weights aggregation. The side rungs carry the families between: 3-10 s (1/12000°: ESA WorldCover and the Lang et al. canopy height), 9-10 s (1/4000°: Hansen Global Forest Change, JRC Global Surface Water, GLAD), 3 s (the 90 m family: SRTM 3s, GLO-90, TanDEM-X 90, MERIT DEM and Hydro, HydroSHEDS, WorldPop, GHSL), 15 s (HydroSHEDS 15s, GEBCO), 180 s (CHIRPS and MODIS CMG at 0.05°), 360 s (ERA5-Land at 0.1°), 600 s (WorldClim 10’), and 9 s and 90 s, which own no product but give the 9-10 s family factor-10 steps to its join (overviews at about 280 m and 2.8 km rather than none between 28 m and 28 km). Every aligned grid has a rational cell size, so the p-q notation names every rung there could be.
The declared variable class and its metadata. POG_VARIABLE_CLASS is extensive, intensive, categorical or covariate; an intensive raster also declares POG_INTENSIVE_WEIGHTING (area, the default, or none) and, for area, POG_DENOMINATOR (the token ha_per_cell, or the observed-area POG). POG_OBSERVED_AREA names the companion where coverage is incomplete, and POG_REGISTRATION_SHIFT records a shift. Companion paths are stored relative to the POG’s folder.
The nodata convention of its class. Every POG declares the per-type nodata value (-9999 for signed integers and floats, the type maximum for unsigned integers, e.g. 255 for Byte). In extensive, intensive and categorical rasters no cell holds it; in a covariate it marks missing cells. make_path_pog converts the values, not just the declaration, and the validator checks both (the cell check reads the raster only when the value falls inside the stored exact statistics’ range).
Compressed with DEFLATE. This is a choice we made and in most tests deflate performs better than the more common LZW. We have also tried out ZSTD which is way better than DEFLATE but is not universally supported (yet), so a file compressed with it (or with LZW) is not a POG.
Internal overviews at exactly the prescribed levels, derived from the ladder rather than chosen, asymmetrically: a main-rung base carries one overview for every coarser main rung, up to the 180-degree top, and no side-rung levels; a side-rung base carries every side rung that is a multiple of it and a divisor of its join rung, then every main rung from the join up. Each overview is therefore an exact union of cells of the one before it, and only the top rung has none. The chain derivation raises on any non-integer ratio. Overviews are validated by dimensions, exactly, on read as on validation: each factor implies each overview’s size, and a missing level, an extra level or a near-miss factor all fail, since an extra level would be read as a rung that does not exist. Overhead is the sum of the squared inverse factors. The mapping is hb.pyramid_compatible_overview_levels:

(Rule formalized 2026-09-24. Before that the levels came from a draft in which every coarser rung that was a multiple of the base counted, so 1 s files carried 3 s and 15 s levels; before that, from a hand-written table with 2° and 4° rungs that could not nest into 10°. POGs written under either fail the level check and must be regenerated.)
Overviews that follow the class rule. A file records no resampling method, so is_path_pog checks the numbers: in each overview it recomputes a few cells, spread from pole to pole, from the level directly below by the declared rule, so every link of the chain is sampled. Integer levels must agree exactly and floating-point levels to a relative 1e-5 (float32 storage). Categorical and covariate POGs make no exactness claim and pass. hb.is_path_pog_overview_conformant(path, verbose=True) runs this check alone.
Exact statistics stored internally. Band statistics must be present and computed exactly (STATISTICS_APPROXIMATE=NO), with no stale .aux.xml sidecar shadowing them. Together with sum overviews, this makes the header of an extensive POG a source of its exact global total.

2. It is a valid COG: it passes GDAL’s COG validation — tiled layout, properly ordered internal overviews, cloud-readable header structure. The validator’s errors fail a file; its advisory warnings (e.g. “recommended to include internal overviews” on a rung with none) do not, because the exact level check above supersedes them. make_path_pog writes through the GDAL COG driver (BigTIFF, 512-pixel blocks by default) with the overviews it built and no others: left to itself the driver inserts dyadic 2, 4, 8… levels into any file that has none.



Three separate claims, each with its own evidence:

A POG is a valid OGC GeoTIFF and a valid OGC Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF. COG has been an OGC standard since 2023 (OGC 21-026). hb.is_path_cog runs GDAL’s validator, which implements that standard, and make_path_pog writes through GDAL’s COG driver.
The pyramid tiling scheme is a valid OGC Tile Matrix Set (OGC 17-083r4, “Two Dimensional Tile Matrix Set and Tile Set Metadata” 2.0). hb.get_pyramid_tile_matrix_set() publishes it: one tile matrix per rung in CRS84 with the origin at the top-left (-180, 90), id EEPyramidCRS84. It is not a quadtree — the scale progression follows the rungs, so it is not the registered WorldCRS84Quad set — which the standard explicitly allows for custom sets. Tile sizes vary by rung (below), which is why the set must be published with all twenty-five matrices (sixteen main, nine side) rather than inferred. hb.validate_tile_matrix_set_json validates the document against the schemas OGC publishes, shipped verbatim in hazelbean/ogc_schemas/tms_2.0/; that validation runs in the unit suite (test_tiles.py) and is the compliance test. hb.write_pyramid_tile_matrix_set_json(path) writes the document for use by OGC API Tiles servers or QGIS.
A subpog tile set is addressable through that tile matrix set. Tiles are named on disk by their south-west corner (below); hb.tile_corner_string_to_tile_matrix_index converts a corner name to the standard’s (tileMatrix, tileRow, tileCol) and hb.tile_matrix_index_to_tile_corner_string converts back. The unit suite checks the two are a bijection over every tile of a matrix.




Five things that are easy to conflate, defined so they stay apart:

POG — the global raster meeting the full spec above.
Subpog — a raster meeting the spec in every respect except extent. Its extent is a whole number of cells from the pyramid origin (-180, 90) at its rung (snap a box with hb.snap_bb_to_pyramid(bb, arcseconds)), and its overview levels are the global chain truncated to the levels whose cell size divides its extent (hb.get_pyramid_overview_levels_for_bb) — so every overview still lands on a rung, and the coarsest is bounded by the extent. A 1-degree tile of 1-second data therefore stops at level 3600; a 10-degree tile of 10-second data carries the chain through level 3600 (10°) and nothing coarser. Make one with hb.make_path_pog(path, expand_to_global_extent=False) (the parallel converter forwards the same flag); check with hb.is_path_subpog; a POG is a degenerate subpog. A seals AOI clip is a subpog and not a tile. The input’s footprint is snapped outward, so an input that straddles cell edges grows by up to a cell per side rather than losing data; such an extent may support no overview level at all, which is legal (the top rung has none either).
Tile — a subpog whose extent is exactly one cell of the published tile grid for its rung. Every tile is a subpog; most subpogs are not tiles.
Tile set — the tiles of one dataset at one rung and tiling, in one folder, plus the VRT that indexes them. A tile set may be sparse: tiles that would hold nothing need not exist.
VRT — not a raster. An XML index (gdalbuildvrt) that presents the tiles of a tile set to GDAL as one global raster: it carries the exact global geotransform, lists which tiles exist and where, and reads anything not listed as zero — what an empty cell of a POG holds — or, for a covariate tile set, as the per-type nodata. It holds no pixels, has no overviews of its own (coarse reads go to the tiles’ internal overviews), and cannot be a COG. hb.is_path_pog_tileset(vrt) checks the VRT frame is global, every source is a corner-named tile of one dataset, rung and edge covering the extent its name claims, and every tile is a subpog.



Corner-based, following SRTM, NASADEM, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover: the south-west corner in whole degrees, latitude then longitude, each with its cardinal letter, followed by the height and width of the extent in whole degrees. The extent is in the name, so a file is interpretable without the tile matrix set, a subpog spanning several tiles is named the same way, and the same dataset may exist at more than one tiling:
lulc_esa_2020_10sec.tif                       the global POG
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_10deg/                    its tile set (folder)
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_40N_130W_10_10.tif        one tile: south-west corner 40N 130W, 10 by 10 degrees
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_10deg.vrt                 the index, beside the folder
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_20N_30E_30_60.tif         a subpog spanning 20N to 50N and 30E to 90E
Helpers: hb.get_tile_filename, hb.get_tile_filename_from_bb (names a whole-degree subpog), hb.parse_tile_filename (returns stem, rung, corner, height, width), hb.get_tile_corner_string, hb.parse_tile_corner_string, hb.get_tile_bb_from_corner_string, hb.list_tile_corner_strings. The VRT uses relative source paths, so the folder and its VRT move together. (Names of the form …_10deg_N40W130.tif, used before 2026-09-24, no longer parse.)

They solve different problems. HTTP range requests fetch only the bytes touching a window from inside one COG — exactly what COG was designed for — and work on a global POG directly, with no tiles and no VRT. So the global POG is the default form and range requests are the default subset mechanism (planned for get_path; not yet built). Tile sets earn their place where a single file is operationally impractical: 1 second and every rung finer (a global Byte raster at 1 s is over 800 GB uncompressed), datasets regenerated or checksummed piecewise, and the Drive mirror, which syncs whole files. There the VRT is the manifest telling get_path which tile files a requested box touches. Both paths converge on a future bounding-box argument to get_path; they differ only in what is fetched — byte ranges of one file, or whole tiles named in a manifest. A dataset’s entry in base_data should say which form it uses.
Round trips: hb.tile_pog_to_tileset(pog_path, tile_degrees=None) cuts a POG into a tile set (omitting tiles that hold nothing) and returns the VRT; hb.write_subpog_from_pog_window(pog_path, bb, output_path) cuts one aligned window, carrying the variable class and its metadata; any raster becomes a subpog with make_path_pog(..., expand_to_global_extent=False); a tile set becomes a global POG again by running make_path_pog on its VRT, which reads the class from the tiles and is byte-identical to the original (test_pog_spec.py checks it).





hb.make_paths_pogs_in_parallel(...) converts a list of rasters across multiple processes, forwarding variable_class, intensive_weighting, categorical_none_value, allow_registration_shift, observed_area_path='derive' and expand_to_global_extent to every file.
hb.write_pog_of_value_from_scratch(output_path, value, arcsecond_resolution, output_data_type, variable_class=None) and hb.write_pog_of_value_from_match(output_path, match_path, value, variable_class=None) create constant-valued POGs, useful as templates or masks.
hb.write_ha_per_cell_pog(output_path, arcseconds, bb=None) writes the canonical hectares-per-cell POG of any rung (extensive, Float64).
hb.get_pog_metadata(path) returns a file’s POG_* items (for a tile-set VRT, its first tile’s).
make_path_pog also accepts ndv_above / ndv_below (censor out-of-range values before the nodata rule) and value_reclassification_dict (reclassify while converting) so you can clean a raster in the same pass that pog-ifies it.

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
Solves zonal statistics inaccuracy once and for all (and is about 10-100x faster than QGIS/ArcGIS)
Solves the hectare at different latitudes problem once and for all and greatly enhances accuracy (Never, never, NERVER use projected data again!)

The function for making a pog is in Hazelbean at make_path_pog. Point it at any GeoTIFF and declare what the values are:
import hazelbean as hb

# Rewrite the file in place as a POG
hb.make_path_pog('cropland_share.tif', variable_class='intensive')

# Or write to a new file and control the details
hb.make_path_pog(
    'cropland_ha.tif',
    output_raster_path='cropland_ha_pog.tif',
    variable_class='extensive',  # hectares: summed at every coarser rung
    output_data_type=None,       # optional; defaults to the input's data type (integer extensive -> Int64)
    output_arcseconds=None,      # optional; see below
    observed_area_path=None,     # 'derive' when the input's nodata means "not observed"; see below
    compression='DEFLATE',       # default
    blocksize=512,               # default
)
variable_class is one of four, and it fixes both how the overviews aggregate and how nodata is carried:









Class
Examples
Overviews
Nodata (declared value / cells holding it)




extensive
hectares, tonnes, counts
sum of the children, in double precision; integer types are promoted to Int64 so the top rung cannot overflow
the per-type value / none: empty cells hold 0


intensive
proportions, densities, yields per ha
area-weighted mean: the block sum of value × hectares divided by the block sum of hectares, written into the overview directly. intensive_weighting='none' declares the plain mean instead, a fast approximation with no exactness claim
the per-type value / none: empty cells hold 0


categorical
land-use classes, zone ids
mode, for display only; model with per-class intensive proportion POGs
the per-type value / none: empty cells hold the none class (categorical_none_value, default 0)


covariate
elevation, temperature, slope
unweighted mean over valid children, no exactness claim
the per-type value / missing cells



The per-type value is -9999 for signed integers and floats and the type maximum for unsigned integers (255 for Byte).
An input that declares no class (no POG_VARIABLE_CLASS in its metadata, no variable_class argument) is taken as categorical if its data type is an integer and covariate otherwise, with a log line saying so. Those are the two classes that promise nothing, so a guess never manufactures an exactness claim, but declare the class: averaging hectares or summing proportions silently corrupts every coarser rung.
If the input is not already on the canonical grid, make_path_pog places it there. The steps, in order: snap the cell size to the nearest rung (or take output_arcseconds); if the input is point-registered with samples on canonical grid lines (SRTM, NASADEM, the Copernicus DEM), apply the registration shift instead of resampling (below); otherwise resample once onto the rung’s grid (a copy when already aligned; sum for extensive; nearest for categorical and integer data; bilinear for floats; the class aggregation when the target is coarser); apply any ndv_above / ndv_below censoring and value_reclassification_dict; apply the nodata rule of the class; then compute exact statistics, build the overviews by the class rule, and write through GDAL’s COG driver. If the input already validates as a POG, it does nothing.
Nodata and observed area. Every POG declares the per-type nodata value, so tools that expect a declaration (and code that copies one from a match raster) find it. In extensive, intensive and categorical POGs no cell holds it, so sums, means and zonal statistics never have to tell a missing observation from a true zero; a raster whose real values include the per-type value needs a wider type, and make_path_pog refuses it. When the input’s nodata means not observed rather than empty, pass observed_area_path='derive': make_path_pog writes <output stem>_observed_area.tif beside the output, an extensive POG of the hectares observed in each cell, derived from the nodata mask, and records it in POG_OBSERVED_AREA. An intensive raster is then weighted by the observed area rather than by ha_per_cell (POG_DENOMINATOR names it). The coverage of a zone is then itself a zonal statistic, the zone’s sum of observed area over its area. Pass a path instead of 'derive' to attach an observed-area POG you already have.
Registration shift. SRTM, NASADEM and ASTER GDEM are point-registered, with samples on whole arcseconds, half a cell off the canonical area-registered grid. Rather than resampling them, make_path_pog reads each sample as the canonical cell whose north-west corner it occupies: the geotransform moves half a cell east and half a cell south, the values are copied unchanged, the duplicated edge row and column of a 3601 × 3601 tile are dropped, and POG_REGISTRATION_SHIFT=+0.5,-0.5 is recorded. Slope, flow direction and every other derivative of the field are unchanged to the bit; the shift (15 m at 1 arcsecond) is inside the products’ own horizontal accuracy. Pass allow_registration_shift=False to resample instead.

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
make_path_pog detects the input’s resolution and snaps it to the nearest rung within a tight tolerance. The target grid is synthesized from the ladder tables (hb.write_pyramid_frame_raster, a sparse raster), so no match raster needs to exist at any rung.
That automatic detection only works when the input is already close to a rung. When it isn’t (say, 0.3-degree cells), or when you deliberately want a different rung than the input’s, pass output_arcseconds:
# An input far from any rung: choose the target explicitly
hb.make_path_pog('weird_resolution.tif', 'now_a_pog.tif', output_arcseconds=1800, variable_class='covariate')

# Deliberate cross-rung conversion: 10 s cropland hectares become 900 s cropland hectares
hb.make_path_pog('crop_ha_10sec.tif', 'crop_ha_900sec.tif', output_arcseconds=900, variable_class='extensive')
When the requested rung is coarser than the input, the conversion aggregates by the class rule. If the input sits aligned on a rung that divides the target (10 s into 900 s, say), the aggregation is exact: block sums for extensive, area-weighted block means for intensive, with nodata children left out and, under observed_area_path='derive', the observed hectares under each coarse cell carried along. Otherwise it is one GDAL resample, sum for extensive, average for intensive and covariate, mode for categorical: a single documented entry, the only resampling that product will undergo on the lattice. Without output_arcseconds, an input far from every rung raises an error that names its CRS and cell size and suggests the rung to pass.
The EE Spec convention still holds: compute in proportions or per-hectare intensities and multiply by the canonical ha_per_cell of the rung as the last step. hb.write_ha_per_cell_pog(path, arcseconds) writes that raster for any rung, and hb.ha_per_cell_rows(arcseconds, first_row, n_rows) gives the same numbers for a block of rows. It is the single definition: rows are addressed by their global index (row 0 touches 90°N), and row k’s top edge is the exact rational (324000 − k × arcseconds)/3600 degrees rounded to a double once, so a row has the same bits in a global POG, a tile, a column file or an aggregation, however the raster is split. Row areas are differences of one cumulative function at those edges, so the areas of the children of a coarse cell sum to its area, which is what makes area-weighted aggregation exact.
You can verify the result (and see exactly which criterion fails, if one does) with:
hb.is_path_pog('my_raster_pog.tif', verbose=True)

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
The pyramids paper (Colesanti Senni and Johnson, in prep.) defines the spec in full; this page is its operational summary. A POG is a GeoTIFF that passes both checks below (this is literally what hb.is_path_pog tests — is_path_global_pyramid and is_path_cog).
1. It is a global pyramid:

Global extent, exact geotransform. The raster spans the whole globe, (-180, res, 0, 90, 0, -res), matching the canonical geotransform for its rung bit for bit. The canonical cell size of a rung of a arcseconds is the double nearest the reduced fraction a/3600 degrees (for 300 s, the double nearest 1/12, 0.08333333333333333); a value that is merely close is a different grid. The CRS is EPSG:4326 and the file is area-registered (AREA_OR_POINT=Area or absent).
A rung of the ladder. The ladder has main rungs and side rungs. A main rung stands in an exact integer ratio to every other main rung, so the main set is closed under divisibility and every path of block sums between two main rungs gives the same result; successive main ratios are 3, 3, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 2, 3, 3, 2. A side rung is a rational cell that divides at least one main rung but not all of them; it joins the main ladder at the finest main rung it divides. Both are asserted when hazelbean is imported, and ratios are tested as reduced fractions, never as floats. Fractional rungs are named as reduced fractions, 3-10sec for 3/10 arcsecond:

Main rungs from 1/9 s to one degree sit where WGS84 product families live: the USGS 3DEP 1/9” and 1/3” DEMs, SRTM, NASADEM, Copernicus GLO-30 and FABDEM at 1 s, 3DEP 2” (Alaska) at 2 s, ESA CCI at 10 s, WorldClim and GPW at 30 s, WorldClim 2.5’ at 150 s, MapSPAM and EarthStat at 300 s, LUH2 and GTAP-AEZ at 900 s, and the half- and one-degree climate grids. Above one degree they nest toward the 180-degree top rung, a 2 × 1 grid: the two faces of the equirectangular map. 5° is HadCRUT and NOAA GlobalTemp, 10° is the zoning and tile edge, and 30°, 90° and 180° are structural. The top rung is the aspect ratio of the map itself, so the ladder is body-independent: the one body-specific parameter is the area stack that weights aggregation. The side rungs carry the families between: 3-10 s (1/12000°: ESA WorldCover and the Lang et al. canopy height), 9-10 s (1/4000°: Hansen Global Forest Change, JRC Global Surface Water, GLAD), 3 s (the 90 m family: SRTM 3s, GLO-90, TanDEM-X 90, MERIT DEM and Hydro, HydroSHEDS, WorldPop, GHSL), 15 s (HydroSHEDS 15s, GEBCO), 180 s (CHIRPS and MODIS CMG at 0.05°), 360 s (ERA5-Land at 0.1°), 600 s (WorldClim 10’), and 9 s and 90 s, which own no product but give the 9-10 s family factor-10 steps to its join (overviews at about 280 m and 2.8 km rather than none between 28 m and 28 km). Every aligned grid has a rational cell size, so the p-q notation names every rung there could be.
The declared variable class and its metadata. POG_VARIABLE_CLASS is extensive, intensive, categorical or covariate; an intensive raster also declares POG_INTENSIVE_WEIGHTING (area, the default, or none) and, for area, POG_DENOMINATOR (the token ha_per_cell, or the observed-area POG). POG_OBSERVED_AREA names the companion where coverage is incomplete, and POG_REGISTRATION_SHIFT records a shift. Companion paths are stored relative to the POG’s folder.
The nodata convention of its class. Every POG declares the per-type nodata value (-9999 for signed integers and floats, the type maximum for unsigned integers, e.g. 255 for Byte). In extensive, intensive and categorical rasters no cell holds it; in a covariate it marks missing cells. make_path_pog converts the values, not just the declaration, and the validator checks both (the cell check reads the raster only when the value falls inside the stored exact statistics’ range).
Compressed with DEFLATE. This is a choice we made and in most tests deflate performs better than the more common LZW. We have also tried out ZSTD which is way better than DEFLATE but is not universally supported (yet), so a file compressed with it (or with LZW) is not a POG.
Internal overviews at exactly the prescribed levels, derived from the ladder rather than chosen, asymmetrically: a main-rung base carries one overview for every coarser main rung, up to the 180-degree top, and no side-rung levels; a side-rung base carries every side rung that is a multiple of it and a divisor of its join rung, then every main rung from the join up. Each overview is therefore an exact union of cells of the one before it, and only the top rung has none. The chain derivation raises on any non-integer ratio. Overviews are validated by dimensions, exactly, on read as on validation: each factor implies each overview’s size, and a missing level, an extra level or a near-miss factor all fail, since an extra level would be read as a rung that does not exist. (Rule formalized 2026-09-24. Before that the levels came from a draft in which every coarser rung that was a multiple of the base counted, so 1 s files carried 3 s and 15 s levels; before that, from a hand-written table with 2° and 4° rungs that could not nest into 10°. POGs written under either fail the level check and must be regenerated.)
Overviews that follow the class rule. A file records no resampling method, so is_path_pog checks the numbers: in each overview it recomputes a few cells, spread from pole to pole, from the level directly below by the declared rule, so every link of the chain is sampled. Integer levels must agree exactly and floating-point levels to a relative 1e-5 (float32 storage). Categorical and covariate POGs make no exactness claim and pass. hb.is_path_pog_overview_conformant(path, verbose=True) runs this check alone.
Exact statistics stored internally. Band statistics must be present and computed exactly (STATISTICS_APPROXIMATE=NO), with no stale .aux.xml sidecar shadowing them. Together with sum overviews, this makes the header of an extensive POG a source of its exact global total.

2. It is a valid COG: it passes GDAL’s COG validation — tiled layout, properly ordered internal overviews, cloud-readable header structure. The validator’s errors fail a file; its advisory warnings (e.g. “recommended to include internal overviews” on a rung with none) do not, because the exact level check above supersedes them. make_path_pog writes through the GDAL COG driver (BigTIFF, 512-pixel blocks by default) with the overviews it built and no others: left to itself the driver inserts dyadic 2, 4, 8… levels into any file that has none.

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
Three separate claims, each with its own evidence:

A POG is a valid OGC GeoTIFF and a valid OGC Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF. COG has been an OGC standard since 2023 (OGC 21-026). hb.is_path_cog runs GDAL’s validator, which implements that standard, and make_path_pog writes through GDAL’s COG driver.
The pyramid tiling scheme is a valid OGC Tile Matrix Set (OGC 17-083r4, “Two Dimensional Tile Matrix Set and Tile Set Metadata” 2.0). hb.get_pyramid_tile_matrix_set() publishes it: one tile matrix per rung in CRS84 with the origin at the top-left (-180, 90), id EEPyramidCRS84. It is not a quadtree — the scale progression follows the rungs, so it is not the registered WorldCRS84Quad set — which the standard explicitly allows for custom sets. Tile sizes vary by rung (below), which is why the set must be published with all twenty-five matrices (sixteen main, nine side) rather than inferred. hb.validate_tile_matrix_set_json validates the document against the schemas OGC publishes, shipped verbatim in hazelbean/ogc_schemas/tms_2.0/; that validation runs in the unit suite (test_tiles.py) and is the compliance test. hb.write_pyramid_tile_matrix_set_json(path) writes the document for use by OGC API Tiles servers or QGIS.
A subpog tile set is addressable through that tile matrix set. Tiles are named on disk by their south-west corner (below); hb.tile_corner_string_to_tile_matrix_index converts a corner name to the standard’s (tileMatrix, tileRow, tileCol) and hb.tile_matrix_index_to_tile_corner_string converts back. The unit suite checks the two are a bijection over every tile of a matrix.

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
Five things that are easy to conflate, defined so they stay apart:

POG — the global raster meeting the full spec above.
Subpog — a raster meeting the spec in every respect except extent. Its extent is a whole number of cells from the pyramid origin (-180, 90) at its rung (snap a box with hb.snap_bb_to_pyramid(bb, arcseconds)), and its overview levels are the global chain truncated to the levels whose cell size divides its extent (hb.get_pyramid_overview_levels_for_bb) — so every overview still lands on a rung, and the coarsest is bounded by the extent. A 1-degree tile of 1-second data therefore stops at level 3600; a 10-degree tile of 10-second data carries the chain through level 3600 (10°) and nothing coarser. Make one with hb.make_path_pog(path, expand_to_global_extent=False) (the parallel converter forwards the same flag); check with hb.is_path_subpog; a POG is a degenerate subpog. A seals AOI clip is a subpog and not a tile. The input’s footprint is snapped outward, so an input that straddles cell edges grows by up to a cell per side rather than losing data; such an extent may support no overview level at all, which is legal (the top rung has none either).
Tile — a subpog whose extent is exactly one cell of the published tile grid for its rung. Every tile is a subpog; most subpogs are not tiles.
Tile set — the tiles of one dataset at one rung and tiling, in one folder, plus the VRT that indexes them. A tile set may be sparse: tiles that would hold nothing need not exist.
VRT — not a raster. An XML index (gdalbuildvrt) that presents the tiles of a tile set to GDAL as one global raster: it carries the exact global geotransform, lists which tiles exist and where, and reads anything not listed as zero — what an empty cell of a POG holds — or, for a covariate tile set, as the per-type nodata. It holds no pixels, has no overviews of its own (coarse reads go to the tiles’ internal overviews), and cannot be a COG. hb.is_path_pog_tileset(vrt) checks the VRT frame is global, every source is a corner-named tile of one dataset, rung and edge covering the extent its name claims, and every tile is a subpog.



Corner-based, following SRTM, NASADEM, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover: the south-west corner in whole degrees, latitude then longitude, each with its cardinal letter, followed by the height and width of the extent in whole degrees. The extent is in the name, so a file is interpretable without the tile matrix set, a subpog spanning several tiles is named the same way, and the same dataset may exist at more than one tiling:
lulc_esa_2020_10sec.tif                       the global POG
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_10deg/                    its tile set (folder)
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_40N_130W_10_10.tif        one tile: south-west corner 40N 130W, 10 by 10 degrees
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_10deg.vrt                 the index, beside the folder
lulc_esa_2020_10sec_20N_30E_30_60.tif         a subpog spanning 20N to 50N and 30E to 90E
Helpers: hb.get_tile_filename, hb.get_tile_filename_from_bb (names a whole-degree subpog), hb.parse_tile_filename (returns stem, rung, corner, height, width), hb.get_tile_corner_string, hb.parse_tile_corner_string, hb.get_tile_bb_from_corner_string, hb.list_tile_corner_strings. The VRT uses relative source paths, so the folder and its VRT move together. (Names of the form …_10deg_N40W130.tif, used before 2026-09-24, no longer parse.)
Tile edges are chosen so a tile is a few thousand pixels per side, and every default edge is itself a main rung (1°, 5° or 10°), so tile sets at different rungs nest exactly. They are the scheme’s hb.pyramid_tile_degrees:

Products delivered in a projected CRS (Sentinel-2, Landsat, NAIP and Planet in UTM; MODIS in sinusoidal; SoilGrids in Homolosine; older GHSL releases in Mollweide), products on a geographic grid that is not a rung (Copernicus Global Land Cover at 1/1008°), and products whose cells widen at high latitude (the Copernicus DEM above 50°) enter the lattice by one resample onto the rung recorded for them, so the choice is made once per product rather than once per project. The entry is a resample, never an alignment: a 10 m UTM cell is not a 3/10-arcsecond cell, and the paper’s non-nested-support treatment applies. The paper’s Table E2 is the authoritative entry table; in brief:

They solve different problems. HTTP range requests fetch only the bytes touching a window from inside one COG — exactly what COG was designed for — and work on a global POG directly, with no tiles and no VRT. So the global POG is the default form and range requests are the default subset mechanism (planned for get_path; not yet built). Tile sets earn their place where a single file is operationally impractical: 1 second and every rung finer (a global Byte raster at 1 s is over 800 GB uncompressed), datasets regenerated or checksummed piecewise, and the Drive mirror, which syncs whole files. There the VRT is the manifest telling get_path which tile files a requested box touches. Both paths converge on a future bounding-box argument to get_path; they differ only in what is fetched — byte ranges of one file, or whole tiles named in a manifest. A dataset’s entry in base_data should say which form it uses.
Round trips: hb.tile_pog_to_tileset(pog_path, tile_degrees=None) cuts a POG into a tile set (omitting tiles that hold nothing) and returns the VRT; hb.write_subpog_from_pog_window(pog_path, bb, output_path) cuts one aligned window, carrying the variable class and its metadata; any raster becomes a subpog with make_path_pog(..., expand_to_global_extent=False); a tile set becomes a global POG again by running make_path_pog on its VRT, which reads the class from the tiles and is byte-identical to the original (test_pog_spec.py checks it).

title: Pyramidal Cloud-Optimized Geotiffs (POGs)
text:
hb.make_paths_pogs_in_parallel(...) converts a list of rasters across multiple processes, forwarding variable_class, intensive_weighting, categorical_none_value, allow_registration_shift, observed_area_path='derive' and expand_to_global_extent to every file.
hb.write_pog_of_value_from_scratch(output_path, value, arcsecond_resolution, output_data_type, variable_class=None) and hb.write_pog_of_value_from_match(output_path, match_path, value, variable_class=None) create constant-valued POGs, useful as templates or masks.
hb.write_ha_per_cell_pog(output_path, arcseconds, bb=None) writes the canonical hectares-per-cell POG of any rung (extensive, Float64).
hb.get_pog_metadata(path) returns a file’s POG_* items (for a tile-set VRT, its first tile’s).
make_path_pog also accepts ndv_above / ndv_below (censor out-of-range values before the nodata rule) and value_reclassification_dict (reclassify while converting) so you can clean a raster in the same pass that pog-ifies it.

Learning Time: 5 minutes

NoteLearning Objectives

Initialize a Hazelbean ProjectFlow for organized geospatial workflows
Understand the intelligent directory structure that Hazelbean creates

Master the data discovery hierarchy and how get_path() searches for files

TipKey Takeaway



ProjectFlow is the foundation of every Hazelbean workflow. It creates an organized directory structure and provides intelligent file path resolution that makes your analysis reproducible and professional. Think of it as your “project manager” that keeps everything organized automatically.








NoteReal-World Application



In research and professional work, you’ll often work with multiple datasets across different projects. ProjectFlow ensures that your analysis remains organized and reproducible, whether you’re analyzing land cover changes, environmental impact assessments, or climate modeling.



Example Code
"""
Step 1: Project Setup and Directory Management
Learn how to initialize a Hazelbean ProjectFlow for organized geospatial workflows.
"""

import os
import hazelbean as hb

def main():
    """
    Demonstrates ProjectFlow initialization and basic project organization.
    """
    
    # Create a new project with automatic directory structure
    project_name = 'hazelbean_tutorial'
    # Keyword, not positional: the first positional argument is project_dir, so
    # hb.ProjectFlow(project_name) would create a bare relative directory here.
    p = hb.ProjectFlow(project_name=project_name)
    
    print("=== Hazelbean Project Setup Demo ===")
    print(f"Project name: {project_name}")
    print(f"Project directory: {p.project_dir}")
    
    # ProjectFlow automatically creates these standard directories:
    print("=== Standard Project Directories ===")
    print(f"Input directory: {p.input_dir}")
    print(f"Intermediate directory: {p.intermediate_dir}")
    print(f"Output directory: {p.output_dir}")
    
    # Show data discovery paths
    print("=== Data Discovery Hierarchy ===")
    print("When you use p.get_path(), Hazelbean searches in this order:")
    print(f"1. Base data directory: {p.base_data_dir}")
    print(f"2. Model base data directory: {p.model_base_data_dir}")
    print(f"3. Project base data directory: {p.project_base_data_dir}")
    print(f"4. Current directory: {p.project_dir}")
    
    print("Project setup complete!")
    print("Next: Run step_2_data_loading.py")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

title: GTAPPy
text:
GTAPPy is the Python package that drives the Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) computable general equilibrium model from a run file instead of from a GUI. GTAP itself is written in TABLO and solved by GEMPACK; the usual way to run it is by clicking through RunGTAP one experiment at a time. That does not scale to the kind of work the devstack does, where a single study sweeps many scenarios across several database aggregations and each run has to be reproducible from a script.
GTAPPy sits on top of the GEMPACK executables and supplies the parts around them:

A ProjectFlow task tree. Directory layout, skip-if-already-computed re-runs, automatic base-data download, and parallel iteration all come from ProjectFlow in Hazelbean, the same engine SEALS and GTAP-InVEST use.
CMF generation. GEMPACK is configured by a command file (.cmf) per experiment. GTAPPy writes those files from Python, so sets, subsets, shocks and closure swaps are defined once in code rather than typed into a dialog.
Parallel execution across aggregations and experiments. The same shock can be run against a 10×10 aggregation and a fully disaggregated 141×65 one in the same job.
Output processing. GEMPACK writes .sl4 solution files; GTAPPy converts, filters and aggregates them into the tables a study actually needs, usually tidy CSVs indexed by region, sector and year.



1. The user writes a run file. A run file (e.g. run_gtappy.py, run_process_aez_results.py) follows the devstack run-file convention: a run_project(p) entry point that creates a ProjectFlow object, sets run_mode, points at the base data directory, and builds a task tree. Machine-specific configuration lives in a *_parameters.csv and the scenarios in a *_scenarios.csv (templates ship in gtappy/input_template/), so changing what is run does not mean editing Python.
2. The user runs it, preferably in VS Code’s debugger with the Earth-Economy Devstack workspace open, so a failure inside a task drops you at the frame that raised it.
3. GTAPPy builds the task tree. Functions in gtappy_initialize_project.py (build_standard_task_tree, build_extract_and_run_aez_task_tree, and so on) assemble tasks from gtappy_tasks.py and register the dependencies between them, which is what lets independent branches run in parallel.
4. GTAPPy generates the CMF files. gtappy_cmf_generation.py fills a template command file per experiment — generate_cmf_file_for_scenario — with that experiment’s sets, shocks, closure and input/output paths.
5. GEMPACK solves. run_gtap_cmf in gtappy_runner.py invokes the compiled GTAP executable against the generated CMF. (There is also a run_gtap_cmf_on_vm path, because GEMPACK is Windows-only and is often driven from a Mac or Linux workstation over SSH.)
6. GTAPPy processes the outputs. Solution files are read back, aggregated to the reporting dimensions, and written as CSV — welfare, volumes, trade (TRAD.csv) and so on — into the project’s output directory. GEMPACK’s own log files are kept alongside them, since a failed solve is usually diagnosed there.



GTAPPy is built to run the same experiment against several database aggregations at once. The premise is that for a well-specified model the results should be qualitatively similar whichever aggregation you use — if a 10-region run and a 141-region run disagree about the sign of an effect, that is a finding about the model, not about the aggregation. Running the set of them is a cheap standing check, in the spirit of leave-one-out testing in regression.
This is also why so much of the setup work below is about producing aggregated databases: each aggregation is a separate GTAPAgg2 product that GTAPPy then treats as one more axis to iterate over.

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
text: Status: proposal 2026-09-18; adopted 2026-09-24. The 180, 360 and 600 s batch was admitted together with 9 and 90 s (the 9-10 s family’s chain), in the pyramids paper’s revised ladder of 16 main and 9 side rungs; see pogs.qmd. The ladder below this line is the pre-adoption one (13 spine rungs, 6 side rungs) and is kept as the record of the decision. This document states the rule that decides whether a resolution becomes a side rung or is resampled on entry, records what that decision costs, and applies it to the case that triggered it.

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
text:
The trigger
Converting WorldClim 2.1 at 10 arcminutes (wc2.1_10m_prec_*.tif) with make_paths_pogs_in_parallel fails:
make_path_pog cannot infer an output resolution ... its cell size is 0.16666667 degrees
(600 arcseconds), which is not one of the supported pyramid resolutions
(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 3, 10, 15, 30, 150, 300, 900, 1800, 3600, 18000, 36000, 108000, 324000, 648000).
Suggested output_arcseconds=900: the closest supported resolution at or coarser than the
native cell, so no detail is invented. Use 300 to upsample instead.
WorldClim 2.1 is distributed at four tiers: 30 s, 2.5′, 5′ and 10′. Three of them are rungs (30, 150, 300 s). The fourth, 600 s = 1/6°, is not. The two exits the message offers are both wrong for this file, and the message itself is wrong in two places (see What the error message gets wrong).

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
text:
What the code enforces today
Three mechanisms in hazelbean/pyramids.py decide everything about a rung:

Admissibility. pyramid_side_arcseconds is asserted at import: every side rung must be an integer divisor of at least one spine rung, tested as reduced fractions. Nothing else is checked.
Overview derivation. A rung’s overview levels are every coarser rung, spine or side, that is an integer multiple of it. The table is not written; it is computed.
Publication. Every rung gets a tile-matrix entry (get_pyramid_tile_matrix_set) and a tile-edge entry (pyramid_tile_degrees).

Mechanism 1 makes admission nearly free: any grid of 1/n° divides the 1° rung. Mechanism 2 is what makes admission expensive, and it is the issue this proposal formalizes:

Admitting a rung R adds one overview level to every existing rung that divides R. Every POG at those rungs then fails is_path_pog (overviews are matched by exact dimensions) and must be regenerated.

An admission is therefore a lattice-wide event, never a local one. The manuscript’s criterion, “join height, not divisibility, is the binding constraint”, is prose: no code expresses a join-height bound, a consumption rung, or the churn a candidate would cause.

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
text:
The rule
A candidate resolution R becomes a side rung only if it passes all four tests, in order.

Admissible. R is rational and divides at least one spine rung. Mechanical; already asserted at import. The smallest spine rung R divides is its join rung J.
Owned. A named product family is distributed natively at R on a lat/lon grid. No owner, no rung. This is why 2° and 4° were removed and why 30°, 90°, 180° exist only as structural bridges.
Served. Every rung at which the devstack consumes the family is either R itself or at or above J. Below J, reading the family at a spine rung is a non-block resample whether or not R is a rung, so the rung buys native storage only, and resample-on-entry to the consumption rung is equivalent. A family that fails this test is entered by resampling and recorded in the entry table (A.1 of the manuscript; the “Products with no lat/lon grid” table in pogs.qmd).
Batched. Admissions are made in a batch aligned with a base_data regeneration, never singly, because of the churn in mechanism 2. Each batch records, per admitted rung, the finer rungs whose chains changed.

Test 3 is the manuscript’s “join height” criterion made checkable. Tests 2 and 4 are the parts the manuscript does not state.

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
text:
Applying the rule
600 s, WorldClim 10′. Admissible; owned; served, because the 10′ tier is the one used where half-degree and one-degree grids are the target, and its join is 1800 s. It has one property no other candidate has: 600 is an integer multiple of 300, 150 and 30, so with it admitted the four WorldClim tiers nest as exact block sums (30 → 150 → 300 → 600 by factors 5, 2, 2). Without it the family is split, three tiers native and one resampled. Verdict: admit.
180 s, CHIRPS and MODIS CMG. Admissible; owned; join 900 s, which is the LUH2 and GTAP-AEZ rung, so it is served for Earth-economy work (not for SEALS covariates at 30 s or 300 s, which get a resample either way). The manuscript currently lists it as resample-on-entry because it “joins too high”. That position is not consistent with admitting 600 s, whose join is higher. Verdict: admit in the same batch as 600 s, or reject both.
360 s, ERA5-Land. Admissible; owned by the dominant reanalysis; same join as 600 s. Verdict: same decision as 600 s.
9000 s, 2.5°. Admissible, but no devstack consumer, and it churns thirteen rungs. Verdict: reject; resample on entry.

Recommendation
Admit 180, 360 and 600 s as one batch, timed with the base_data regeneration that the 2026-09-16 overview-rule change already requires, so the regeneration happens once. The cost is concentrated in one place, 300 s POGs gaining a factor-2 overview (about a quarter more overview bytes on files that are 4,320 × 2,160 cells, so megabytes), and the benefit is that the three most-used coarse climate families in the stack become native rungs with exact paths to the spine. The alternative, admit none and enter all three by resampling, is coherent too; what is not coherent is the manuscript’s current state, which admits WorldClim’s finer tiers and rejects its coarsest on a criterion that would also reject nothing else on the list.
Either way, the lattice after this batch is 13 spine + 9 side = 22 matrices, or stays at 19.

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
section: What the error message gets wrong
text:
What the error message gets wrong
Recorded here for the fix, not fixed in this proposal.

Side rungs print as 0, 0, 0, 0. _explain_unsupported_resolution in hazelbean/pog.py formats every supported rung with int(), so the four fractional rungs print as zero. It should use hb.arcseconds_to_token.
The lossy and lossless exits are labelled backwards for this file. The message calls 900 s the choice where “no detail is invented” and 300 s an “upsample”. For a 600 s input, 600 → 900 is a ratio of 1.5: a resample that mixes cells and cannot be undone. 600 → 300 is an integer refinement by 2: nearest-neighbour replication invents nothing, and a block sum back to 600 s recovers the input exactly. The suggestion rule should be: prefer the coarsest rung that divides the native cell (lossless refinement); else the finest rung the native cell divides (exact aggregation); else the nearest coarser rung, and say that this last case is a true resample.
The entry table is prose only. The manuscript’s A.1 says resample-on-entry products are “recorded in an entry table kept beside the rung table”. No such table exists in code; a small registry (product, native cell, enters-at rung, method) would let make_path_pog suggest the recorded rung by filename or metadata instead of by arithmetic.

title: Proposal: a side-rung admission rule
text:
What adopting this would touch

hazelbean/pyramids.py: pyramid_side_arcseconds, pyramid_compatible_resolution_bounds, pyramid_tile_degrees (all three candidates untiled), the shapes and geotransform dicts; the derived overview table and the tile matrix set update themselves. test_tiles.py matrix count.
hazelbean/pog.py: the error message fixes above.
docs/pogs.qmd resolution and overview tables; docs/_conventions_reference.md (its supported-set sentence still lists 7200 and 14400); manuscript A.1, A.6 and Appendix E.
Regeneration of every existing POG at the ten rungs 600 s divides, which the pending regeneration covers.

title: Troubleshooting Guide
text:
This guide covers common issues you might encounter while working with Hazelbean documentation and development environment.




Symptom: quarto preview command fails or hangs
Solutions:

Check if Quarto is installed:
quarto --version
If not installed, follow Quarto installation guide
Port already in use:
# Check if port 4200 is occupied
lsof -i :4200

# Kill the process if needed
kill <PID>

# Or use a different port
quarto preview --port 4201
Permission issues:
# Ensure you're in the correct directory
cd docs-site/quarto-docs

# Check file permissions
ls -la _quarto.yml




Symptom: quarto preview keeps rebuilding endlessly, never stabilizing
Cause: A pre-render hook in _quarto.yml generates .qmd files, which triggers Quarto’s file watcher, which re-runs the pre-render hook, creating an infinite loop.
Solution:

Check for pre-render hooks that generate files:
grep -n "pre-render" docs-site/quarto-docs/_quarto.yml
Run report generation manually instead:
# From project root
python tools/generate_all_reports.py

# Then preview
cd docs-site/quarto-docs
quarto preview
Or use the convenience script:
./tools/preview_docs.sh

Note: The pre-render hook works fine with quarto render (one-time build), but causes issues with quarto preview (live file watching).



Symptom: quarto render produces errors
Common causes and fixes:

Missing dependencies:
conda activate <your_env>
conda install -c conda-forge quarto
Broken links in QMD files:

Check error messages for specific file paths
Verify all referenced files exist
Use relative paths consistently

Malformed markdown:

Check fenced code blocks are properly closed
Verify YAML front matter is valid
Ensure callout blocks have proper syntax: ::: {.callout-note}








Symptom: conda: command not found or environment won’t activate
Solutions:

Initialize conda:
# For bash
conda init bash

# For zsh
conda init zsh

# Restart your shell
Verify environment exists:
conda env list
Recreate environment if corrupted:
conda env remove -n <your_env>
conda env create -f environment.yml




Symptom: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'hazelbean'
Solutions:

Ensure environment is activated:
conda activate <your_env>
python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
Reinstall hazelbean:
cd /path/to/hazelbean_dev
pip install -e . --no-deps
Check Python path:
python -c "import sys; print('\n'.join(sys.path))"







Symptom:
error: Microsoft Visual C++ 14.0 or greater is required
Solutions:

Install conda compiler (recommended):
conda activate <your_env>
conda install -c conda-forge m2w64-toolchain libpython
pip install -e . --no-deps --force-reinstall
Install Visual Studio Build Tools:

Download from https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/downloads/
Select “Build Tools for Visual Studio 2022”
Check “Desktop development with C++”
After install: pip install -e . --no-deps --force-reinstall





Symptom:
ImportError: cannot import name 'cython_functions' from 'hazelbean.calculation_core'
Solution:
python scripts/verify_installation.py
This script will diagnose the issue and provide specific solutions.






Symptom: Coverage reports show 0.0% coverage or no data
Solution:

Run tests with coverage:
cd hazelbean_tests
conda activate <your_env>
pytest --cov=hazelbean --cov-report=json --cov-report=term
Regenerate coverage report:
cd tools
python generate_coverage_report.py
Verify coverage.json was created:
ls -lh hazelbean_tests/.coverage*
ls -lh hazelbean_tests/coverage.json




Common issues:

Missing test data:

Check data/ directories exist
Verify test fixtures are properly set up
Some tests auto-generate synthetic data if real data is missing

Environment issues:

Always activate <your_env> before running tests
Verify all dependencies are installed: conda list

Path issues:

Run tests from hazelbean_tests/ directory
Use relative paths in test configurations








Symptom: Documentation shows old or stale data
Solution:

Regenerate all reports:
cd tools
./generate_reports.sh
Regenerate specific reports:
python generate_test_results_report.py ../hazelbean_tests/test-results.json
python generate_coverage_report.py
python generate_baseline_report.py
python generate_benchmark_summary.py
Re-render Quarto site:
cd docs-site/quarto-docs
quarto render




Symptom: test-results.json not found
Solution:
cd hazelbean_tests
conda activate <your_env>
pytest --json-report --json-report-file=test-results.json --quiet






Symptom: “Address already in use” error
Common ports: - 4200 - Quarto preview - 8000 - MkDocs serve
Solution:
# Check what's using the port
lsof -i :4200
lsof -i :8000

# Kill the process
kill <PID>

# Or use a different port
quarto preview --port 4201
mkdocs serve --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8001






Symptom: Links to documentation pages return 404
Solutions:

Ensure site is rendered:
cd docs-site/quarto-docs
quarto render
ls -la _site/  # Should contain HTML files
Check link paths:

Use relative paths (e.g., ../reports/test-results.html)
Don’t include .qmd extension in links
Quarto converts page.qmd to page.html

Verify navigation configuration:

Check _quarto.yml for proper page structure
Ensure all referenced files exist








Symptom: Search bar doesn’t return results
Solution:

Rebuild search index:
cd docs-site/quarto-docs
quarto render
Check browser console:

Open browser dev tools (F12)
Look for JavaScript errors
Check if search.json was generated in _site/






If you’re still experiencing issues:

Check logs:

Review terminal output for error messages
Check browser console for JavaScript errors
Look for .log files in the project

Verify installation:
python scripts/verify_installation.py
GitHub Issues:

Search existing issues: https://github.com/jandrewjohnson/hazelbean_dev/issues
Create a new issue with:

OS and Python version
Complete error message
Steps to reproduce
Output of conda list


Documentation:

Getting Started Guide
Windows Setup Guide
GitHub Workflows





Run these to quickly diagnose your setup:
# Environment check
conda activate <your_env>
python -c "import hazelbean as hb; print('Hazelbean imported successfully')"

# Quarto check
quarto --version

# Location check
pwd  # Should be in hazelbean_dev directory

# Dependencies check
conda list | grep -E "hazelbean|quarto|mkdocs|pytest"

# File check
ls -la environment.yml
ls -la docs-site/quarto-docs/_quarto.yml
